quotes.text: An inkeeper is one who holds himself out to the public as engaged in the business of keeping a house for the lodging and entertainment of travellers and passengers, their horses and attendants, for reasonable compensation.

There are numerous farmers situated on the public roads of the country, who occasionally, and even frequently, take in and accommodate travellers, and receive compensation for it, who are not innkeepers, and are not liable as such. It is not their business or occupation, nor do they prepare and fit up their establishments for it. They yield to the laws of hospitality, in receiving and entertaining the stranger and the traveller, yet they cannot afford to do so without some compensation.

If the defendant only occasionally entertained travellers for compensation, when it suited his pleasure to do so, and did not hold himself out to the public as the keeper of an inn, or house for the accommodation of the travelling public, then the defendant was only bound to take that ordinary care of property committed to his keeping, that a prudent man usually takes of his own property, of the same kind ; and he would not be liable for a loss, unless it was shown that he had failed to use ordinary diligence in the care of the property committed to him.

quotes.text: See Siegman v. Keeler (4 Misc. Rep. 528; 24 N. Y. Supp. 821), which holds that a boarding house keeper is liable for the loss of goods belonging to a boarder only if he has omitted to exercise ordinary care to prevent it.
I think, therefore, the judgment must be reversed for the reason that no negligence was proved.

It granted relief only as to officers affirmatively telling prospective customers that the place was a disorderly house likely to be raided, holding that tactic exceeded lawful police authority even if the underlying suspicion were justified.

The motion will be denied so far as it seeks to obtain an injunction preventing the posting of officers and inspection of the premises, and granted so far as it relates to the interference with proposed customers by volunteered statements and threats.

new.holding_summary: The Appellate Division held that a private family's taking of boarders in its own dwelling does not violate a restrictive covenant limiting occupancy to no more than two families, nor a covenant against any dangerous, noxious, noisy, or objectionable business, even where some boarders behaved noisily; such conduct is to be addressed by other legal means, not by treating ordinary householder boarding as a covenant violation. The court separately held that operating a general store in one of the dwellings did violate covenants restricting buildings to residential use.

quotes.text: Taking boarders by a private family is not a violation of a restriction in a deed that a dwelling shall not be occupied by more than two families.
Taking boarders by a private family is not a violation of a restriction against any noxious, noisy or objectionable business, though the boarders are allowed to be noisy.
the taking of boarders in private houses in such sections has been carried on for years, without any question of its violating such a restriction having been even raised.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
new.holding_summary: In a conversion action over a piano stored with a boarding and lodging house keeper, the Appellate Term held the statutory lien for 'accommodation, board, lodging, and extras furnished' could not be extended to cover a claim for future rent or damages under an alleged yearly room hiring, and that the tenant's surrender of the keys followed by the keeper's re-renting of the room constituted a surrender and acceptance cutting off rent liability from that date, with the keeper bearing the burden of proving the surrender's exact date.

quotes.text: where the defendant is a boarding and lodging house keeper.
The statute, however, gives a lien only for accommodation, board, lodging, and extras furnished. Its language cannot possibly be extended to cover future rent, or damages under a yearly hiring.
Concededly these acts on the part of the defendant constituted a surrender and acceptance, at least from the date of the re-renting.

The court defined 'board' as receiving food as a lodger for compensation, a 'boarder' as one who has food and lodging in another's family for a stipulated price, and a 'guest' as a transient received at an inn.

new.holding_summary: The court reversed a disorderly-house conviction, holding the trial court erred by failing to charge on accomplice testimony where the State's key witness was herself an accomplice. It further held the evidence insufficient because it showed only that appellant kept a boarding house with boarders, without establishing her legal relation (lessee or tenant) to the premises.

quotes.text: There is evidence that she kept a boarding house and had boarders.
Outside of this there is no testimony that shows she was the lessee or tenant.
With the exception in the most inferential way, the evidence is silent as to her relations to the house.

new.holding_summary: The court held unconstitutional a Texarkana ordinance criminalizing men and women 'associating together for immoral purposes,' whose provisions swept in any male and female found together in the bedroom of any hotel, rooming house, boarding house, lodging house, or inn, or registering there as man and wife. The ordinance was found overbroad, penalizing innocent conduct (doctors, relatives, delivery agents), and the relator was discharged.

quotes.text: its terms are too broad and many of its sections make penal acts and persons which and who by no construction could be held to be crimes or criminals, and against whose inclusion as such, reason and common sense would revolt.
The ordinance in question being unconstitutional, it would follow that the arrest and conviction of relator was without authority of law, and Ms discharge will be ordered.

new.holding_summary: The Texas Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the state zoning enabling statute and the City of Dallas zoning ordinance excluding business, apartment, and other non-residential uses from single-family residential districts, as a valid exercise of the police power. In doing so the court reasoned at length that apartment and tenement houses have historically been treated as a class 'peculiarly subject to' police-power regulation because of associated overcrowding, disease, and crime concerns, and affirmed exclusion of a gasoline filling station from a residential district on that reasoning.

quotes.text: Apartment or Tenement Houses have always been regarded as peculiarly subject to the police power.

What we have determined here is that the zoning statutes are valid and that the ordinance before us in its general scope and dominant features, so far as its provisions are here involved, is a valid exercise of authority.

new.holding_summary: An oil-lease pumper was injured in a gas explosion inside a small lease house on his employer's property, which he occupied under an arrangement deducting $10 per month from his wages as rent. quotes.text: there is no inconsistency between the relation of landlord and tenant and that of master and servant.

quotes.text: The defendant was an innkeeper. He kept a house of reception and entertainment for all comers, but more especially for the accommodation of that class of persons known as emigrants. This constitutes an inn.

In a boarding house, the guest is under an express contract, at a certain rate, for a certain period of time; but in an inn there is no express engagement; the guest being on his way, is entertained from day to day, according to his business, upon an implied contract

quotes.text: The defendant occupied rooms in the plaintiff's building, under a hiring by the month, the rent being payable in advance.

the occupant of any building which shall without any fault or neglect on his part be destroyed, or be so injured by the elements or any other cause, as to be untenantable and unfit for occupancy, shall not be liable or bound to pay rent after such destruction or injury

As an occupant of apartments in. a tenement house, the defendant was not bound to either see to the erection of a proper sink or privy upon the premises, or to cause it to be emptied, to prevent an overflow.

new.holding_summary: In an action for rent where the defendant, a married woman, raised coverture for the first time after judgment, the court denied her motion to set aside the judgment and execution because the evidence showed her husband had long been absent from the state and tended to show she kept a boarding house on her own account, occupying the plaintiff's premises for that purpose.

quotes.text: The defence was, surrender of the lease and payment.
The opposing affidavits tended to show that defendant was keeping a boarding-house on her own account, and had occupied the plaintiff's said premises for that purpose.
the evidence showing that her husband had been absent from the state a long time, and tending to show that she kept a boarding-house on her own account, that the motion be denied, with costs.

new.holding_summary: The 1885 act limiting the height of dwelling-houses and of houses used as dwellings for more than one family was a valid exercise of the police power, but the court held it did not apply to hotels, which are occupied by temporary adult guests under one management, so a mandamus was granted compelling approval of plans for a hotel addition exceeding the height limit.

quotes.text: hotels not usually built in the midst of dwelling-houses, which are mainly occupied by temporary adult guests, which are under the supervision of one management and which can never become very numerous.
We have no doubt of the competency of the legislature in the exercise of the police power under the Constitution to pass such an act
a dwelling-house is not a hotel .and a hotel is not a.dwelling-house.

quotes.text: The defendant kept an emigrant boarding house or inn.
He received every person that came, accommodating them by the day or by the week, at a charge of one dollar per day.
If the guest is notified to put his baggage in a particular place where it will be safely kept, and he neglects to do so, the innkeeper, if it is lost, is not liable.

new.holding_summary: In an action for the last quarter's rent under a one-year lease of a furnished dwelling-house, the court held there was no implied covenant that the house was fit for habitation where noxious odors from a neighboring livery stable, unknown to either party when the lease was made and not originating on the demised premises, made the house unhealthy; the tenant, who had examined the premises and continued to occupy them, remained liable for the rent.

quotes.text: In an action to recover the last quarter of rent reserved by a lease for one year of a furnished dwelling-house, the answer set up as a counter-claim damages alleged to have been sustained on account of the breach of an implied covenant that said house was fit for immediate and permanent occupation.
It is uniformly held in this state that the lessee of real property must run the risk of its condition, unless he has an express agreement on the part of the lessor covering that subject.

We do not think that there was any covenant in the lease in question, implied either by common law or from the acts or relations of the parties, that extended to the grievance of which the defendant complains.

new.holding_summary: The court affirmed disallowance of a claim for board and lodging furnished to a decedent because the claimant failed to prove how much time the decedent actually lived with him and because the evidence showed the decedent had in fact paid for his board. The court held that no presumption of gratuitous boarding arose merely from the family relationship between the parties, and that recovery, if any, would rest on an implied contract to pay for boarding and lodging furnished.

quotes.text: A claim against a decedent’s estate for board and lodging, furnished to the decedent for a period of three years before his death, will be refused, where the evidence failed to establish how much of the time during the period in question the decedent lived with the claimant, and where there was ample evidence to show that the deceased had paid for his boarding.
The court properly held that the relationship between the decedent and the wife of the claimant did not give rise to a presumption that the boarding was to be furnished gratuitously.
if the claimant was entitled to recovery it was upon an implied contract to pay for the boarding and lodging which he furnished.

new.notes: Household boarding-for-pay dispute; claim ultimately denied on evidentiary grounds (duration unproven, decedent shown to have paid already), but the legal principle recognized boarding-for-pay as an enforceable implied contract not presumed gratuitous.

In this State, boroughs may enact such regulatory ordinances under the police power

new.holding_summary: The court held that a surviving spouse's homestead right encompasses exclusive title to the rents and income from the homestead property -- here a 40-room rooming house that had served as the family's business homestead -- regardless of whether the property is rented out in whole or part or operated as the survivor's own business, and such income is not subject to partition among the heirs. The survivor was nonetheless treated as a life tenant, liable for ordinary current taxes but without a right to reimbursement for ordinary repairs from the remaindermen.

quotes.text: all revenues, rents, and income derived from the homestead, as such, are the separate and individual property of the survivor and that without any reference whatever to whether the same is rented out either in whole or in part by the survivor, or used by him in a business of his own

all revenues, rents, and income derived from the homestead, as such, are the separate and individual property of the survivor and that without any reference whatever to whether the same is rented out either in whole or in part by the survivor, or used by him in a business of his own

quotes.text: Under these circumstances, apartment houses, which in a different environment would be not only entirely unobjectionable but highly desirable, come very near to being nuisances.
the enactment of the amendatory ordinance was not within the scope of the police power of the City, and that the same is unconstitutional and void.

new.holding_summary: The court construed Article 4592, under which a hotel, apartment hotel, or boarding-house keeper may limit liability for a guest's lost valuables to $50 by maintaining a safe and posting the statutory notice on the guest's sleeping-room door. It held that posting the notice inside the bathroom door within the suite, rather than on the sleeping-room door itself, did not satisfy the statute. Because the hotel had not complied, its liability for the guests' stolen jewelry was to be determined under ordinary negligence principles rather than the statutory cap.

quotes.text: Any hotel, apartment hotel or boarding house keeper, who constantly has in his hotel, apartment hotel or boarding house a metal safe or vault in good order and fit for the custody of money, jewelry, articles of gold or silver manufacture, precious stones, personal ornaments, or documents of any kind, and who keeps on the doors of the sleeping rooms used by guests suitable locks or bolts and proper fastening on the transom and window of said room, shall not be liable for the loss or injury suffered by any guest on account of the loss of said valuables in excess of the sum of fifty dollars

It is evident that the Legislature enacted this law for the benefit of the hotel keepers in this state, and to relieve them from burdens imposed by • the common law in case of loss of property by guests.

We think that the Article requires that such printed copy be posted on the door of .the sleeping room' used by the guest, on which the hotel is required to keep a suitable lock or bolt. Posting the copy of Article 4592 on the bath room door, as was done in this case, was not a compliance with such Article.

new.notes: polarity marked favorable because the statute is legislature-granted protection treating hotel/boarding-house keeping as a recognized, protected trade; it is a liability-limitation statute rather than a right-to-let holding, so the favorable/adverse fit is imperfect. duration_of_occupancy set to 'months' because the injured guests had resided at the hotel continuously since September 1942 through trial.

new.holding_summary: A city sought to enjoin a developer from operating an 8.17-acre, 128-space mobile home/recreational vehicle rental park in the city's extraterritorial jurisdiction until it complied with subdivision platting standards. The court held that dividing land into rental spaces is a 'subdivision' subject to city platting regulation even without any sale or transfer of ownership, and upheld the city's use of its police power to require compliance before the park could operate.

quotes.text: Appellant is a home rule municipal corporation which sought to permanently enjoin appellee from constructing a mobile home and/or recreational vehicle park within appellant’s extraterritorial jurisdiction until appellee complied with city code standards for subdivision developments.

The concomitant need for city services, in addition to the predictable problems generated by such intensive population of the land, justify appellant’s use of its police power in protecting the general welfare.

Having given careful consideration to the argument and all of the authorities called to our attention, we find that the City of Weslaco discharged its burden of showing that it was entitled to the issuance of the permanent injunction and that the trial court erred in denying such relief.

new.notes: Borderline relevance: this is a mobile-home/RV rental-space development, not a traditional boarding house, but it is doctrinally analogous adverse authority — a municipality using platting/subdivision regulation under the police power to control a commercial operator's business of renting occupancy spaces to the public. Use-and-occupation action between an assignee-owner and tenants over an assigned commercial lease and a rent set-off claim; not about lodging or short-term letting.

Plaintiff's prior boarding-house keeping is mentioned only as the source of separate earnings in a dispute over whether property (a piano) is exempt from her husband's creditors under coverture law; the letting/boarding relationship itself is not adjudicated. New trial ordered on an unrelated procedural ground.
Dispute over the city's liability for use of a private pier in offal removal under a municipal contracting statute; no connection to lodging or boarding houses.

Nuisance/street-obstruction suit by the proprietor of an eating-and-lodging house against the city over market sheds blocking access to his premises; his lodging-house business is incidental identification, not the subject of adjudication.
Dispute over an assignee-for-creditors' personal liability for quarterly rent on a commercial lofts lease; no lodging/boarding issue.
Will/codicil construction case concerning executors' power of sale over a decedent's real estate; unrelated to short-term letting or lodging.
Summary dispossession proceeding for nonpayment of rent and the scope of equitable relief from a warrant of ejectment; concerns a commercial tenancy repair covenant, not lodging or boarding.

Attachment case turning on whether the defendant's hotel-room stays in New York City (as opposed to his family's home in Connecticut) made him a 'resident' for jurisdictional purposes; hotel boarding is incidental to the domicile analysis, not to the legal character of letting/lodging.
False-imprisonment action arising from a conviction for driving an unlicensed express wagon for hire under a municipal cartmen ordinance; unrelated to lodging or boarding houses.

Negotiable-instruments case on the diligence required to locate a note's maker before presentment; the maker's occupation as a boarding-house keeper is mentioned only to establish her whereabouts, not the legal character of boarding.

Married woman's separate-estate liability for furniture she purchased intending to use in keeping a boarding-house; the boarding-house use is incidental context for a coverture/separate-property holding, not an adjudication of the boarding relationship itself.
Dispute over which municipal officer had authority to permit or order removal of building materials obstructing a street; unrelated to lodging or boarding houses.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a house is treated as an inn, rather than a mere boarding-house, when it receives all who choose to visit without any prior agreement as to duration of stay or terms of entertainment. An innkeeper's strict liability for a guest's property lasts only while the guest relation continues, and ceases once the guest pays his bill and leaves with a declared intent not to return, after which any baggage left behind is at the guest's own risk. Because the trial court did not let the jury decide whether the guest relation had already ended when the trunk was lost, a new trial was ordered.

quotes.text: To charge a defendant, as an innkeeper, it is sufficient to prove, that he received, as guests, all who chose to visit his house, without any previous agreement, as to the duration of their stay, or the terms of their entertainment.

There may be a distinction between the liability of the keeper of an inn and of a mere boarding-house, where transient persons are not received at all, and none are received but for a certain time and upon certain terms. But it is not pretended that the defendant’s house was a mere boarding-house. It was a public house of entertainment for all who chose to visit it, which is the true definition of an inn.

That relation ceases, when the guest pays his bill and leaves the house, with the declared intention of not returning. In such a case it is at his own peril, we apprehend, that he leaves his baggage or other property behind him.

new.notes: Foundational innkeeper/boarding-house distinction case: relevant to the characterization taxonomy for short-term commercial lodging, though the dispute itself concerns baggage-bailment liability rather than the right to let or its regulation.
Trespass action over a rope/sign fixture attached to a roof, turning on a tenant's authority to license the act and resulting costs rule; unrelated to lodging or boarding houses.

Injunction against a soap factory as a nuisance to a nearby hotel (Irving House); the hotel is merely the injured neighboring business, and the case does not address the legal character of letting or lodging.

new.holding_summary: The Court of Appeals upheld Long Beach's residential zoning ordinance restricting property to a single one-family housekeeping unit, holding it validly excluded operating the property as a boarding or rooming house business. The court's dictum, however, recognized that a homeowner may still occasionally take in roomers or boarders as an incident to using the house as a family home.

quotes.text: It is not unreasonable to prohibit its use as a boarding or rooming house as a business.

The fact that the property may not be used for the business of keeping roomers and boarders does not bar the occupant from occasionally taking roomers or boarders, upon special considerations, where the practice is merely incidental and accessory to the principal use of the house as a home by the family of the occupant.
Using the dwelling as a rooming or boarding house within the above definitions is not a proper accessory use within the residential district and is prohibited by the ordinance.
The judgment appealed from should be affirmed, with costs.

new.notes: Leading case; adverse as to business-scale boarding but favorable dictum for incidental household letting.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a large lakeside establishment catering to vacationers who stayed for fixed periods at fixed rates was a "boarding house," not a "hotel," and therefore a use permitted under the town's residential zoning ordinance. The neighbor's suit to enjoin it as an unlawful hotel was dismissed.

quotes.text: it is not a hotel. It is a boarding house notwithstanding its size (forty-five rooms) and the number of its possible guests (100), which features do not characterize the ordinary smaller type of boarding house.

the evidence as a whole demonstrates that this place is not for the accommodation of merely transient guests, but is used wholly as a place for boarders who come to spend either part or all of their vacations for fixed periods and at fixed rates.
Complaint dismissed, in all circumstances, without costs in favor of any defendant.

new.notes: Concerns innkeeper's tort liability for a guest's lost property; the guest-vs-roomer distinction is collateral to bailment/insurer liability, not to the right to let or to boarding-house regulation.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a church building housing the pastor's family together with three paying female roomers (who ate separately, cooked for by a matron) was not a "multiple dwelling" under the Multiple Dwelling Law, because the roomers did not constitute a separate "family" living independently. Consequently the statutory lighting-duty claim against the landlord failed.

quotes.text: The building was occupied by one family, the pastor's. The matron was merely a domestic and the three women were roomers or lodgers.
There were not three or more families living independently of each other.
The motion to set aside the verdict is granted.

new.notes: Favorable in the sense that a small paying-lodger arrangement did not trigger heavier multiple-dwelling regulatory duties.

new.holding_summary: The County Court affirmed a conviction under the Long Beach zoning ordinance for operating premises in a residential district as a boarding/rooming house business, rejecting the defendant's claim of a protected legal nonconforming use. The trial court's finding that the current use was a business use, not a continuation of the prior use, was sustained on the evidence.

quotes.text: the trial court was justified in its conclusion that the present use of the premises was for a boarding or rooming house as a business, and that such use was not the use to which the premises were being put when the ordinance was enacted

the trial court was justified in its conclusion that the present use of the premises was for a boarding or rooming house as a business, and that such use was not the use to which the premises were being put when the ordinance was enacted
The judgment of conviction is, therefore, affirmed.

new.notes: Applies and extends Baddour.

new.holding_summary: The court held that renting out apartments in the plaintiff's subdivided dwelling did not violate a restrictive covenant against business use, since an apartment landlord performs no personal services and is not comparable to a boarding house keeper. However, because plaintiff separately violated the covenant by running a real estate office on the premises, she came to equity with unclean hands and her complaint was dismissed.

quotes.text: A person who owns and rents out apartments on the other hand, performs no personal services and can scarcely be placed in the category of a boarding house keeper.
A person who owns and rents out apartments on the other hand, performs no personal services and can scarcely be placed in the category of a boarding house keeper.
Complaint dismissed.

new.notes: Plaintiff lost on unclean-hands grounds unrelated to the apartment-letting question itself.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a proposed motel did not fall within a zoning ordinance's permitted "inn" use for a business district, because a motel is commonly understood as materially different from a full-service inn or hotel. The zoning board's denial of a building permit for the motel was accordingly sustained.

quotes.text: But a motel is commonly understood to be an establishment essentially different from an inn or hotel in design, purpose and use.
the court believes that the determination of the zoning board of appeals is to be sustained
The proceeding is dismissed, without costs.

new.holding_summary: The court convicted a homeowner of violating a single-family zoning ordinance for renting a complete, separate apartment within his house to a tenant family under a long-term lease at substantial rent. This was distinguished from the occasional, incidental boarding permitted as an accessory use under Baddour and held to constitute an illegal second housekeeping unit.

quotes.text: here, on the contrary, he rented a complete apartment to a single tenant for an extended period of time and at a substantial rental.
It is therefore found and determined that defendant is guilty of count 1 of the information here under review.
It is therefore found and determined that defendant is guilty of count 1 of the information here under review.

new.notes: Directly distinguishes the favorable Baddour dictum from an unprotected disguised two-family conversion.

new.holding_summary: In a declaratory judgment action, the court held that a 52-room single-room-occupancy establishment was legally a "hotel" rather than a "rooming house" under the New York City Administrative Code, because it was commonly regarded as a hotel and provided customary hotel services. The owner was therefore not required to obtain a rooming-house operating permit.

quotes.text: the subject premises meets the definition of a hotel within the meaning of the definition of subdivision i of section D26-3.22 of the Administrative Code.

the court finds and declares that the subject premises fall within the Administrative Code definition of hotel under section D26-3.22; and a permit for a rooming house should not be required of plaintiffs.

the court finds and declares that the subject premises fall within the Administrative Code definition of hotel under section D26-3.22; and a permit for a rooming house should not be required of plaintiffs.

new.holding_summary: The Court of Appeals reversed convictions under a village lodging-house ordinance for housing hospital employees, paid and unpaid, in two adjoining dwellings. It held that such employee housing was an accessory use customarily incidental and subordinate to the hospital's principal use, not an illegal unlicensed lodging house.

quotes.text: constitutes within the meaning of the village ordinance an accessory use customarily incidental to and subordinate to the principal use of the main building.
The judgments should be reversed, and the cash fine remitted in each instance, and the information dismissed.
The judgments should be reversed, and the cash fine remitted in each instance, and the information dismissed.

new.notes: Regulatory conviction for maintaining an unlicensed lodging house was reversed, favoring the letting arrangement.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
new.holding_summary: The Appellate Division upheld the State Rent Administrator's certificate of eviction permitting a landlord to recover the portion of a ten-room house that the tenant used to operate a rooming house, while protecting the tenant's own separate two-room basement dwelling. The rooming-house business space was held separable from the tenant's actual living quarters.

quotes.text: the part of the housing accommodations occupied by the tenants was entirely separable and separate from the accommodations employed as a rooming house

the part of the housing accommodations occupied by the tenants was entirely separable and separate from the accommodations employed as a rooming house

new.holding_summary: The court held that a lease requiring the premises to be used and occupied "only for furnished rooms" became void once operating the building as a rooming house was found to violate the newly effective Multiple Dwelling Law's licensing requirements. The landlord could not recover rent under the illegal lease, though the tenant also could not recover the security deposit.

quotes.text: The use of the premises specified in the lease being illegal the lease was void.
The high purposes of the Multiple Dwelling Law — the protection of human life and limb — is far more important than the preservation of alleged contract rights.

new.notes: Dispute over waste-paper haulers' access to a commercial loft building's freight elevators; no bearing on residential letting or boarding/lodging-house regulation.

Concerns hotel guests' claim to rent-control tenant status when the landlord seeks to close the hotel for redevelopment; the guest-vs-tenant characterization is collateral to the landlord's right to withdraw property from the rental market, not to the right to let or to boarding-house regulation.
Commercial office-space sublease and rent-law assignment dispute between a law firm and its landlord's assignees; no bearing on residential lodging, boarding, or short-term letting.

new.holding_summary: The court held that the plaintiff's property retained a valid legal nonconforming use as a rooming and boarding house despite a wartime interruption and intervening ownership by a church, because the right had never been abandoned. Plaintiff was entitled to operate the rooming/boarding house subject to compliance with any valid licensing ordinance.

quotes.text: the house in question was used as a rooming and boarding house prior to the enactment of the zoning ordinance and continuously thereafter until it was interrupted by the onerous wartime restrictions placed upon all seaside resorts.
The court finds that at the time of the interruption of the boarding and rooming house business occasioned by wartime restrictions, the premises were vested with a valid nonconforming use.
The plaintiff is entitled to judgment for the relief demanded in the complaint; he must, of course, comply with any valid licensing ordinance of the city.

new.holding_summary: The court denied a residence-club landlord's attempt to evict professional tenants under the Business Rent Law's "immediate and personal use" exception, holding that the landlord's proposed expansion of its room-and-board club was really the renting of rooms to others, equivalent to operating a rooming/boarding house under the Multiple Dwelling Law. quotes.text: The proposed use in the opinion of the court is for the renting of rooms to others.
He is not, in other words, permitted to oust the tenant for the purpose of reletting the space to others.
The landlord’s petitions must, therefore, be dismissed and final order entered in favor of the tenants.

new.notes: Court equates a paid 'residence club' arrangement with rooming/boarding-house operation for Multiple Dwelling Law purposes.

new.holding_summary: The court upheld as valid a town zoning ordinance restricting operation of boarding houses for institutional mental-health patients and parolees in residential districts, holding it did not conflict with the Mental Hygiene Law's family-care placement provisions. quotes.text: The conducting of such a boardinghouse is in the nature of a business properly excluded from a residential district.

quotes.text:
LODGING HOUSE:

A building containing not more than fifteen (15) rooms with sleeping facilities where lodging only is provided for compensation and by previous arrangement to three (3) or more persons but not exceeding twenty (20) persons.

new.holding_summary: The court affirmed that several apartment buildings retained legal nonconforming-use status because owners timely obtained post-Katrina restoration permits, and held that a nineteen-room boarding house exceeding fifteen rooms fell outside the City's rooming-house ordinance (which only reaches houses under fifteen rooms) and was instead governed by the state sanitary code.

quotes.text: A lodging house, which is analogous to a rooming house, is defined as “a building where persons are supplied with, and charged for, sleeping accommodations but not meals.”

new.notes: Community home for mentally handicapped adults zoning dispute; the 'lodging house'/'family' definitions are discussed only to decide whether the residents constitute a family, with no compensated letting arrangement at issue.

new.holding_summary: The court affirmed the Board of Zoning Adjustments' denial of an off-street-parking variance for a youth hostel converted from a licensed rooming house, rejecting the operator's argument that reliance on an erroneously issued occupational license entitled him to the variance.

the hostel, with its transient occupancy, would significantly alter the neighborhood’s residential character, and that the increased vehicular congestion caused by the hostel would be detrimental and injurious to the surrounding properties.

new.notes: The hotel's practice of renting rooms to transient guests is undisputed background fact; the actual holding concerns whether an accessory bar/restaurant/party-room expansion at 'The Columns Hotel' exceeded the scope of its nonconforming hotel use, not the legality of the room letting itself.

new.notes: Personal-injury/invitee-status case arising from a health-studio weightlifting accident; no lodging or letting arrangement is involved.

new.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, First Circuit
new.notes: Premises-liability (custody/garde) case about a collapsed vanity stool at a condo resort operated much like a hotel; the plaintiffs' status as paying guests is incidental — the holding addresses only the owner/custodian's knowledge of the furniture defect, not the character or legality of the short-term rental arrangement.

new.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Fourth Circuit
new.holding_summary: The court affirmed a permanent injunction barring condominium-owner LLCs from operating short-term/transient rentals in violation of a condominium bylaw — validly adopted by a supermajority vote as a use restriction rather than a building restriction — that prohibited overnight, bed-and-breakfast, guest-house, hotel, or transient paid use of units.

new.notes: Vicinage-nuisance suit over noise/dust from a commercial automobile racetrack; no lodging or letting issue.

new.notes: Vicinage-nuisance suit over dust/noise from a concrete-recycling construction operation adjacent to plaintiffs' mobile homes; no lodging or letting issue.

new.court: Civil Court of the City of New York, New York County
new.holding_summary: A hotel occupant who had resided and paid rent intermittently for about three months but who had registered for a short stay was locked out by the hotel as a 'transient.' The court held she was not a transient because she had no other home, and as an occupant in possession over 30 days she qualified as a 'tenant' under RPAPL 711, so the hotel could not remove her without legal process and had to restore her to possession.

quotes.text: There is nothing to indicate that she has any other residence, and although hotels normally require a transient guest to provide a home address, the hotel has no other address for her.
Consequently, the hotel acted improperly in locking Ms. Mann out of her rooms.

“Transient” has been considered the opposite of “resident” (see The Leontios Teryazos, 45 F Supp 618), and with respect to a hotel, is one who has a home elsewhere and is staying at the hotel for a short period in connection with a trip away from home.

new.court: Civil Court of the City of New York, Queens County
new.holding_summary: The City sought to close six rooming houses for violating a code provision barring rooming units not registered before 1954, effectively requiring eviction of roughly 95 low-income roomers. Although the code's constitutionality had already been upheld, the court stayed the consent decree requiring eviction and adopted an interpretation of the 'family' definition allowing the buildings to be reorganized so small groups of tenants and boarders could remain, reasoning enforcement compelling eviction into homelessness would produce an unintended injustice.

quotes.text: DHPD alleged that the defendants were operating these buildings in violation of New York City Housing Maintenance Code § D26-33.07

this court will stay the enforcement of the consent decree entered into by the parties and will allow the tenants to remain in their residences, within the limits defined by this court under the statutory language of Code article 33.

Under the Code, a “family” is defined as (i) a single person, or (ii) two or more persons related by blood or marriage occupying a common household, with not more than two boarders, and (iii) not more than three unrelated persons occupying a dwelling unit and maintaining a common household.

new.court: Justice Court of Village of Elmsford, Westchester County
new.holding_summary: A motel owner sought summary eviction of a homeless woman placed there by the county Department of Social Services and residing there over two years, arguing she was a mere transient licensee. The court held she was not a transient because she had no other home, making her a month-to-month tenant under RPAPL 711 entitled to a 30-day notice to vacate, which the motel had not given, so the eviction proceeding was dismissed.

quotes.text: respondent here is a homeless person not a transient, is for the reasons noted a month-to-month tenant, and may not be evicted without being given a 30-day notice to vacate — which was not afforded her in this case.
In the opinion of this court respondent’s argument as presented by Westchester Legal Services is more persuasive.
For the reasons heretofore noted this proceeding is dismissed.

new.court: Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
new.holding_summary: A landlord sought to evict a tenant occupying a partitioned 'cubicle' in a Manhattan lodging house on the theory the tenancy was an unregulated nightly arrangement. The Appellate Term affirmed dismissal of the holdover proceeding, holding that lodging-house housing accommodations, including cubicles used as a tenant's residence, are covered by rent stabilization because lodging houses are class B multiple dwellings not excluded from that coverage.

quotes.text: Petitioner concedes that a lodging house constitutes a class B multiple dwelling (see, Multiple Dwelling Law § 4 [9], [14]), and can point to no specific ETPA exemption removing lodging houses from the ambit of rent stabilization.
The cubicle space here in issue was intended to and has in fact served as this tenant’s “residence, home [and] dwelling unit” for a period of years
Order entered September 16, 1991 affirmed with $10 costs.

new.notes: duration_of_occupancy mapped to 'months' as the closest available bucket; the opinion states occupancy 'for a period of years,' which exceeds all enumerated options.

new.holding_summary: The City sought reimbursement from a building owner for relocating 55 people found illegally residing in cubicles built into a commercial basement lacking secondary egress, heat, or sanitary facilities, after a fire department vacate order. The court held the relocated occupants were not 'tenants' entitled to trigger owner reimbursement liability under the Administrative Code because the record did not establish that they had occupied the illegal basement lodging for a sufficient, verified period to be more than transient occupants, though the owner was found negligent for the illegal buildout.

quotes.text: No secondary means of egress from cellar, Inadequate fire protection, Overcrowding, Illegal single room occupancies.
the court finds that the persons relocated were not “tenants,” defendant is not liable for the relocation expenses for these 55 individuals.

new.notes: Characterization left null: the court addressed only whether the relocated individuals were 'tenants' vs. mere 'occupants' for municipal reimbursement purposes and did not classify the underlying arrangement as lease/license/lodging/innkeeping.

new.court: Civil Court of the City of New York, New York County
new.holding_summary: A resident of a hotel under an 11-month written lease sued for property stolen from his room, invoking the innkeeper's strict-liability rule applicable to transient guests. The court held that, given the duration of occupancy, the written lease, and the hotel's monthly rental services, plaintiff was a tenant rather than a transient guest, so the innkeeper's insurer-liability rule did not apply and, absent proven negligence, the complaint was dismissed.

quotes.text: At common law, the liability of an insurer was imposed on an innkeeper to protect travelers who, while on their journey had stopped in transit for food and lodging.
I conclude that the plaintiff is not a guest, to be treated like a transient or traveler at an inn, but rather is a tenant on a regular and permanent basis.
since there was no negligence on the part of the defendant and since plaintiff was not a “ guest ” in defendant’s hotel, judgment will be entered for the defendant dismissing the complaint herein.

new.court: Supreme Court, Special Term, Nassau County
new.holding_summary: The Town sued to enjoin the owner of a legally two-family residence from housing far more than two families, having converted the premises into a rooming-house-like arrangement with locked individual rooms occupied by numerous unrelated persons receiving mail there. The court found the ordinance's two-family occupancy limit a valid exercise of the police power and permanently enjoined the owner from permitting occupancy by more than two families, ordering him to remedy the violation.

quotes.text: The maintenance of a rooming house on premises legally zoned for a two-family dwelling is a continuing violation calling for immediate appropriate legal action.
The maintenance of a rooming house on premises legally zoned for a two-family dwelling is a continuing violation calling for immediate appropriate legal action.

the defendant is maintaining premises at 63 Allen Drive, Great Neck, New York, in violation of the Building Zone Ordinance as well as section 3(d) of article II of the Housing and Rehabilitation Code of the Town of North Hempstead in that he is permitting the use of said premises by more than two families as defined in the Building Zone Ordinance.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a restrictive covenant limiting land to "residential, camping or picnicing purposes," which also deemed "[m]otel, tourist courts, and trailer parks" a business use, prohibited appellants from renting their house to vacationers for short stays as transient housing. The temporary injunction was modified to enjoin only rental of the property "for temporary or transient housing purposes."

quotes.text: We further believe that the nature of the rental activity in which appellants have been engaged results in the property being used for the type of transient housing that the third sentence of paragraph six intended to designate as a business use.
Appellees have established a probable Adoption of the restrictive covenant at issue by appellants; therefore, they are entitled to a temporary injunction.
Therefore, the temporary injunction is modified to enjoin appellants from “renting and/or leasing said property to the public for temporary or transient housing purposes.”

new.notes: Restrictive-covenant case (private, not government police power) enforcing a residential-use limitation against short-term vacation rentals; 'characterization' marked other because the court classified the use as transient/business under the covenant rather than in lease/license/lodging/innkeeping terms.

new.holding_summary: The court affirmed the trial court's finding that a nonprofit corporation's residential facility for former psychiatric patients, who paid no fees themselves and received counseling but no medical treatment, constituted a "lodging or boarding house" rather than an establishment for treatment of alcoholic, narcotic, or psychiatric patients, and was therefore a lawful nonconforming use under the zoning ordinance.

quotes.text: Lodging shall mean where one or more dwelling units are occupied or intended to be occupied by five or more persons who are not husband and wife, son or daughter, mother or father, sister or brother of the owner or operator. Boarding shall mean where meals are provided by the operation of a lodging house.
It was conceded by the City that the operation of a lodging and boarding house was permitted at 2707 Routh Street as a nonconforming use.

the trial judge found as a fact that the present use of the property was not for the treatment of alcoholic, narcotic or psychiatric patients, but was for a lodging or boarding house. We find the evidence sufficient to support that conclusion.

new.notes: Zoning-enforcement dispute over a halfway house for former psychiatric patients; relevant mainly for its definitional treatment of 'lodging or boarding' but residents did not pay for occupancy themselves and stayed indefinitely, so duration is marked unclear.

new.court: Court of Appeals of Texas, Corpus Christi-Edinburg
new.holding_summary: The court held that neither the Dwelling Restriction (a structural limitation on the type of building) nor the Occupancy Restriction (which merely defined permissible household composition) prohibited Raub's short-term rental of his home to vacationer groups, and upheld the jury's finding that the operation was not a prohibited "commercial enterprise" because no indicia of business existed on the property itself.

quotes.text: The agreements described two groups of parties: the guests and the “landlords,” which were Raub, Rosa, and Raub Properties, LLC.

The ownership of land, when the estate is a fee, carries with it the right to use the land in any manner not hurtful to others; and the right to lease it to others, and therefore derive profit, is an incident of such ownership.
The Occupancy Restriction does not prohibit short-term rentals, so long as the renters meet the Declaration's definition of "family."

new.notes: Raub formed an LLC to manage the single rental property but did not operate multiple properties or live off-site as a business; classified as householder rather than commercial_operator.

new.holding_summary: The Texas Supreme Court held that unambiguous deed restrictions limiting tracts to "residential purposes" and prohibiting "business" use do not restrict a homeowner's right to lease his home for short-term vacation rentals, because occupants who use the home for ordinary residential activities satisfy "residential purposes" regardless of the duration of their stay. It reversed summary judgment for the homeowners' association.

quotes.text: we hold that so long as the occupants to whom Tarr rents his single-family residence use the home for a "residential purpose," no matter how short-lived, neither their on-property use nor Tarr's off-property use violates the restrictive covenants in the Timberwood deeds.

For this reason, we disapprove of the cases that impose an intent or physical-presence requirement when the covenant's language includes no such specification and remains otherwise silent as to durational requirements.
So long as the renters continue to relax, eat, sleep, bathe, and engage in other incidental activities, they are using the cabin for residential purposes.

new.notes: Landmark favorable authority; characterization marked 'other' because the Court classified the use as residential (not business/transient) rather than in lease/license/lodging/innkeeping terms.

Municipal bond-validation dispute over pledging hotel-occupancy-tax revenue to finance a convention-center/hotel project; the tax code's definition of 'hotel' is quoted only for that fiscal purpose, not compensated short-term occupancy of a dwelling or its regulation.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a restriction limiting a lot to "residential purposes" was satisfied by a group home for four mentally retarded men and supervising houseparents functioning as a single housekeeping unit, distinguishing this from a prohibited "boarding, lodging house, or hotel," and that a separate structural single-family-dwelling provision was not violated because the home was designed for and occupied by one household.

quotes.text: the Collinses, as lessors, leased their property to the Advisory Board of the El Campo Area Adult Center for the Developmentally Disabled, Inc., for the purpose of establishing a group home for not more than four mentally retarded adults, plus one supervising couple.

Family: One or more persons occupying a dwelling and living as a single housekeeping unit and doing their own cooking on the premises, as distinguished from a group occupying a boarding, lodging house, or hotel, as herein defined.

Since the evidence shows that the home is “used for residential purposes only” by the four men and their supervising parents, there is no violation of the pertinent provisions of the restrictive covenant.

new.notes: Not a short-term paid stay; occupancy was long-term/permanent, so duration is marked unclear (no enum value for indefinite/permanent occupancy). Relevant for its treatment of leasing residential property and the boarding/lodging-house distinction.

Zoning dispute over a religious college's dormitories, cafeteria, and day-care use; the ordinance's separate prohibition on 'boarding house, rooming house' is listed only as one of several banned uses tied to the college, not independently litigated or about compensated short-term occupancy.

new.holding_summary: The court held that four unrelated handicapped women living with a paid, unrelated houseparent did not constitute a "family" under the Southampton Civic Club definition (a household including parents, children, servants, and incidentally lodgers or boarders), so the arrangement violated a restrictive covenant limiting the property to single-family residential use.

quotes.text: The defendant leases all of his property to the Lubbock Area Extended Rehabilitation Services, a non-profit corporation.
the generally accepted definition of the word “family” is “a household, including parents, children and servants, and, as the case may be, lodgers or boarders.”
In this instance, the occupants of the property in question do not constitute a family under the Southampton definition.

new.notes: Marked mixed: the opinion approvingly restates the Southampton doctrine that taking in lodgers/boarders is an ordinary incident of family residential use (favorable to letting generally), while itself ruling against this defendant's non-family group-home leasing arrangement (adverse outcome).

Premises-liability tort suit by a paying motel guest's child injured by a defective wall structure; addresses landlord-lessee tort liability and nuisance doctrine, not the legality or regulation of short-term letting itself.

Premises-liability case concerning a criminal sexual assault in a commercial parking garage; addresses landowner duty and foreseeability of third-party crime, unrelated to lodging or short-term rental regulation.

new.holding_summary: The court affirmed a declaratory judgment that renting homes on a weekly or weekend "vacation rental" basis to different groups violated a deed restriction limiting lots to "single-family residence purposes," and held that any rental for a period of less than ninety days would likewise violate the restriction, drawing on statutory residency-duration analogies.

quotes.text: The trial court held that the use of the property in question “as a vacation rental for weekends and/or weekly rentals to different groups of people by JENNIE ATTAWAY BENARD is a violation of Deed Restriction No. 1” for Point Lookout Estates.
The trial court further held that any renting for a period of less than ninety days would also be a violation of Deed Restriction No. 1.
We cannot say that the trial court abused its discretion in declaring that Appellants use of their property violated the deed restrictions in question.

new.notes: Wrongful-death premises-liability case about a social guest killed while cutting down a tree at a private home; addresses invitee/licensee tort duties, unrelated to compensated occupancy or lodging regulation.
Intermediate appellate decision in the same parking-garage sexual-assault premises-liability litigation as Mellon Mortgage Co. v. Holder; unrelated to short-term lodging or its regulation.

new.holding_summary: The court of appeals held that Tarr's short-term rental practice -- fixed check-in/check-out times, a two-night minimum, and payment of hotel occupancy taxes -- showed the home was used for "transient" rather than "residential" purposes, violating the covenant requiring tracts to be used "solely for residential purposes," and affirmed summary judgment and a take-nothing judgment against Tarr (later reversed by the Texas Supreme Court).

quotes.text: We also agree with Munson that the term “residence” “generally requires both physical presence and an intention to remain.”
One leasing his home to be used for transient purposes is not complying with the restrictive covenant that it be used solely for residential purposes.

new.notes: This intermediate decision was subsequently reversed by the Texas Supreme Court (see cite 556 S.W.3d 274 in this batch); recorded here as adverse authority reflecting the doctrine at that stage of the litigation.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a restrictive covenant limiting use to "single family residence purposes" was ambiguous as to whether it excluded short-term rentals, and, resolving the ambiguity against the enforcing homeowners and in favor of free use, held the Garretts' short-term VRBO rentals violated neither that restriction nor the covenant's prohibition on commercial use; it reversed the temporary injunction.

quotes.text: if a vacation renter uses a home "for the purposes of eating, sleeping, and other residential purposes," as was done in the present case, "this use is residential, not commercial, no matter how short the rental duration."

Because we conclude that the Restriction requiring the Property to be used for “single family residence purposes” is ambiguous, we must strictly construe the ambiguity against Appellees and resolve all doubts in favor of the free-and-unrestricted use of the Property.
Accordingly, we hold that the trial court abused its discretion by granting Appellees’ application for temporary injunction, and we sustain the Garretts’ first issue.

new.notes: Governmental-immunity and premises-defect suit arising from an employee's injury at a leased airport cargo warehouse; the licensee/invitee duty analysis concerns a commercial cargo lease, not residential short-term letting.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a homeowner who had operated short-term rentals on Tiki Island for years before the Village enacted an ordinance banning short-term rentals pleaded and presented sufficient evidence of a viable regulatory-takings claim -- economic impact and reasonable investment-backed expectations -- to support a temporary injunction restraining enforcement of the ban against her, while dismissing her duplicative declaratory-judgment claim and declining jurisdiction over relief granted to other homeowners due to an untimely notice of appeal.

quotes.text: short term rentals have occurred on Tiki Island for over 20 years,” and that, “prior to passage of Ordinance 05-14-02, Plaintiffs were able to do short term lease/rentals.”

We hold that we lack jurisdiction over the Village’s challenge to the trial court’s temporary injunction order in favor of the Ronquille and Changs. We also hold that the trial court lacked jurisdiction over Hill’s declaratory judgment action. We otherwise affirm the trial court’s temporary injunction in Hill’s favor.

new.notes: Directly on point ADVERSE-domain material: a municipal ordinance outright banning short-term rentals, challenged as a taking. Marked mixed because the ordinance itself is a police-power prohibition while the court's disposition favored the property owner by enjoining its enforcement. Characterization left null because the case adjudicates the ordinance's validity/takings status rather than the private-law lease/license/lodging character of the rental arrangement.

Forcible-detainer eviction appeal from an extended-stay hotel, resolved as moot; the opinion notes a hotel guest is 'a mere licensee, not a tenant' with no landlord-tenant relationship to the hotel, but the case is a commercial-hotel eviction/mootness holding, not a dispute about householder short-term letting or its regulation.

new.holding_summary: A lessor sought to cancel a lease because the lessee's wife received paying Christian Science patients in the dwelling; the court held this was not a violation of a 'dwelling only' use covenant, reasoning the reception of visitors or patients was merely incidental to residential use. In reaching this result the court relied on and extended its own precedent holding that a householder may admit into his home whomever he chooses, including boarders and lodgers, without the home ceasing to be a private dwelling.

quotes.text: A dwelling-house is a place for the accommodation and shelter of human beings, and the householde r may admit into his house whomsoever he pleases even boarders and lodgers; nor does his home thereby cease to be his private dwelling house

We do not see how it can be said that the actions of the defendant detailed above can be construed into making another use of the property; it still remained a dwelling and the receiving of visitors or patients was only incidental.

new.notes: This case's own facts concern a Christian Science healer's patients, not a lodger/boarder occupancy; characterization left null because no letting-of-rooms arrangement is characterized here. The doctrine quoted from Moreira v. Heckman (case_id 8502118) is the substantively relevant material, cited here as controlling precedent.

new.holding_summary: A landlord provisionally seized all effects in premises leased to a boarding house keeper for unpaid rent; boarders intervened to recover their own furniture. The court held that boarders are sub-tenants (undertenants) to the extent they occupy rooms in the leased premises and keep their own furniture there, and since these boarders owed the boarding house keeper nothing at the time of seizure, their property was properly released.

quotes.text: Boarders are in a sense sub-tenants, and where the sub-lessee agreed in good faith to pay the rent in advance payment made in accordance with the terms of the contract is riot a payment made in anticipation under the meaning of R. C. C. 2706
A boarder is an undertenant to the extent that he occupies apartments in the leased premises and keeps his own furniture and effects there.

new.holding_summary: A lessor sought to annul a lease and dispossess a tenant who had taken in boarders, lodgers, and roomers, on the ground the premises were rented only as a dwelling and the arrangement was an unconsented sublease. The court held a householder may admit into her house, on whatever condition she chooses, whomever she will, including boarders, lodgers and roomers, without her home ceasing to be a private dwelling, and further held that renting rooms to friends while the tenant retains overall superintendence of the premises is not a 'sublease' requiring the lessor's written consent.

quotes.text: But certainly a householder may admit into his house, and on whatever condition he chooses, -whomsoever he will, including boarders, lodgers and roomers; nor does his home thereby cease to be his private dwelling.

Concerns a brewery's alleged disguised ownership interest in a barroom lease, prohibited by statute; wholly unrelated to lodging or boarding houses.

new.holding_summary: Plaintiff, a practical nurse, rented a room from Mrs. Agnew (the building's lessee) and was injured when defective stairs collapsed; the courts below found plaintiff was not a subtenant but merely a 'roomer or lodger' in the leased premises, and that this did not violate the lessee's covenant not to sublease. The Supreme Court held the building owner could not, by contract with the lessee, escape ex delicto liability to such a lodger for injuries caused by the owner's neglect to keep the building in repair.

quotes.text: 4. Landlord and tenant <@=>164(5) — Landlord cannot, by contract with lessee, escape obligation arising ex delicto for injuries to roomer of lessee, resulting from collapse of stairs (Civ. Code, arts. 670, 2315, 2322, 2693-2695).

Landlord-tenant dispute over the landlord's duty to protect one apartment tenant from disturbance caused by a disorderly co-tenant in the same duplex; does not involve lodger/boarder letting or its regulation.

new.holding_summary: Plaintiff and her husband occupied a hotel room that its registered occupant had turned over to them with the desk clerk's knowledge and consent, without themselves registering. The court held that hotel registration is not essential to guest status: when a registered occupant, with the hotel management's knowledge and consent, turns his room over to another person to whom the clerk delivers the key, that person becomes an accepted guest of the hotel and not a mere licensee.

quotes.text: The fact that such person fails to register, or is not required to register, is immaterial; as the registration , of guests at a hotel is no part of the contract between the hotel proprietor and the guest

when the registered occupant of a room, with the knowledge and consent of the hotel management, turns his room over to another person, and the hotel clerk delivers the key of the room to that person, he becomes an accepted guest of the hotel, and is not a mere licensee.

new.holding_summary: Plaintiff operated a business of renting furnished rooms in premises leased from defendant, a purpose known to both parties at the time of leasing; when a neighboring hotel's excavation work destroyed the building's usability for that purpose, the court held plaintiff entitled to cancel the lease and be relieved of rent from judicial demand, since the lessor's warranty extends to the tenant's known business purpose. A keeper of a hotel, inn, boarding house or lodging house, except an emigrant lodging house, has a lien upon, while in possession, and may detain the baggage and other property brought upon their premises by a guest, boarder or lodger, for the proper charges due from him, on account of his accommodation, board and lodging, and such extras as are furnished at his request.

The evidence in the case does not bring respondent within the requirements of the provisions of section 71 of the Lien Law, essential to a valid lien in her favor as a boarding-house or lodging-house keeper.

new.notes: Polarity marked mixed: the Lien Law's recognition of lodger/boarder arrangements is protective, but on these facts the boarding-house keeper's lien claim failed for lack of proof.
Water-power rights dispute arising from nineteenth-century perpetual leases; discusses feudal landlord-tenant tenure doctrine, not residential letting or lodging house regulation.

new.holding_summary: The court granted certiorari to correct a hotel-classification tax assessment, holding that a fifteen-story building whose rooms were mostly leased to permanent tenants, with roughly twenty percent temporarily let to transients pending long-term leasing, retained its character as an apartment house rather than a hotel and therefore qualified for the new-building tax exemption for buildings 'planned for dwelling purposes exclusively, except hotels.'

quotes.text: One hundred and thirteen rooms are leased to permanent tenants; twenty-eight rooms are used by transients; seventy-four rooms were furnished by the landlord, of which fifty-six have been leased on long-term leases, and twenty-eight rooms devoted to transients.
I think that it may safely be said that the character of the building as an apartment house was practically adjudicated.

The rooms occupied by transients, forming but twenty per cent of the total number of rooms, are being so used only temporarily in order to derive an income therefrom pending attempts to lease them for .long terms, like the rest of the rooms.

new.notes: Characterization marked 'other' because the court's classification turns on the hotel-versus-apartment-house tax distinction rather than lease/license/lodging/innkeeping.
Summary proceeding over alleged illegal use of a leased loft as a place of public assembly under the building code; unrelated to residential letting or lodging house regulation.

Zoning-classification dispute over whether a sorority/chapter house qualifies as a 'family' single dwelling; concerns communal student cooperative living, not compensated letting of rooms to lodgers or boarders.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
new.notes: Dispute over right to possession of a building hallway/stairway among landlord, tenant, and a third-party squatter; not concerned with letting of rooms or lodging house regulation.

Zoning ordinance dispute over erection of apartment houses in a restricted single/two-family residence district; concerns multi-family apartment-house zoning generally, not letting of rooms by householders or regulation of boarding/lodging houses specifically.
Mandamus proceeding over a zoning-map amendment reclassifying property from residence to business district for an office building; unrelated to residential letting or lodging.
