new.holding_summary: Reviewing a claim against a decedent's estate for table board, room rent, and nursing care, the court held that although the decedent had for years boarded weekly with claimant's household at an agreed price he had paid up to the week of his death, the evidence failed to establish any express or implied contract to pay for room rent, laundering, or nursing services beyond that board, and reversed the surrogate's allowance of those additional charges.

quotes.text: Board ” is- defined as “ To receive food as a lodger, or without lodgings, for a compensation”
Dr. Clyde had boarded with the claimant’s mother and with the claimant for a long term of years
it is very evident, from the claimant’s own showing, that Dr. Clyde intended to and did pay his board in the agreed amount of three dollars and fifty cents during his lifetime

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
new.notes: Criminal rape prosecution where the defendant took the complainant to a furnished-room house; the furnished-room setting is mentioned only as the location of the offense, with no discussion of the legal character of letting or lodging.

Landlord-tenant dispute over tenancy-at-sufferance and use-and-occupation liability after a partition; defendant happened to run a hotel in the demised premises, but the holding addresses holding-over/assumpsit doctrine, not lodging or boarding practice or its regulation.
Appeal in the same Sutmeyer/Thornton litigation as case 457003; again turns on use-and-occupation/estoppel doctrine for a holdover hotel tenant, not on lodging/boarding practice or its regulation.

Hotel room let by the day (up to a month) for use as a millinery shop and private trade display, not as a dwelling or lodging; dispute concerns advertising rights and eviction, not compensated residential occupancy or its regulation.
Municipal negligence case over an icy sidewalk and a snow-removal ordinance's application to a commercial tenant (telegraph office); no lodging, boarding, or short-term residential letting involved.

new.holding_summary: A constable who broke into a hotel boarder's room and seized her piano under a landlord's distress warrant for rent owed by the hotel keeper was liable in trespass, because a boarder's goods are not subject to distraint for the boarding-house keeper's rent. The court also permitted amendment to drop the landlord as a defendant since the case had proceeded against the constable alone.

quotes.text: Where a constable at the instance of the lessor of a hotel breaks into the room of a boarder, and seizes and sells for rent a piano belonging to the boarder, he will be liable in damages to the boarder in an action of trespass.
The goods of a boarder are not liable to be distrained for rent due by the keeper of a boarding house
The goods of a boarder are not liable to be distrained for rent due by the keeper of a boarding house

new.notes: Facts do not state how long plaintiff had boarded at the hotel, so duration is left unclear.
Trade-fixture removal dispute between a commercial landlord and outgoing tenant; no lodging, boarding, or dwelling-occupancy issue.
Municipal borough renting excess office space in its own building to raise revenue; not a householder or commercial lodging operator, and no lodger/boarder occupancy at issue.
Dispute over use of a fraternal meeting hall (GAR Memorial Hall) among veterans' organizations under a deed of trust; not compensated residential occupancy or boarding-house regulation.

new.holding_summary: The hotel proprietor was not liable when a bottle fell from an upper window and injured a passerby below, because there was no proof connecting the fall to any act or knowledge of the proprietor or a guest under his control. The court held a hotel proprietor is not liable for an occupant's negligent placement of an article on a window sill absent notice of the danger.

quotes.text: it is his living quarters or residence as a home
the guest or boarder has an absolute right to the free enjoyment of his room or apartment without interference from anyone

Nor would he be liable for the result of articles placed on the window sill falling to the street unless he knew, or had reason to know, the thing placed there was of a dangerous nature, or likely to fall to the street.

new.notes: Court draws a doctrinally rich distinction between transient hotel guests and 'permanent guests' using rooms partly for light housekeeping (a recurring boarding/lodging-adjacent term); the specific room from which the bottle fell was never identified, so duration is unclear from the facts. Characterization set to innkeeping as the dominant frame, though lodging-type occupancy is also discussed.

new.court: Butler County Court of Common Pleas
new.holding_summary: A tenant holding a hotel building under a twenty-year lease is an 'owner' within the meaning of the fire-escape statute and may be compelled to erect and maintain fire-escapes, even though the lease imposed no such duty on him and made no provision for repairs by the landlord.

quotes.text: The building is a four-story brick, used in its entirety for hotel purposes.
the hotel building and the use made of it by the relator is such as to require fire-escapes, under the provisions of the Act of May 3, 1909, P. L. 417
A tenant for years may he compelled to erect fire-escapes under the Act of May 3, 1909, P. L. 417

new.notes: Sustains a police-power safety regulation (fire-escapes) against a hotel operator, extending statutory 'owner' liability to a tenant for years; classified adverse as an upheld regulation of a lodging establishment. Duration of individual occupants' stays is not addressed.

Bailment dispute over a trunk stored in a hotel baggage room before the owner's arrival; discusses when the guest/innkeeper relation begins only to resolve bailment liability for lost trunk contents, not the legality or character of room-letting itself.

Bailment dispute over a traveling bag left at a hotel desk while plaintiff sought a room elsewhere and eventually stayed at a different hotel; concerns bailment-for-mutual-benefit liability standards, not lodging/boarding doctrine.

Private nuisance/trespass dispute between adjoining landowners over a roof spout and boarded-up windows; the covenant of quiet enjoyment is discussed only as to a commercial tenant's shop, unrelated to short-term letting or boarding-house regulation.
Dispute over the form of a landlord's distress warrant and whether it reaches a stranger's goods on leased business premises; no lodging or boarding element.
Dispute over 19th-century deed covenants for a public wharf/pier and municipal wharfage fees; commercial dockage rights, not residential lodging.
Equity suit over the power to execute oil and gas leases reserved under a family partition deed; no lodging/boarding element.

new.holding_summary: Hotel guests whose room was broken into and clothing stolen during a night's absence could recover from the innkeeper, who is practically an insurer of property properly kept in a guest's assigned room while the guest remains in the house. The Act of 1913 did not diminish this common-law responsibility for goods left in the room.

quotes.text: The innkeeper, as to articles properly retained by guests in their room, is practically in the position of an insurer while the guest remains in his house
The guests had the reasonable right to expect that their room would be protected from unlawful intrusion or thefts.
The guests had the reasonable right to expect that their room would be protected from unlawful intrusion or thefts.

new.notes: Plaintiffs registered and occupied the room jointly for one night before the theft was discovered the next evening.

new.holding_summary: The Act of May 8, 1876, permitting hotel, inn, and boarding-house keepers to attach a debtor-employee's wages for up to four weeks' board, is constitutional special legislation for a properly recognized class. The judgment against the garnishee was nonetheless reversed because the record failed to show the plaintiff was a boarding-house keeper and affirmatively showed the claim included board for persons other than the laborer.

quotes.text: Hotelkeepers and innkeepers have from time immemorial been recognized as a distinct class, owing special duties to their patrons and possessing special corresponding rights.
Hotelkeepers and innkeepers have from time immemorial been recognized as a distinct class, owing special duties to their patrons and possessing special corresponding rights.
The Act of May 8, 1876, P. L. 139, authorizing hotel and hoarding house keepers to attach wages due such employees as may be indebted to them is constitutional.

new.notes: Underlying justice-of-the-peace judgment was for four weeks' board and lodging. Holding_summary quote reproduces the source's OCR rendering of 'boarding' as 'hoarding' verbatim, per source-fidelity requirement.
Guardian-and-ward dispute over authority to lease ward's commercial store buildings and subletting rights; no lodging/boarding-house occupancy involved.
Ordinary landlord-tenant rent dispute over a house leased by church trustees to tenants; no lodger/boarder or regulatory issue present.
Facts recite a rooming house being leased/subleased with furniture, but the adjudicated issue is conversion of chattels and limitations, not the legal character of the letting.

Nuisance-abatement statute lists 'hotel, rooming house or boarding house' as one category of premises subject to closure for liquor/gambling/prostitution, but the actual premises is a social club and the holding is purely procedural (ex parte closure order improper).
Railway station premises-liability case regarding duty owed to a licensee bidding a passenger farewell; no dwelling/lodging occupancy issue.
Gambling-control prosecution; defendant's operation of the second story as a 'rooming house' is mentioned only to establish control of premises over an attic used for gaming.
Injunction case concerning bawdyhouses/disorderly houses and a municipal ordinance confining them to a district; does not involve boarding/lodging houses or compensated room-letting.
Partnership/adverse-possession dispute over an employee's occupancy of a firm-owned house as part of employment consideration; not a compensated lodging arrangement.
Tenancy-in-common land partition dispute; no dwelling/lodging occupancy issue.
Agricultural cropper/landlord-tenant classification dispute over a farm rental; incidental mention of the cropper living in one room does not implicate the lodging/boarding doctrine.

new.holding_summary: In a libel suit by a man who ran a rooming house in his own home near the Union Station, the court held the petition insufficient because the libelous article referred to a 'bunch of whorehouses ... placarded as "Rooming Houses"' and no facts were pled connecting plaintiff's single rooming house to that class. The court refused to infer, from the mere fact that a house is placarded as offering furnished rooms for rent, that it is therefore a whorehouse.

quotes.text: such rooms in the house as were not occupied for family purposes by plaintiff and his father and mother were held out to the traveling public and the public in general for rent, and were on divers occasions rented to other persons

It may be conceded that a whorehouse may be so placarded as to appear to be a rooming house, but we cannot agree to the converse of the proposition which plaintiff seems to urge in his petition, without sufficient averments of fact to sustain his conclusion that a rooming house, or a house with furnished rooms for rent, and so placarded, may reasonably be considered to be a whorehouse by reason of its placards.
No allegation by way of colloquium was made to show that plaintiff’s house was included in the class denominated “whorehouses.”
“Crawford House. Rooms 50‡, & $1.00 per Day;”

new.notes: Householder rented rooms not needed for family use to the traveling public at nightly/daily rates; court treats such a legitimate furnished-rooms business as distinct from a disorderly house.
Fire-insurance occupancy-warranty dispute over a sanitarium building; not a lodging/boarding-house occupancy case.

quotes.text: the tenant reconvened for damages from being compelled to abandon the premises, preventing her from keeping boarders therein
the profits alleged and attempted to be proven were too vague, uncertain, and speculative to be recoverable in an action at law.

new.notes: Tenant's boarding-house business is treated as an ordinary commercial tenancy (favorable), but her damages claim tied to it was rejected under general speculative-profits doctrine, not on grounds specific to boarding-house legality (adverse-leaning); no clear lease/license/lodging characterization of the boarder relationship is stated, so characterization left null.
Concerns whether a private country club's dispensing of liquor to members constitutes 'selling' under tax/injunction statutes; no lodging or boarding-house issue.

Suit is a landlord-tenant dispute over rent and lease extension of a lodging-house building among successive operators; the legal character of the operator's letting to roomers/lodgers is never adjudicated.
Dispute over rent under a land lease and the mental competency of the lessor at the time of a deed; no dwelling/lodging occupancy issue.
Farm-land rent dispute between a life tenant and her tenant; no dwelling/lodging occupancy issue.

quotes.text: Mrs. Dubose testified that appellant came to her house in Uvalde about the 12th of September and she let him have two furnished rooms in which he and his wife and child lived until the 23d of October, when they moved to Mrs. Greaves where they resided at the time of the trial. They did their own cooking and ate in the rooms and slept there.

if you believe from the evidence that J. Less was an actual dweller in Uvalde County, Texas, at the time that he practiced medicine, if he did so, and that he had removed from some other place, and brought his wife and child with him, and was keeping house with such wife and child in said Uvalde County, Texas, and had come to Uvalde County, Texas, for the purpose of remaining some time, and practicing medicine (if he did so intend) . . . then and in that case he would be residing in Uvalde County, Texas, within the purview of said law.

new.notes: A householder's short-term letting of furnished rooms to a family is treated as an unremarkable, lawful basis for establishing actual residence; the letting arrangement itself is never questioned.
License-tax dispute over a bank leasing surplus office space in its own commercial office building; discusses 'right to lease as incident of ownership' but involves no dwelling/lodging occupancy.
Summary-eviction pleading case under La. C.C.P. art. 4702 against a 'former owner' occupant; no compensated lodging or dwelling-letting arrangement at issue.
Summary eviction of an occupant (living in a camp boat) holding 'through the accommodation of the owner'; not a compensated boarding/lodging dispute.
Agricultural lessor's-privilege dispute over cotton crops removed between farm properties; no dwelling/lodging occupancy involved.

Premises-liability case turning on a child's licensee status near a garage-apartment driveway; the underlying sublease of the apartment's living quarters is background fact only, not the arrangement actually adjudicated.
Ordinance case regulating door-to-door peddlers/solicitors entering private residences without invitation; unrelated to letting rooms or lodging houses.

Gambling-ordinance ultra vires case; the ordinance's quoted definitional clause excluding a 'hotel, rooming house or place of transient residence' from 'bona fide private residence' is background text, not an issue actually litigated or adjudicated on appeal.
Murder-trial insanity-plea appeal; tourist camps appear only within defendant's confession narrating his flight, with no doctrinal treatment of lodging law.

Burglary appeal reversing a conviction on evidentiary/impeachment grounds; 'rooming house' and 'tourist court' are mentioned only to test witness credibility/alibi, not adjudicated as lodging-law issues.

new.holding_summary: On rehearing, the Louisiana Supreme Court reversed course and upheld Act No. 18 of 1886, which exempts hotels and boarding houses -- but not restaurants -- from the Sunday prohibition on selling wine for table use, holding the classification a permissible legislative judgment based on the nature of the hotel and boarding house business rather than unconstitutional discrimination. The restaurant proprietor's conviction was reinstated, though the charge against his clerk-employee was dismissed because the statute's penalty reaches only 'proprietors.'

quotes.text: there may still be good reason, because of the nature of the hotel and boarding house business, the investment therein, etc., for the legislature to place them in a separate and distinct class in regulating the operation of business which may be pursued on Sundays.

Act No. 18 of 1886 withstood attack, similar to that presented here, in State ex rel. Walker v. Judge, 39 La.Ann. 132, 1 So. 437. After a reconsideration, we see no reason to disturb the ruling in that case.

new.notes: Case concerns statutory classification of hotels/boarding houses versus restaurants under a Sunday liquor law, not a specific occupant's arrangement, so characterization/who_was_letting/duration are not applicable to a particular occupancy. On rehearing the court reversed its original opinion's discrimination holding (which had favored the restaurant) and upheld the boarding-house/hotel exemption as constitutional -- hence 'mixed' polarity.
Nuisance/zoning suit over a restaurant's driveways and customer parking lot; no lodging or boarding-house issue is involved.
Attorney disbarment proceeding for bar-exam cheating; hotel rooms are mentioned only as the meeting location for the conspiracy, not a lodging-law issue.

License-tax case on operating a commercial office building, again invoking the 'right to lease as incident of ownership' doctrine from State v. City Savings Bank; involves office space, not dwelling occupancy.
Burglary conspiracy appeal; a tourist camp is mentioned only as a stop on the getaway route, with no doctrinal discussion of lodging.
Auto-theft/confession appeal; defendant was arrested at a Mississippi tourist camp cabin, mentioned only as an investigative fact, not adjudicated lodging law.
Junk-yard fencing ordinance case decided under the police power; unrelated to residential lodging or boarding houses.
Barber minimum-price regulation case under the police power; unrelated to lodging or boarding houses.

new.notes: Upholds a 4-week duration limit on occupied house trailers under a town's police-power ordinance; concerns trailer-camp regulation, not compensated letting of rooms/dwellings by a householder, and no payment for the trailer occupancy is shown.

new.notes: Dispute over whether ground beneath tenant-owned bungalows is a 'housing accommodation' under rent control; the statutory list including boarding/lodging house is quoted only as part of definitional analysis, not adjudicated on the letting practice itself.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Onondaga County
new.holding_summary: A prior owner who lived on the first floor and boarded elderly paying occupants on the second floor for weekly fees committed no nuisance; the court held that maintaining a boarding house is not itself a nuisance. The successor owner was enjoined not because boarding paying occupants was unlawful, but because she radically changed the use to house alcoholics, drug addicts, and the mentally ill in a manner that disturbed the residential neighborhood.

quotes.text: it might be called a boarding house or private home for elderly people; it served a useful purpose, and the use to which it was put caused no annoyance to the neighborhood during all the years that Mrs. Owens occupied and used the premises for such purposes.
To maintain a boarding house or a hospital or a restaurant or any other legitimate business does not, in and of itself, constitute a nuisance.
The plaintiffs are entitled to an injunction restraining the defendant from receiving alcoholic or drug addicts or insane or demented people as patients

new.notes: Mixed result on the facts (injunction issued against successor owner), but the operative legal doctrine — boarding paying lodgers is a lawful, ordinary use, not per se a nuisance — is favorable; marked favorable for the doctrinal holding rather than the ultimate outcome against this defendant.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Niagara County
new.notes: Landlord-tenant dispute over loss of light/air from a neighboring garage after a zoning amendment; the leased premises' intended use as a 'rooming house, boarding house or hotel' is incidental background, not at issue.
Ordinary apartment lease surrender/reletting dispute; no boarding, lodging, or short-term letting issue present.

Criminal fraud prosecution over misrepresentations (hotel's 'respectability,' occupancy rate) inducing a lease of an entire hotel business; concerns fraud in a commercial lease transaction, not the legal character or regulation of room letting.

new.court: New York Surrogate's Court, New York County
new.notes: Dispute over which of two claimants (paramount landlord vs. tenant's assignee) is owed use-and-occupancy payments after a summary dispossess proceeding against a subtenant's estate; ordinary apartment sublease priority dispute, no lodging/boarding issue.

new.holding_summary: Plaintiff, as assignee of a lease authorizing use of a 42-room building 'in the business of subletting the apartments thereof... for residential and living purposes' (a rooming-house operation), was compelled by a pre-existing tenement house department fire-safety violation to convert the building, reducing legal sleeping rooms from 42 to 15 and destroying her profit margin. The court held the lease placed the obligation to cure such regulatory violations on the tenant, not the landlord, and denied return of her security deposit after she was evicted for nonpayment of rent.

quotes.text: to be used in the business of subletting the apartments thereof, furnished or unfurnished, for residential and living purposes.
a violation order on the premises in question was issued by the tenement house department, the violation charging a serious infringment of fire regulations.
the intent of the lease is clear in its requirement that the removal of violations placed against the premises was an obligation cast upon the tenant, and not the landlord.

new.notes: Regulation (fire-safety violation limiting sleeping rooms) is treated as valid and enforced against the rooming-house operation, with the economic burden of compliance falling on the letting party; marked adverse for that regulatory backdrop, though the court's actual holding is a lease-allocation-of-cost ruling.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
new.notes: Holds an innkeeper's statutory lien inapplicable where an apartment was occupied under a yearly lease (landlord-tenant relationship) rather than as hotel accommodation; occupancy was long-term leasehold, not short-term letting or boarding.
Dispute over whether hotel house laundries require licenses under a laundry-licensing ordinance; unrelated to room/dwelling letting.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Erie County
new.notes: Zoning-district and private-nuisance dispute over an apartment hotel's guest parking lot; the hotel's 'permanent and transient guests' are mentioned only as background, not the subject of the ruling.

new.court: New York Court of General Sessions
new.notes: Manslaughter prosecution over a fatal rooming-house fire; the building's classification as a 'Converted Class B' furnished-room house and its fire-safety requirements are recited only as background to the culpable-negligence analysis, a passing mention.

new.court: County Court of New York, Nassau County
new.holding_summary: Defendant was convicted of maintaining a building with separate housekeeping units as a rooming/apartment house in a single-family residence zoning district. The court found the multi-unit use had legally existed since 1919, predating the zoning ordinance and surviving despite a restrictive covenant (which had been released or waived by the original grantor), and reversed the conviction as an unlawfully prosecuted non-conforming use.

quotes.text: It was proven and not disputed that the defendant’s building was not used for one housekeeping unit only, but was used as an apartment house with separate housekeeping units
That defense is amply supported by the proof, and does not seem to be seriously disputed.
The judgment of conviction should, therefore, be reversed and the information dismissed.

new.notes: Favorable in that the court protected the owner's pre-existing right to let multiple housekeeping units against a later-enacted single-family zoning restriction.
Restrictive-covenant dispute between a luncheonette and a competing drink stand in a retail arcade lease; no lodging/boarding content.

Invalidates a permit requirement for a married couple occupying their own house trailer as a residence; no compensated occupancy of another's dwelling/rooms is involved — the occupants own the trailer itself.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Monroe County
new.notes: Zoning variance case for a gasoline station on an obsolete residential corner lot; expert testimony that the houses could only be rented to 'rooming-house operators' is passing valuation testimony, not an adjudicated issue.
Injunction dispute over building-tenants' right to use a waste-paper removal contractor of their choice; no lodging/boarding content.
Concerns building-code regulation of house trailers used as permanent owner-occupied dwellings; not about letting rooms/dwellings to others for pay.

new.court: Monroe County Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Tort/premises-liability demurrer case concerning an innkeeper's duty of care to injured paying guests at a tourist lodge; does not address the legality or regulation of letting rooms/dwellings for pay.

Zoning nonconforming-use dispute over converting a store to a restaurant/tavern with a liquor license; no lodging or room-letting issue.
Child-custody habeas corpus case; father's rooming/boarding arrangement and grandparents' tourist camp are passing background facts only.
Fire-insurance case construing 'vacant or unoccupied'; cites lodger/occupancy case law only as interpretive dicta, not concerning a letting arrangement itself.

Criminal conviction for maintaining a disorderly house/prostitution in furnished rooms; the opinion's holding addresses evidentiary/cross-examination rules, not the legality or regulation of room-letting as such.
Divorce/indignities case; a tourist camp is mentioned only as the site of the parties' honeymoon, a purely incidental detail.

new.holding_summary: The court held that plaintiff's presence in her brother's leased apartment, where she paid $2 a week for lodging when able and helped with housework, did not constitute a sub-letting forbidden by the lease's no-subletting clause; her status more closely resembled that of a servant than an independent lodger or sublessee, and the landlord owed her, as an invitee, a duty of reasonable care on the common fire-escape passageway.

quotes.text: She can hardly be said to have been a lodger (cf. Davis v. Hartel, 56 Pa. Superior Ct. 557, 564) as that designation would imply some status more independent of Whitton than the evidence discloses; the relationship had more of the characteristics of master and servant and it was in this relationship that she was employed when injured, as she had been washing dishes and “was starting down to empty the rubbish.”

We think the provision in the lease was intended to prohibit a more substantial change in possession than resulted from plaintiff’s presence in the household. It is not conceivable that by the words of the provision the parties intended to prevent the tenant’s taking a servant who worked outside for others part of the time and also did the family household work in whole or part consideration of the accommodation received.

In support of her position, appellant cites Peaks v. Cobb, 197 Mass. 554, 83 N. E. 1106, and Gardiner v. DeSalles, 13 La. App. 83, 126 So. 739, holding that a lodger is not a sublessee within such a provision.

new.notes: Trade-fixtures dispute over bowling alleys in a commercial lease; unrelated to lodging or room-letting.
Tort case turning on invitee-versus-licensee status of a hotel guest's visitor injured on a balcony; does not address the character or regulation of letting rooms for pay.
Commercial lease assignment/holdover dispute over a restaurant-liquor business; not about lodging or room-letting.

Concerns a zoning ordinance's attempt to bar liquor sales at an otherwise-permitted hotel; the regulatory dispute is about liquor licensing within the hotel business, not the legality or regulation of letting/lodging itself.

new.holding_summary: The Supreme Court affirmed a zoning variance permitting a restaurant lessee to also operate its property as a hotel/guest house, holding that although the ordinance's special-exception provision for 'hotel, boarding house or restaurant' use lacked governing standards, the commercial character of the surrounding neighborhood and the proven financial hardship of restricting the business to a restaurant justified granting a variance.

quotes.text: Among the possible uses, by special exception, is a “hotel, boarding house or restaurant”.
entered a decree nisi reversing the order of the Board of Adjustment and directing the Board to authorize a variance permitting the plaintiff to use the demised premises as a hotel.
The hardship to the plaintiff, if it were prevented from using the premises as a hotel, was satisfactorily established.

new.holding_summary: The court affirmed defendants' summary conviction for beginning excavation and construction of a motel/automobile tourist camp without a zoning permit, holding that the newly enacted R-1 residential zoning ordinance validly barred the commercial tourist-camp use in that district and that defendants' pre-ordinance architect's fees and post-injunction construction expenditures did not vest a right to complete the project.

quotes.text: an area including defendants’ land became classified as an R-1 Residence Zone, in which there were permitted only single family detached dwellings, churches, schools, libraries, government buildings and parks.
The decree of the court below affirming the judgment of the alderman is affirmed at the cost of appellants.

new.holding_summary: In a homestead-partition dispute, the court held that a 21-unit tourist court built and operated by the widow on the same tract as her residence constituted both her personal and business homestead, exempt from partition, because operating and renting the cabins occupied all of her time and effort as an ordinary business. The court treated running a tourist court renting cabins by the day or week as no different in kind from operating a grocery store, gristmill, or print shop.

quotes.text: the evidence conclusively reveals that the land was purchased for the purpose of establishing thereon a tourist court to be occupied as a personal and business homestead

is that which occupies the time, labor, and efforts of its owner or operator, and we think it is doing no violence to the term to say that operating a tourist camp is as distinctive a business as operating a grocery store, a gristmill, or a print shop.

new.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Fourth Circuit
new.holding_summary: The court held that the City's suit to enjoin a guest house from renting rooms for transient (under-sixty-day) occupancy in a residential zoning district was barred by the two-year peremptive period of La. R.S. 9:5625, because the City had actual written notice of the zoning violation by October 31, 1989, before it filed suit on November 15, 1991. As a result, the guest house's expanded transient-occupancy use acquired legal nonconforming status.

quotes.text: from renting rooms at 705 and 709 Burgundy Street for transient occupancy (less than sixty days) in violation of the Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance (CZO Art. 5, § 18.2 and Art. 12, § 5).

St. Peter, Inc. caused, allowed and/or permitted the expansion of a nonconforming use by allowing 705 and 709 Burgundy to be utilized as part of St. Peter House (a |2guest house used for transient occupation).
the units of St. Peter Guest House at 705-709 Burgundy St. acquired and shall enjoy legal non-conforming status.
Prescription had accrued and the City’s petition for an injunction | gwas barred when it was filed on November 15, 1991.

new.notes: Substantive dispute is procedural (peremption/notice), not a holding on the legality of transient letting itself; adverse regulatory framework (CZO bar on transient occupancy) coexists with a practical favorable outcome (continued nonconforming use) for the operator.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
new.holding_summary: A rent-stabilized tenant who sublet her apartment to 93 different Airbnb guests over 338 days across 18 months, charging nightly rates far exceeding the lawful 10% sublet premium, engaged in unlawful profiteering as a matter of law. Because the conduct was sustained and substantial rather than isolated, she was not entitled to a right to cure, and the landlord was entitled to terminate the lease and evict her.

quotes.text: the record establishes that defendant’s “guests” were, as a matter of law, subtenants, and this matter is therefore governed by RSC § 2525.6
defendant’s systematic commercial exploitation of her rent-stabilized leasehold fully warrants the termination of her lease.
Turning her rent-stabilized apartment into a single-unit tourist hotel in this fashion enabled defendant to earn substantial profits, far in excess of the legally permissible 10% premium.

new.notes: Property tax exemption dispute over ownership of a college dormitory built under a ground lease/master lease structure; no bearing on short-term letting or lodging house regulation.
Landlord-tenant attornment dispute after a building was sold to a new owner; addresses licensee-vs-month-to-month-tenant status, not compensated lodging or boarding.

Religious corporation governance and trespass dispute over control of a church and its pastor; boarding/lodging arrangements are not at issue.

new.holding_summary: A restrictive covenant barring 'business' use — defined to include operating a hotel or boarding/lodging house and housing paying guests for profit — does not bar a homeowner from leasing his or her entire home to a tenant on an ordinary lease. Because the covenant contemplates the possibility of leasing (by barring both owners and tenants from business use) and does not expressly prohibit residential leasing, a two-year lease of the defendants' home did not violate it.

quotes.text: the subject covenant prohibits any “owner, tenant or occupant” of premises located in Edgewater Point from operating a boarding or lodging house for paying guests. However, the covenant does not expressly bar a property owner from leasing his or her home, and, in fact, contemplates the possibility that homes will be leased by barring both tenants and owners from using premises for business purposes.
It is well settled that the law favors the free and unobstructed use of real property
the Supreme Court properly dismissed the complaint on the ground that the restrictive covenant does not bar an Edgewater Point property owner from leasing his or her home.

new.holding_summary: In a companion zoning-enforcement action, the court held that a cottage containing a bathroom and two bedrooms, moved onto defendants' lot and given a permanent foundation, violated the town's single-family zoning ordinance's ban on accessory structures containing 'living quarters.' The court reasoned the ordinance validly confined each lot to one household, a concern it linked to the tourist area's pattern of short-term rental of extra living quarters, and ordered the cottage removed.

quotes.text: No accessory structure having living quarters is permitted.

The obvious legislative planning scheme in the ordinance is the recognition of residential control over a household unit in one building with all rooms accessible from inside. What is prohibited in the ordinance are separate buildings with living quarters. The reason is obvious especially in this tourist area where high rents and overnight and weekend occupancy are common with or without kitchen facilities.

new.notes: Loft Law coverage dispute over whether bare residential occupancy without physical conversion counts as use 'for residential purposes'; concerns loft-conversion doctrine, not boarding/lodging for pay.

new.notes: Roommate-law (Real Property Law § 235-f) dispute over the number of co-tenant roommates permitted in a leased apartment; concerns tenant occupancy-sharing rights among unrelated cohabitants, not compensated lodging/boarding by a householder taking in paying guests.

Zoning dispute over a methadone clinic use permit; references Thomason (bed-and-breakfast exclusionary zoning) only in passing as a distinguishable precedent. Does not itself address short-term letting, boarding houses, or lodger status.

new.holding_summary: The Commonwealth Court affirmed dimensional variances allowing a nonprofit to convert a vacant former motel/dormitory into a fifty-unit single-room-occupancy residence for low-income and homeless persons, holding the proposed use fit within zoning categories such as apartment/multiple-family dwelling, group care facility, rooming/boarding home, or tourist home that are all expressly permitted uses in the T-1 district.

quotes.text: Community Services’ Executive Director, Kitty Cancilla, testified that the intended purpose of the building would be to provide low-income and homeless persons with a place to live and that their average stay would be six to nine months.
Accordingly, we affirm the judgment of the Court of Common Pleas of Erie County and the grant of the two dimensional variances to Community Services.

new.notes: Court treats the converted motel/dormitory as fitting several permitted zoning categories (apartment/multiple-family dwelling, group care facility, rooming/boarding home, tourist home) without settling on a single characterization of the arrangement; characterization left null.

new.holding_summary: The Commonwealth Court held that a six-room boarding house with a communal kitchen qualifies as a 'residential building' under the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act, affirming an injunction requiring the water authority to restore and maintain water service to boarder-tenants despite the landlord's nonpayment, because occupants who treat their rooms as a permanent domicile and pay rent are the tenants USTRA was meant to protect.

quotes.text: Appellees live as tenants in the building and pay the landlord rent for the right to do so.
The legislature, in enacting USTRA, clearly intended to combat against an innocent tenant suffering the loss of utility service because of a landlord’s failure to pay.

Therefore, if the Authority could simply ignore USTRA in this case, the Appellees would innocently suffer the loss of water service to the residence, even though they maintain payment to the landlord for the use of their room and common areas.

new.notes: Home occupation special exception dispute over a dog-breeding business; 'kennel license'/floor-area/employee language matched lodging-adjacent selectors but the case does not involve letting rooms or dwellings for pay.

new.holding_summary: The Commonwealth Court upheld a municipal ordinance requiring landlords to notify the health officer and pass an inspection before re-letting a vacant rental dwelling, holding it a valid exercise of police power that neither denies due process nor violates equal protection, and that distinguishing rental from owner-occupied housing for inspection purposes is rationally related to protecting tenant health and safety.

quotes.text: No dwelling or dwelling unit hereafter becoming vacant and available for occupancy or reoccupancy shall be leased, rented, or occupied for dwelling purposes by other than the lawful owner until the Health Officer has certified in writing on a form provided by the City that such dwelling or dwelling unit substantially conforms with the provisions of this ordinance.

As a measure taken by the City of Farrell to ensure that rental property within the City is safe, healthful, and habitable, the ordinance requiring landlords to notify the City of a change in tenants in rental property and allow inspection of the premises for health and safety violations is a proper exercise of the City’s police powers.

In light of these principles, it is clear that the trial court was correct in finding that the ordinance is a constitutional exercise of the City’s police power, and that the appellant has failed to carry his burden of proving otherwise.

new.notes: Concerns ordinary rental dwellings citywide rather than a specific boarding/lodging house; record does not indicate whether appellant was an individual landlord or larger operator, so who_was_letting and duration are unclear.

new.holding_summary: The trial court held that a six-room rooming house with a communal kitchen, where boarders held oral leases and paid weekly or monthly rent to the landlord's agent, is a 'residential building' under the Utility Service Tenant's Rights Act, entitling the long-term boarders to USTRA's protections against termination of water service for the landlord's nonpayment.

quotes.text: Both plaintiffs Mark Sisco and Van Thompson have oral leases with the landlord owner of 1117 Vine Avenue, John Bricker Jr.
These plaintiffs have resided at 1117 Vine Avenue for a significant period of time. This is their home.

In conclusion, based on the foregoing discussion the court finds that the Utility Service Tenant’s Rights Act applies to plaintiffs Mark Sisco and Van Thompson and the defendant Williamsport Municipal Water Authority must comply with this act and allow plaintiffs the opportunity to be availed of this act.

Eminent-domain dispute over rent owed by a commercial fruit-market tenant who remained in possession after condemnation; concerns Eminent Domain Code compensation procedure, not residential lodging or boarding houses.

new.holding_summary: The Superior Court held that a motor lodge remained subject to the innkeeper's strict common-law liability for a paying guest's stolen property because it had not complied with the notice-posting and safe-provision requirements of the Act of 1913 that would otherwise have limited its liability, affirming liability and remanding only for a jury determination of the amount of the guest's loss.

quotes.text: Plaintiff, H. George Buck, was a paying guest of the defendant George Washington Motor Lodge on October 22, 1965, when, at sometime after midnight, while he was in bed in the room assigned him, he was awakened by the noise of an intruder in his room.

He held himself out as an innkeeper, and was required by law to receive all persons coming and desiring lodgings, and upon him was imposed the duty of strict care of the property of his guests whilst in his hotel.
However, defendant did not comply with the requirements of the Statute and therefore remained in the domain of common law liability.

new.notes: Concerns commercial innkeeping (a motor lodge) rather than household letting; included because the case directly addresses the legal character of a short-term paying-guest occupancy (the 'innkeeping' characterization category).

Fire-injury suit turning on whether an implied residential landlord-tenant relationship arose between a redevelopment authority and a family remaining rent-free in an apartment after condemnation; ordinary apartment tenancy formation, not boarding/lodging houses or short-term letting.

new.holding_summary: The Dallas Court of Appeals affirmed judgment for the apartment complex owner, holding the City failed to prove that the property was being operated as a zoning-restricted 'residential hotel,' because current tenants signed apartment leases for whole units (with optional roommate agreements) rather than six or more separately rented, individually secured guest rooms. The trial court's refusal to permanently enjoin the owner's use of the property was therefore upheld.

quotes.text: All current tenants had entered into an apartment lease for a particular apartment unit.

we cannot conclude the evidence established conclusively Billinglsey was separately renting six or more guestrooms at the time of trial or that the trial court's finding to the contrary was against the great weight and preponderance of the evidence.
The zoning ordinance, however, does not permit Bill-ingsley's property to be used as a residential hotel or motel.

new.notes: Complex previously advertised 'Rooms for Rent' at $105/week/$420/month but had switched to month-to-month apartment leases with roommate agreements by trial; city's 'residential hotel' zoning theory failed on proof of separately-rented rooms, so outcome favors owner's leasing practice even though the underlying regulatory scheme (adverse-type) targets room-by-room lodging use.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a mobile-home owner's informal, no-fixed-term rental of her own mobile home to a tenant who was 'desperate for a place to live' was an ordinary landlord-tenant rental, not a 'bailment lease' (a financing device carrying an eventual right to ownership), so the fire policy's bailment-lease exclusion did not bar recovery.

quotes.text: There was nothing in the agreement that gave the tenant the right to use and enjoy the mobile home as long as she paid the rental, or the right to ever become the owner of the mobile home.
The subject exclusion is directed solely to a security transaction and not to a simple landlord-tenant relationship.
we hold that the verbal agreement in question in this case did not create a “bailment lease” as we have defined that term.

new.holding_summary: The court held that condominium unit owners have an 'absolute right to lease' their units as guaranteed by the condominium declaration, but that right is 'subject to all provisions and restrictions applicable to the Project'; it reversed the trial court and upheld the condo association's fees on units rented outside its rental pool and its prohibition on outside leasing agents as reasonably necessary to the project's operation, not arbitrary, capricious, or discriminatory.

quotes.text: Each Apartment Owner shall have an absolute right to lease or rent his apartment upon such terms as he shall approve, subject to all provisions and restrictions applicable to the Project.
We conclude the prohibition and fees were necessary to achieve the purpose of creating a uniform plan for the development and operation of the condominium project.

We hold there is no evidence to support the jury’s conclusion that the assessment of the fee and later prohibition against the use of outside rental agents was arbitrary, capricious, and discriminatory.

new.notes: Beach-condo (Port Aransas) rental-pool dispute; owner held investment units through a family limited partnership and used an outside leasing agent instead of the condo's rent pool. Court recognizes letting as an incident of ownership but sustains private (HOA-level) regulation restricting how that letting may occur; exact rental duration (nightly/weekly) not stated in excerpt.

new.holding_summary: The court upheld a city zoning ordinance barring 'correctional or rehabilitation facilities'—including a religious ministry's homes for parolees and probationers—within 1000 feet of residential areas, schools, parks, and churches, holding the ordinance was a valid, generally applicable exercise of the city's police power that did not violate the operator's free-exercise, free-speech, assembly, equal-protection rights, or the Texas Religious Freedom Act.

quotes.text: The purpose of the legislation was not to stifle speech but rather to protect the public by regulating the location of correctional and rehabilitation facilities.
We conclude Pastor Barr’s religious rights were not substantially burdened by the City ordinance. Therefore, the Religious Freedom Act has not been violated.

new.holding_summary: A school-master's claim against a deceased ward's estate for the pupils' board and lodging is prescribed after one year, the same as an inn-keeper's claim for board and lodging, because by taking persons to board for hire the school-master assimilated himself to an inn-keeper for purposes of the prescription statute.

quotes.text: The claim of one whose occupation is that of a-school-master, for the hoard and lodging Of pupils, is prescribed by one year, under art. 3403 of the Civil Code.
By taking persons to board with him for hire, Roberts assimilated himself to an inn-keeper.

new.court: Superior Court of the Territory of Orleans
new.holding_summary: The court held that the corporation of New Orleans, through rights inherited from the Spanish cabildo and confirmed by its 1805 charter, had authority to license and receive taxes on taverns, billiard-tables, and boarding-houses. It further held the city could require an applicant who in fact applied for and accepted a license covering all three cumulated objects to pay for the cumulated license, absent proof he had sought a license for a single object only.

quotes.text: I feel no difficulty, therefore in saying that the city may exact the tax from every tavern, billiard-table and boarding-house.

new.holding_summary: New York's lien law gives keepers of hotels, boarding houses, and lodging houses a statutory lien on a boarder's or lodger's property for proper charges due for accommodation, board, and lodging. Because the respondent failed to prove that the $600 owed to her by the decedent was specifically for board and lodging charges rather than some other debt, the court held she had no valid lien and ordered the decedent's property turned over to the estate's administrator.

quotes.text: Q. Mr. Stiens had been a lodger and boarder of yours for some time previous to his death? A. Tes, sir; ever since coming to Utica.

A keeper of a hotel, inn, boarding house or lodging house, except an emigrant lodging house, has a lien upon, while in possession, and may detain the baggage and other property brought upon their premises by a guest, boarder or lodger for the proper charges due from him, on account of his accommodation, board and lodging, and such extras as are furnished at his request.

The evidence in the case does not bring respondent within the requirements of the provisions of section 71 of the lien law, essential to a valid lien in her favor as a boarding house or lodging house keeper.

new.notes: Duration of the lodging relationship given only as 'ever since coming to Utica,' with no specific length stated.

new.holding_summary: A woman who resided in a hotel annex for seventeen months, moved substantial personal property including a piano into her rooms, and dealt directly with the proprietors rather than hotel staff was not a transient 'guest' for purposes of the innkeeper's strict insurer liability, even though no fixed lodging term was ever agreed and she changed rooms several times. Because the relationship of innkeeper and guest did not exist, her complaint for loss of property was dismissed.

quotes.text: who had lived for 17 months in an inn which accommodated both transient and permanent lodgers

A woman, who had lived for 17 months in an inn which accommodated both transient and permanent lodgers, and had moved property into her rooms, which indicated an intention to make more than a temporary sojourn, and had made the arrangements for her stay with the proprietors themselves, instead of the clerk, was not a traveler and guest, within the rule which makes an innkeeper an insurer of the property of his guest, although, when she first went to the inn, she contemplated housekeeping, and never made any agreement for lodging for a definite time, and had frequently changed her apartments during her stay at the inn.

new.notes: Bears centrally on duration-of-occupancy doctrine (transient guest vs. permanent lodger) rather than on the favorable/adverse letting question directly; marked mixed.
Restrictive-covenant dispute over building-line/first-class-dwelling requirements; a boarding house is mentioned only once, in passing, as evidence of neighborhood commercial change.

new.holding_summary: An undelivered memorandum in which a decedent stated he owed his wife for seventeen years of 'home keep' did not create an enforceable claim against his estate, because it was never delivered and no contract or consideration was shown. The marital relationship raised a presumption that the board and lodging she furnished him in the boarding house she operated were gratuitous, not for hire.

quotes.text: It was shown that, prior to the marriage of the decedent, the claimant was carrying on the business of keeping a boarding-house, and the decedent was one of her boarders. Subsequent to the marriage, the claimant continued to keep' boarders, in a house owned and furnished by her, for nearly the entire seventeen years of her married life, and the business was only interrupted for a few years during which she rented part of her house in furnished rooms.

It was shown that, prior to the marriage of the decedent, the claimant was carrying on the business of keeping a boarding-house, and the decedent was one of her boarders. Subsequent to the marriage, the claimant continued to keep' boarders, in a house owned and furnished by her, for nearly the entire seventeen years of her married life, and the business was only interrupted for a few years during which she rented part of her house in furnished rooms.
The relation of the parties repels any presumption of a promise to pay for food and lodging furnished, and requires a presumption that such food and lodging were gratuitous.

new.notes: Parallel report (Mills Surr.) of the same underlying dispute as case_id 7701664 (70 N.Y.S. 426); recorded as a separate case per batch instructions. Same duration caveat applies.
Murder appeal; sole reference is that the defendant 'went to boarding with his brother' after a marital estrangement, a passing biographical detail with no bearing on lodging doctrine.
Cigar-sale-to-minor prosecution; the boy's mother 'kept a boarding house' is a passing background fact, not a lodging-law issue.
Restrictive-covenant dispute between adjoining lot owners over a private-first-class-residence covenant; no boarding, lodging, or letting issue in the case.
Municipal lateral-support-of-streets/highway law case involving excavation adjacent to a public street; unrelated to lodging or letting.

Police-power licensing case, but the subject is public dancing academies, not lodging or boarding houses; outside corpus scope despite structural similarity to boarding-house licensing cases (statute struck down as arbitrary discrimination).
Riparian rights/erosion and railroad right-of-way condemnation dispute; unrelated to lodging or letting of dwellings.
Zoning setback-line dispute over an enclosed porch; no letting, lodging, or boarding of any kind at issue.
Zoning side-yard/lot-area requirements for one- and two-family dwellings; no compensated occupancy or lodging issue.

Landlord-tenant possession-proceeding jurisdiction case; the 'license/occupation for indeterminate time' at issue is a divorced wife's continued occupancy of the marital home, not a paid lodging/letting arrangement. Doctrinal license-vs-lease language present but no compensated-occupancy facts.
Retail liquor license refusal tied to a 'place of amusement' in the same building; no dwelling-letting or lodging issue.
Ground-rent grantee liability under Act of 1878; purely a real-covenant/retroactivity question, no occupancy-for-pay facts.
Will construction: devise of a house 'for a home' to a life-tenant couple is not conditioned on personal occupancy. No compensated letting or lodging at issue.
Trespass between cotenants over possession of inherited land; occupant held by permission of other cotenants, not as a paying lodger/tenant of a stranger.
Landlord's distress against a commercial store tenant's commission goods; a business-premises lease, not residential lodging.
Lease of vacant-lot space for billboards; no dwelling or lodging occupancy.
Dispute over an agreement for a lease and rent liability for what appears to be industrial/commercial premises; no lodging facts.
Parol contract to split a government damages/rent claim for a farm tenancy disrupted by an army camp; not about letting rooms for pay.
Ordinary month-to-month tenancy/notice-to-quit dispute over leased premises; no facts identifying the property as a lodging arrangement or the letter as a householder.

Retail liquor license case turning on whether the 1856 act's hotel-accommodation requirement (bedrooms/beds for travelers) survives the 1887 licensing act; mentions traveler lodging only as a statutory-repeal question, not a holding on letting/regulation of lodging houses.

Employee occupied a room as part of wages, not as a paying lodger/boarder; wrongful-eviction/trespass claim after discharge. Occupancy was compensation-in-kind for labor, not a householder letting rooms for pay.
Borough building-construction permit ordinance struck down as unreasonable; unrelated to lodging or letting.
Summary conviction for renting an opera house for an immoral exhibition; regulation of entertainment venues, not dwelling/lodging letting.
Easement/right-of-way survival through sheriff's deed and mortgage foreclosure; no letting or lodging issue.
Trade-fixture removal rights of a commercial/industrial tenant (gas engine, dynamos) after lease expiration and holdover; unrelated to residential lodging.

Commercial parol lease of land to liquor dealers for bottling/storage business (tenancy at will) and eminent-domain condemnation by a railroad; no dwelling, lodging, or boarding-house occupancy at issue.
Dispute between commercial landlord and business tenants over removal of trade fixtures at lease renewal; no residential letting or lodging/boarding issue.
Easement/right-of-way dispute over an alley and a theater fire escape; no compensated occupancy of a dwelling at issue.

Will-construction dispute over which relative has first option to occupy the testator's house for an indefinite/life term at a nominal fixed rental plus carrying charges; a testamentary family arrangement, not a market letting of rooms/lodging and not short-term.
Dispute between a mortgagee-purchaser and a lessee over ownership of an amusement-park scenic railway as a trade fixture; no dwelling/lodging occupancy.
Dispute over possession of a public market stall held under a municipal license; commercial vendor space, not a dwelling or lodging arrangement.
Deed construction of an easement/right to build over an alley; no occupancy-for-pay issue.
Commercial lease forfeiture-for-nonpayment procedure (place of rent demand); tenant is a business (A. G. Spalding & Bros.), not a residential lodger/boarder.

Foreign-attachment jurisdiction turning on the meaning of 'residence' vs. 'domicil' for an ambassador; discusses residence generally but not compensated occupancy of another's dwelling or lodging/boarding practice.
Constitutional challenge to the state moving-picture censorship statute as an exercise of the police power; unrelated to lodging or dwelling occupancy.

Landlord-tenant dispute over rent-acceleration and distress on an assigned commercial lease of an entire hotel (Hotel Vannear) to a business operator; the case addresses lease-assignment/rent covenants only and does not discuss the character or regulation of guest occupancy within the hotel, so it is only a passing mention of a hotel.

new.holding_summary: A deed restriction limiting land use to a 'private dwelling house' is violated by an apartment house with a common entrance, hall, and stairway, because the word 'private' excludes buildings used for residential purposes of a public character, such as hotels and general public boarding or apartment houses, as distinguished from a building for the sole and exclusive occupancy of one family.

quotes.text: there is a well defined difference between an apartment house, operated by the owner for profit through leasing different stories or suites of rooms, and a dwelling intended and calculated to be for the sole and exclusive occupancy of one family, suitably constructed for that purpose.
The word “private” further restricts the buildings by excluding all such as are used for residential purposes of a public character, like hotels and general public boarding or apartment houses.
The restriction in this deed prohibits the erection of an apartment house.

new.notes: Restrictive-covenant case classifying multi-family/boarding rental buildings as distinct from and excluded from 'private dwelling' use; relevant to the doctrinal line between ordinary household occupancy and public/commercial letting, though the letting here is by a commercial owner-operator, not a householder.

Constitutional zoning case striking down a building set-back-line ordinance as an unreasonable exercise of the police power; concerns yard/setback space, not the letting or regulation of lodging/boarding occupancy.

new.holding_summary: Construing a deed restriction that permitted 'houses' but barred use as a 'hotel or tavern' or for any purpose 'offensive' to neighboring owners, the court held an apartment house is not a hotel and is not barred: a hotel is a building held out to the public where transient persons are received and entertained as guests for compensation, whereas an apartment house is a dwelling for several families, each living separate and apart, occupied under long-term leases, and its erection was therefore permitted.

quotes.text: A hotel is a building held out to the public as a place where all transient persons who come will be received and entertained as guests for compensation, 32 C. J. 527.
an apartment house is not a hotel, but is a building used as a dwelling for several families, each living separate and apart.

We hold the language “a building for any other purpose offensive to the owners or occupiers of other properties” is not sufficiently clear, explicit or definite in use or reference to restrict the use permitted under clause “(a)” on the word “houses” which concedes the right to erect an apartment house.

new.notes: Favors treating multi-family rental housing as an ordinary, non-offensive use distinct from transient innkeeping, while simultaneously drawing a sharp adverse-leaning line that hotel/innkeeping-for-transients is a different, prohibitable category; marked mixed for that reason. Letting here is long-term apartment tenancy by a commercial building owner, not short-term householder lodging.
Zoning appeal over a garage set-back permit under the Pittsburgh zoning ordinance; no lodging or boarding-house issue.
Commercial store/basement lease dispute over rights to an outer wall and sidewalk for a lunch stand; no residential lodging or boarding occupancy.

new.court: Union County Court of Quarter Sessions
new.notes: Sunday blue-law prosecution for selling ice cream at a shop; discusses 'lodging-houses' and 'inns' only as part of a statutory list of exempted premises, not the character or regulation of letting rooms to lodgers/boarders.

new.court: Erie County Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Party-wall/adverse-possession trespass dispute between adjoining building owners; no dwelling occupancy or lodging issue.

new.court: Lehigh County Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Dispute over borough building-line ordinance, street widening, and eminent domain compensation; no compensated occupancy of a dwelling/rooms or its regulation is at issue.

Elderly relative occupied a house her nephew purchased out of family kindness; court found no implied contract to pay rent. Not a lodger/boarder arrangement, letting for pay, or regulation of letting; purely an intra-family gratuitous occupancy dispute over an estate claim.
Concerns validity of a borough ordinance restricting bill-boards on private property; no bearing on compensated occupancy of dwellings/rooms or lodging regulation.

new.court: Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Dispute over a restaurant occupant's right to a stall/space in a city-owned market-house; occupancy is of commercial market space, not a dwelling or rooms, so it does not bear on residential letting or its regulation despite discussing license-vs-tenancy status.

new.notes: Landlord-tenant covenant dispute over an entire hotel property being handed over wholesale by the lessee to an employee (breach of covenant against subletting) and a penalty-vs-liquidated-damages question; concerns transfer of an entire commercial hotel business between operators, not compensated occupancy of rooms by lodgers/boarders or its regulation.

new.court: Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Routine apartment-house landlord-tenant dispute over the landlord's covenant to enforce quiet-enjoyment rules against a noisy neighboring tenant, resulting in constructive eviction; does not address the legal character of letting or its regulation, only breach of a quiet-enjoyment covenant.
Ground-rent extinguishment and estoppel case; no compensated dwelling occupancy or letting-regulation issue.

Public Service Commission rate-regulation dispute between a bridge company and a street-railway company over lease rental for track space on a bridge; wholly a utility-ratemaking matter, not residential letting.
Mineral/timber reservation deed-construction case; no dwelling occupancy or letting issue.

Building-restriction case about whether a new multi-story porch violates a deed covenant on setback lines; concerns architectural covenant enforcement, not compensated occupancy or letting of rooms/dwellings.
Mining-subsidence/water-supply damages case; no letting or occupancy-for-pay issue.

Building-restriction case enjoining construction of a theatre in violation of a 'dwelling houses only' covenant; concerns building type/use classification for a theatre, not compensated occupancy of rooms/dwellings by lodgers or boarders.

Affidavit-of-defense sufficiency question in an assumpsit action; the underlying facts involve a wife's continued occupancy of her family's former home after mortgage foreclosure, with a set-off claim for reasonable use-and-occupation value — not a householder letting rooms/dwellings to lodgers or boarding-house regulation.
Partition/ejectment dispute among cotenant heirs turning on estoppel and adverse possession; mesne-profits figure is incidental to a title dispute, not a letting or lodging arrangement.
Borough hawker/peddler licensing ordinance applied to door-to-door meat sales; regulates itinerant selling of goods, not lodging/boarding of occupants.
Replevin action over a landlord's illegal distress (picking a lock to seize a tenant's goods); a distress-procedure case, not about the legal character of letting or its regulation.

Wrongful-distress damages action under the Act of 1772 for seizure of a tenant's horse when no rent was actually due; a distress/damages procedure dispute unrelated to letting characterization or its regulation.
Prostitution-procurement prosecution; boarding/rooming houses mentioned only as incidental waypoints in witness travel testimony, not at issue.
Timber-sale and mill-improvement removal-rights dispute; license/property-affixed-to-land discussion concerns sawmill fixtures, not dwelling occupancy.
Gambling-house/vagrancy statutory-repeal case; defendant's rented family residence used for gaming, not compensated lodging.
