In Kieffer v. Keough (Tex. Civ. App.) 188 S. W. 44, the Galveston Court gives an extended review of the authorities, showing the modern trend of decision to abrogate the early common-law distinction between a guest and a boarder.

new.notes: Doctrinally on-point for lodger/boarder characterization in a commercial hotel setting, but the holding reduces (not enforces) protections for the occupant, so it does not cleanly fit the favorable/adverse polarity as defined for the corpus; coded mixed.
Habeas challenge to statute criminalizing nighttime removal of a 'laborer or tenant' from a plantation; concerns agricultural tenancy/labor mobility, not room/dwelling lodging.
Venue/plea-of-privilege dispute over defendant's 'residence' vs 'transient' status; mention of renting a furnished house/apartment is background to a domicile analysis only.
Municipal ordinance licensing/locating tent shows and carnivals; police-power zoning analysis, unrelated to dwelling lodging or boarding houses.

Dispute between lessees over advertising-sign rights in a shared hallway (theater vs. 'Page Hotel' apartments upstairs); a leasehold/easement fixture case, not about the character or regulation of the lodging use itself.
Zoning ordinance restricting private meat markets near a city market house; no connection to residential lodging or boarding houses.
Homestead-exemption dispute over crops raised under a farm cropping/leasing arrangement; the landlord/tenant analysis concerns agricultural land, not room or dwelling lodging.

Injunction over a private-garage setback ordinance violation; defendant's property is described in passing as a 'boarding and rooming house,' but the dispute concerns garage placement, not the lodging use or its regulation.
Ordinance restricting motion-picture theaters in residence districts, struck down as an unconstrained delegation of discretion; unrelated to lodging or boarding houses.

new.holding_summary: The Court of Civil Appeals held that an automobile tourist camp is not a nuisance per se, that a landowner has the right to use his property for such a lawful business so long as it does not impair the use others make of their own property, and that a petition alleging only anticipated noise, odors, and unsightliness was insufficient, absent facts showing a nuisance would inevitably result, to enjoin construction of the camp buildings in a residence district.

quotes.text: Automobile tourist camp in city or town is not a nuisance as a matter of law.
Owner of land has right to the use of his property so long as such use does not impair or destroy the use of others in their property.

It cannot be held as a matter of law that a camp for the use of travelers by automobile is a nuisance. The use of land for the purpose of a camp in a city or town is a lawful use, and may be exercised without thereby creating a nuisance.

new.notes: Analogous short-term-lodging authority: court protects a commercial operator's right to house transient travelers overnight against a neighbor's attempt to enjoin the business as a nuisance in a residential district.

Physician-licensing 'residence' registration prosecution; the fact that defendant rented furnished rooms from a householder is used only to establish domicile for the registration statute, not to characterize the lodging arrangement itself.

Sheriff-liability/homestead-abandonment case; owner rented out an entire former-residence house on his lot for continuous income over two years — a long-term whole-house tenancy for homestead-exemption purposes, not short-term room lodging or boarding-house regulation.
Murder appeal; defendant's flight to a friend's 'lodging house' after the killing is mentioned only in an evidentiary-error analysis, not at issue as a lodging arrangement.
Ordinance defining and abating public dance halls in residence districts as nuisances; entertainment-venue police-power case, not lodging.
Conversion suit turning on whether a landlord's lien for farm supplies attached to cotton crops; agricultural share-cropping/landlord-tenant dispute unrelated to dwelling lodging.

new.holding_summary: Stockholders who furnished supplies to a corporation's farm tenants were not entitled to a landlord's lien because the lien benefits only the landlord (the corporation itself); a prior-recorded crop mortgage with a general description was upheld as valid against a later mortgagee.
new.notes: Landlord's lien priority and crop-mortgage description dispute on farm rental land; no dwelling/room letting issue.

new.holding_summary: A homestead purchased by a married minor for himself and his family was a 'necessary' for which he was liable, and the trial court's definition of necessaries was not erroneous for failing to separately address renting versus buying or a speculative purpose.
new.notes: Necessaries-doctrine case for a minor's home purchase; mentions renting the house out and a precedent about a rooming-house leasehold only in passing, not as an adjudicated letting issue.

new.holding_summary: A landlord who did not participate in her co-defendants' unauthorized entry onto leased farmland was entitled to be sued in her home county rather than the county of the trespass, and the wrongful-dispossession damages charge was remanded for error.
new.notes: Venue and damages dispute over wrongful dispossession of a farm lessee; agricultural land, not dwelling/room letting.

new.holding_summary: An 18-year-old who entered a company's employee shower bath house without permission for his own pleasure was at most a bare licensee owed no duty to keep the premises safe, so a directed verdict for the company was proper.
new.notes: Attractive-nuisance/licensee premises-liability case at an employer's bath house; unrelated to dwelling or room letting.

new.holding_summary: A lessor who sold leased commercial property (a horse/mule barn) before the lease term ended was individually liable, under the lease's own terms, to repay the tenants' rent deposit to the tenants' assignee, notwithstanding the tenants' failure to formally surrender possession within 90 days.
new.notes: Commercial-building lease deposit dispute; not dwelling/room letting by a householder.

new.holding_summary: Commercial lessees forfeited their building lease under the anti-subletting statute by letting sub-tenants occupy part of the premises with their consent, even though the arrangement was accommodative, uncompensated, and conditioned on the landlord's approval.
new.notes: Subletting-forfeiture dispute over commercial office space; not dwelling/room letting.

new.holding_summary: A brewing company's threat not to renew saloon leases unless tenants stopped selling a competitor's beer was a lawful exercise of its rights as landlord over its own leased premises and did not violate the antitrust laws or common law.
new.notes: Antitrust/boycott dispute over saloon lease restrictions; commercial leasing, not dwelling/room letting.

new.holding_summary: Where co-owners' oil and gas lease used language implying fee ownership, title to an undivided interest later acquired by the lessor from her children passed by estoppel to the lessee, validating the lease as to that interest.
new.notes: After-acquired-title estoppel dispute over an oil and gas mineral lease; unrelated to dwelling/room letting.

new.holding_summary: A Dallas ordinance confining bawdy houses to a designated district was upheld as a valid exercise of the police power that neither conflicted with the state's criminal prohibition on bawdy houses nor unconstitutionally damaged nearby property without compensation.
new.notes: Concerns municipal zoning/confinement of bawdy (prostitution) houses under the police power, a distinct vice-regulation category from licensing of ordinary lodging or boarding houses; outside the corpus's short-term letting scope.

new.holding_summary: An employee of a commissary the railroad permitted to operate on its depot grounds was more than a bare licensee while on the grounds for purposes connected to his employment, so a general demurrer to his wrongful-death suit was improperly sustained.
new.notes: Invitee/licensee premises-liability case at a railroad depot commissary; unrelated to dwelling/room letting.

new.holding_summary: A statute criminalizing unauthorized resale of railroad tickets was held unconstitutional because it left it optional with each railroad company, via the notice printed on a ticket, whether resale of that ticket was penal—an unlawful delegation of legislative power.
new.notes: Railroad-ticket scalping statute case; the 'incident of ownership' language matched by the selector concerns ticket property rights, not dwelling letting.

new.holding_summary: A city ordinance confining tenpin (bowling) alleys to a remote, impractical location was an unreasonable exercise of the regulatory power because it effectively prohibited rather than merely regulated the business, and was therefore void.
new.notes: Municipal regulation of tenpin-alley location; unrelated to dwelling or room letting.

new.holding_summary: A conviction for keeping a disorderly house was reversed because the evidence showed only that the defendant occupied one room by sufferance and exercised some supervision, not that she was the owner, lessee, or tenant of the house as the statute requires.
new.notes: Concerns criminal liability for keeping a disorderly (prostitution) house and the owner/lessee/tenant element of that offense, not licensing of lodging/boarding houses or ordinary compensated occupancy.

new.holding_summary: A city ordinance establishing a hack stand near a train depot was a reasonable exercise of the police power, but the provision requiring only hack and omnibus drivers (not street-car conductors) to remain with their vehicles while soliciting patronage was an unlawful discrimination rendering the ordinance void.
new.notes: Municipal regulation of hack/omnibus stands and solicitation at a depot; unrelated to dwelling/room letting.

new.holding_summary: In a murder prosecution arising from resistance to an officer re-executing a writ of possession on leased farmland, the court held the writ was not functus officio and remanded for charge error regarding when a coconspirator's declarations could be considered.
new.notes: Murder/conspiracy case arising from a farmland-eviction dispute; agricultural tenancy, not dwelling/room letting.

new.holding_summary: The private-residence exception to the gaming statute for an ordinary head-to-head dice game does not extend to an exhibitor operating a banking (table) game, so a defendant who ran a craps bank at his residence was properly convicted of exhibiting a banking game.
new.notes: Gaming-statute prosecution turning on a private-residence exception for dice games; unrelated to dwelling letting for pay.

new.holding_summary: A dugout used only occasionally for cooking, sleeping, or as a storm shelter in connection with a private residence was nonetheless an 'outhouse' within the gaming statute, so a conviction for playing cards there was upheld.
new.notes: Gaming-statute case about whether a dugout counted as an outhouse versus part of a private residence; unrelated to dwelling/room letting for pay.
Partition-by-private-sale statute for absentee co-owners; no letting/lodging of dwellings at issue.
Jurisdiction/venue dispute over batture-land expropriation for levee purposes; no compensated occupancy of a dwelling at issue.
Personal-injury/premises-liability case about invitee vs. licensee status of a business visitor at a bottling plant; no dwelling letting involved.
Tenant-vs-landlord repair-duty case (defective gallery plank); plaintiff's rooming-house business mentioned only to compute lost income, not adjudicated as to its legal character or lawfulness.
Party-wall window/servitude dispute under zoning ordinance; no compensated occupancy of dwellings involved.
Zoning-ordinance prosecution over a backyard horseshoe-pitching game in a residential district; no lodging/letting issue.
Commercial store lease dispute over rent diminution following levee/street reconstruction; no dwelling letting or lodging involved.
Ordinance regulating uninvited door-to-door solicitors/peddlers, upheld as police-power measure protecting the home; not about letting or lodging of dwellings.
Possessory action between family members over a store/residence building following a purported lease to a stepson; no compensated-occupancy characterization at issue.
Boundary-fixing action holding a farm lessee is not a necessary/proper party; no dwelling lodging or letting involved.

Movable-vs-immovable classification dispute over air conditioners/outbuildings on a sold home; only a passing treatise quote mentions a house 'leased furnished,' with no bearing on the character or regulation of compensated occupancy.
Zoning special-permit dispute over construction of a Knights of Columbus fraternal 'lodge hall'; this is a private-club meeting hall, not a lodging house for paying occupants.
Plaintiff resided with her mother as an unpaid family guest (invitee) after losing her own home; no compensation for occupancy, so not a letting/lodging arrangement.
Mandamus action over a permit to erect a gasoline filling station on nonconforming-use commercial land; no dwelling letting or lodging involved.
Tort suit over a footbridge collapse during a paid tour of a historic plantation house; a museum-style day visitation attraction, not overnight lodging/letting of a dwelling.
Verbal farm/rice-crop lease dispute between landowner and tenant farmer; agricultural land lease, not dwelling/lodging occupancy.

Premises-liability tort case turning on licensee-vs-invitee status of a warehouse worker unloading crackers; the licensee/invitee terminology is a general tort concept, not lodging-related. No occupancy of a dwelling for pay is at issue.
Zoning nonconforming-use dispute over an ice cream store, liquor store, and refrigerator building added to a grocery; no lodging or boarding house is at issue.

A separately-leased 'cafe and tourist court' is mentioned as backdrop, but the dispute concerns rent-deduction for repair costs between lessor and commercial lessee under civil code lease law; guest occupancy of the tourist court is never addressed.
Zoning rezoning dispute for a neighborhood shopping center (supermarket, drug store, laundry, barber shop); no lodging or boarding house at issue.

new.holding_summary: The City of New Orleans sought to enjoin the owner from using his property as a multiple dwelling or 'rooming house' in a zoned two-family residential district. The court affirmed the injunction because the evidence showed the rooming-house use began around 1933, after the 1929 zoning ordinance's effective date, so no lawful nonconforming use had ever been acquired.

quotes.text: which, prior to the judgment rendered herein, was occupied and used as a multiple dwelling or “rooming house” and that the use thereof, as such, is prohibited by virtue of an appropriate zoning ordinance adopted by the City of New Orleans.

We have made á careful analysis of the record and we are of the opinion that an abundance of evidence is contained therein revealing that the property never acquired a legal non-conforming status and there now exists a glaring violation of the ordinance which unequivocally created a prima facie case in support of the issuance of the preliminary writ of injunction by the trial judge.

quotes.text: They also remain decontrolled and not subject to rent control where the letting is of nonhousekeeping, furnished housing accommodation, located within a single-dwelling unit not used as a rooming or boarding house, provided not more than two tenants pay rent and live in such dwelling unit, and the remaining portion of such dwelling unit is occupied by the landlord or his immediate family.

The landlord respondent having rented part of the dwelling unit for housekeeping purposes, the housing accommodation was occupied for other than single-family occupancy and the exemption from control terminated.
The final order should be reversed, with $30 costs, and final order awarded the tenant dismissing the petition on the merits, with costs.

new.notes: General rule recognizing owner letting of up to two paying lodgers while occupying the remainder is favorable framework; specific application here found the exemption forfeited, hence mixed polarity.
Overcharge dispute about whether a separately-leased private storage room was part of the tenant's 'housing accommodation' essential services; no lodging/boarding issue.

new.holding_summary: The court rejected constitutional challenges to the State and City rent laws' hotel-exclusion provisions, reaffirming (per Hotel Armstrong, Fabian Studios, Sylarn, and Noxon) that establishments not classified as hotels on and after March 1, 1950 are properly regulated as rooming houses and that the implementing regulations validly track the statutory standard.

quotes.text: the amendments are applicable to housing accommodations styled as hotels which do not satisfy the definition of hotels in the statute, even though such housing accommodations have not been subject to rent control since 1950, and even though such accommodations were once properly classified as hotels but have since deteriorated into something less
It appears that the regulations impose the identical standard as prescribed in the act and are in all respects valid.
the conclusion is inescapable that the court is concluded by the prior adjudications and the declarations as sought by the plaintiff are without merit.

new.holding_summary: The court sustained recontrol and denial of decontrol for a rooming house that had been converted to self-contained apartments, holding that decontrol required the conversion to have produced additional self-contained family units of minimum size completed before April 30, 1962, and that the landlord failed to prove timely completion, adequate unit size, or a net increase in legal housing units.

quotes.text: The premises here involved were a one-family house prior to 1947, and thereafter the property was converted into a rooming house.

No regulation or order of the city housing rent agency shall be enjoined or set aside, in whole or in part, unless the petitioner shall establish to the satisfaction of the court that the regulation or order is not in accordance with law, or is arbitrary or capricious.
Sufficient ground exists upon the record herein to support the order and it should not be disturbed.

The court found no triable fact issues and adjudged defendants guilty on all four counts of violating the Long Beach Municipal Code provisions governing rooming houses.

quotes.text: The Court believes also that the statute here under consideration represents a valid exercise of the City’s police powers and of its inherent right and obligation to protect the health, safety and welfare of its citizens.

In conclusion the court finds that the two ordinances here challenged represent valid and reasonable exercises of the legislative function with which this court has neither the right nor the desire to interfere.

A variance for the separate 'guest house,' whose paid rental use began only after the ordinance took effect, was properly denied as a self-imposed hardship.

quotes.text: Petitioners have continued to rent the gatehouse (unfurnished) and receive $145 monthly.
The only practical effect of barring the rental of the gatehouse is to deprive the owners of a beneficial use thereof while forcing them to demolish it or have it remain vacant.

We agree with the Appellate Division that petitioners have demonstrated practical difficulties in the way of carrying out the strict letter of the ordinance, and a variance should be granted in order that the spirit of the ordinance may be observed, public safety and welfare secured and substantial justice done.

new.holding_summary: The court held that plaintiffs' proposed use of their property as a convalescent home for recuperating patients did not violate the village's residential zoning ordinance, which expressly permits 'hotels, rooming or boarding houses' as of right, because a convalescent home differs only slightly from an ordinary boarding house even with attendant nursing care. Declaratory and injunctive relief were granted in plaintiffs' favor.

quotes.text: In the subdivision of the Village of Lancaster known as and designated as Zone 1 A ’, or Residence District, no building or premises shall be used and no building shall lie erected, constructed, altered or used for any purpose other than that of one or two family dwelling houses, or multiple or apartment houses; and hotels, rooming or boarding houses, churches, schools, club houses and private garages, green houses, nurseries or other building accessory to such private dwellings.
They differ in a very small degree from ordinary boarders.
I find the plaintiffs are entitled to a declaratory judgment in accordance with this opinion and the injunctive relief is hereby granted.

new.notes: Zoning ordinance affirmatively lists boarding houses alongside dwellings as a permitted residential use, and the court treats lodging/boarding for hire as an ordinary, non-nuisance use analogous to the plaintiffs' convalescent home.

new.holding_summary: Defendant leased an entire rooming house, furnished the rooms/apartments herself, and sublet them at a profit; the court held the landlord's cancellation of the master lease was ineffective and, independently, that federal rent control barred eviction because defendant's furnished sublettings are 'housing accommodations' including 'rooming- or boarding-house accommodations' protected under the Act.

quotes.text: Section 202, subdivision (b), of said act defines the term “ housing accommodations ” so as to include “ real or personal property rented or offered for rent for living or dwelling purposes (including houses, apartments, rooming- or boarding-house accommodations, and other properties used for living or dwelling purposes) together with all privileges, services, furnishings, furniture, and facilities connected with the use or occupancy of such property.” This includes the defendant in this action, who furnished these rooms and apartments and rented them in a furnished condition.

Section 202, subdivision (b), of said act defines the term “ housing accommodations ” so as to include “ real or personal property rented or offered for rent for living or dwelling purposes (including houses, apartments, rooming- or boarding-house accommodations, and other properties used for living or dwelling purposes) together with all privileges, services, furnishings, furniture, and facilities connected with the use or occupancy of such property.” This includes the defendant in this action, who furnished these rooms and apartments and rented them in a furnished condition.

It is the expressed intention of this law not to dispossess tenants in the situation of this defendant, who have equipped rooms and apartments with furniture and furnishings, and have sublet them as furnished accommodations.

quotes.text: In our view the evidence fully warranted a finding that the relationship between the parties was that of guest and innkeeper.
Plaintiff’s claim on this issue finds support in the weekly bills rendered by the appellant. They show a per diem, and not a charge prorated upon a monthly basis at the rate of $1,500 a month.
We are of opinion, therefore, that under the circumstances here presented the appellant was liable as an innkeeper for the loss of the plaintiff’s baggage.

new.notes: Doctrinally useful for the guest/boarder/duration distinction (citing Hancock v. Rand) even though the immediate holding concerns innkeeper baggage liability rather than letting legality itself.

new.holding_summary: A zoning ordinance permitted 'hotels, lodging and boarding houses' as of right in a business district; the Board of Appeals denied a permit to build a 12-unit motel citing insufficient lot size, but the court found no record support for that finding and ordered the permit issued, noting motels cannot be excluded from all areas of a municipality.

quotes.text: While motels, as such, may properly be excluded from certain areas of a community, they cannot be excluded from all areas.
My decision, however, must be made on the record presented and on the reasons given in the decision of the board. I find these reasons insufficient for a denial of petitioner’s application.

new.notes: Characterization left null: the court expressly declined to decide whether a 'motel' is a 'hotel' under the ordinance, so no lease/license/lodging/innkeeping classification is supported by quotable text.

quotes.text: Defendant’s contention that the moneys received from roomers should not be construed as rent but rather as compensation for personal services cannot be allowed. new.holding_summary: Neighboring property owners bound by a restrictive covenant limiting use to 'a private dwelling house' sued to enjoin defendants from running their home as a tourist house, renting rooms to the traveling public by the day or longer. The court held that renting rooms to transient guests for hire is not use as 'a private dwelling,' is instead akin to a hotel or public boarding house, and enjoined the practice notwithstanding some change in neighborhood character and toleration of a few other similar violations nearby.

quotes.text: Beginning in November 1940, defendants have conducted a tourist house on their premises, without altering the structure of the building thereon, and pursuant thereto have rented rooms to strangers by the day or for any longer period desired.

An invitation to the general traveling public to the facilities of the home for hire certainly deprives a residence of its designation as a ‘private residence’. It comes closer to being a hotel or public boarding house, both held by the Taylor ease to be in violation of such a restriction.

Joseph K. Crager and Mary E. Crager are hereby enjoined from conducting their premises, 5934 Roosevelt Boulevard, Philadelphia, Pa., as a tourist house and from using said premises for any purpose other than as a private dwelling.

new.holding_summary: Reviewing a borough ordinance requiring a license fee to keep inhabited house trailers on land, the court upheld the license as applied to landowners who rent space to trailers for profit as a commercial trailer camp, reasoning the camps impose extraordinary demands on police, fire, sanitation and other municipal services that justify a licensing fee under the police power. But the court struck the ordinance down as applied to a landowner who lived in his own trailer on his own land, holding that the right to occupy one's own home cannot be licensed absent a commercial use of the kind found in a boarding or rooming house.

quotes.text: Unquestionably, the right to have a home can be licensed only where conditions prevail which take the home out of the ordinary category, as for example where it is used for such commercial enterprise as a boarding or rooming house.
The right to live in a home is not a privilege which is subject to license; it is a human right.
But we see no constitutional objection to enforcement of this ordinance as a police measure against those who operate trailer camps for profit.
The effect of this ordinance as to appellant George is that the borough is licensing his right to establish his own home on his own land.

The court also held the rear-yard width requirement of the Housing and Sanitation Act was satisfied notwithstanding an uneven yard depth across the two conjoined buildings.

quotes.text: We therefore hold that the present use of the property as a store, seven housekeeping units and one non-housekeeping unit is a permissible expansion of nonconforming use rights, under section 4 of the Philadelphia Zoning Ordinance of 1933.

We therefore hold that the present use of the property as a store, seven housekeeping units and one non-housekeeping unit is a permissible expansion of nonconforming use rights, under section 4 of the Philadelphia Zoning Ordinance of 1933.

new.court: Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas
new.holding_summary: The court held that YMCA dormitory and food-service facilities, though occupied by paying residents (some 'transient' for under two weeks, most 'permanent' for two weeks or more), were tax-exempt because their actual use was primarily charitable rather than commercial lodging. The court distinguished the case from an earlier ruling taxing a YMCA's dormitory that competed with avowedly commercial lodging houses, finding no comparable competition, advertising, or profit here.

quotes.text: In neither the Salvation Army case nor the instant case was there any testimony of that character; in fact, the evidence shows that there was no advertising of the dormitory facilities in any of the five buildings here involved, and no complaints were heard from hotels or boarding houses that the dormitories were in competition with them.

In the former decision the court held that the part of the building occupied by dormitory facilities was primarily commercial in nature, competing with lodging houses which are avowedly commercial in character.
Having thus disposed of the problem of the dormitories and food service facilities, the incidental problem of bowling alleys, barber shops, and businessmen's health clubs is easily resolved.

The permanent classification included all those who occupied the rooms for two weeks or more and paid rent-on a weekly basis; transients being those whose occupancy was less than two weeks and who paid on a daily basis.

new.notes: A tax-exemption case, not a letting-rights or police-power-licensing case, but it extensively analyzes the line between charitable dormitory lodging and commercial lodging-house/hotel operation, including transient (nights-to-under-two-weeks) versus permanent (two-weeks-plus) occupancy classes -- both are present in the facts, weeks chosen as the predominant occupancy class since a majority of residents were permanent.

quotes.text: conducting, operating or maintaining for profit a commercial boarding home for the aged as defined in the Act of Assembly of September 26, 1951, P. L. 1536, sec. 2, 37 PS §172

The concern for the protection and safety of elderly persons is as much within the exercise of the police powers of the Commonwealth as is the regulation for the protection and welfare of guests in hotels, children in public schools, or patrons in restaurants and theatres, and the fact that such aged persons are ambulatory does not render their classification arbitrary or unreasonable.

quotes.text: In our opinion, the term “rooming house” in common parlance refers to a dwelling in which the owner rents out separate rooms to separate individuals primarily for sleeping purposes, whereas, an apartment house ordinarily means a building consisting of more than one dwelling unit, each of which units may be used by one or more persons as a general dwelling.

Adultery conviction reversed for insufficient evidence; that the co-defendant rented a tourist-camp cottage is one circumstantial fact among several, not a holding on letting.
Burglary appeal; a tourist camp is mentioned only in the defendant's alibi testimony about where an accomplice claimed to be staying.
Companion robbery appeal to Gillard v. State; offense occurred at a tourist camp/restaurant, mentioned only as crime-scene location.
Zoning appeal over a permit to build a gasoline filling station in a residential district; concerns police-power zoning of a filling station, not lodging or boarding houses.
Eminent-domain valuation case; the tourist camp on Mrs. Blair's homestead is only relevant to damages calculation, no bearing on lodging law or its regulation.
Search-warrant/liquor-possession appeal; the rented tourist-camp cabin is only the crime scene, no discussion of lodging arrangements or their regulation.
Robbery appeal; appellant merely slept at a tourist camp awaiting a signal, no legal issue touching lodging or its regulation.
Murder conspiracy appeal; no tourist camp or lodging facts appear in the opinion beyond retrieval noise; irrelevant.
Cotton-theft appeal; a planned overnight stay at a tourist camp is only an evidentiary detail on the conspiracy/accomplice issue, no bearing on lodging law.
Election-contest case; a voter's operation of a tourist camp is used only to assess her residency for voting purposes, not to address lodging law.

Breach-of-contract case over a month-to-month lease of a commercial warehouse building used by a grain company; not a dwelling/rooms letting or lodging/boarding matter despite month-to-month tenancy doctrine discussed.

Nuisance-abatement appeal over a gambling club ('Ringside Club'), not a hotel/boarding/rooming house; only interprets which houses the reputation-evidence statute reaches, no facts about compensated dwelling occupancy.
Robbery appeal; the tourist camp is merely where the proprietor was robbed while renting a cabin, appeal turns on jury-panel procedure, no lodging-law issue.
Venue/plea-of-privilege appeal in an assault suit; tourist camps are just the locations of the alleged assault, no lodging-law issue.
Child-desertion appeal; appellant's stay at an Oklahoma tourist camp is only evidence of his whereabouts, no lodging-law issue.
Trespass-to-try-title dispute over land underlying a tourist-cabin business; holding turns on lease-assignment priority against an unrecorded oral land sale, not on the character of guest lodging.
Rape appeal; a night spent by the prosecutrix at an Oklahoma tourist camp is newly-discovered-evidence fodder on her chastity, no lodging-law issue.
Suit against city for delayed road construction damaging a relocated tourist camp/filling station; dispute is about municipal contract/tort liability, not lodging regulation.

new.holding_summary: Residents of Henrietta sought mandamus to force the city council to reopen a hearing on a permit already issued to S. A. Donnell for a 'transit camp and filling station' in a residential district, arguing it was a fire hazard and would depreciate nearby property. The court held Donnell was a necessary party who had not been joined, and separately held that under the zoning ordinance the board of aldermen had discretion whether to call such a hearing, so mandamus would not lie absent a showing of abused discretion.

quotes.text: Plaintiffs allege that the transit camp' erected by Donnell will work injury and damage and incur fire hazard to plaintiffs and other citizens in the vicinity, and will decrease the value oí their property.

Certainly a mandamus could not be issued to force the board of aldermen to call a hearing where they were vested with a discretion in the first instance as to whether or not the hearing was advisable, unless allegations were made and supported by evidence, tending to show that the officer or officers against whom a mandamus is sought had been guilty of abuse of discretion.

new.notes: Marginal: the zoning ordinance frames a tourist/transit camp as a potential fire hazard/nuisance in a residential district (adverse-type regulatory posture), but the court reaches only procedural mandamus/necessary-party grounds and never characterizes the guest-occupancy arrangement itself, hence characterization left null.
Burglary appeal; appellant and a companion spending a night at a Mineral Wells tourist camp is only an accomplice-witness detail, no lodging-law issue.
Zoning-validity case, but the excluded use is a gasoline/oil filling station in an 'apartment district,' not lodging or boarding of paying occupants; no letting/lodging facts.

new.holding_summary: The city sued to enjoin Hattie Miller from operating two hotels, the Metropolitan Hotel and Grand Central Annex, on the ground that she knowingly permitted prostitutes to ply their trade there, a nuisance under the statutes governing hotels, boarding houses, and rooming houses (Arts. 4664-4667). The Court of Civil Appeals upheld admission of the hotels' general reputation as evidence of the nuisance but reversed because the judgment ordered the hotels closed outright for one year without including the statutory option letting the owner, tenant, or lessee keep them open by posting bond.

quotes.text: This suit as originally filed was brought by the city of Abilene and H. L. De Busk, a citizen of Taylor county, against Hattie Miller to enjoin the latter from operating two hotels in Abilene known as the “Metropolitan Hotel” and “Grand Central Annex.”

Has the defendant, Mrs. Hattie Miller, knowingly permitted prostitutes to remain in the two hotels in question and ply their trade therein? Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘No.’ ” To this question the jury answered, “Yes.”

The court is empowered to order the closing of such house for one year “unless the defendants in said suit or the owner, tenant or lessee of said property make bond payable to' the state at the county site of the county where such nuisance is alleged to exist, in the penal sum of not less than $1,-000.00 nor more than $5,000.00, with sufficient sureties to be approved by the judge trying the case, conditioned that the acts prohibited in this law shall not be done or permitted to be done in said house.”

new.notes: Squarely adverse: hotels regulated/enjoinable as nuisances under police power; characterization left null because the court never classifies the legal nature of any guest's occupancy, only the propriety of nuisance abatement against the operator.

Will contest over testamentary capacity; testator's having operated a rooming house is mentioned only as biographical background (part of her being a 'hard-working, industrious woman'), with no adjudication of any lodging/letting issue.

new.holding_summary: The Court of Civil Appeals held that a homeowner's temporary rental of a second house on his homestead lot to a tenant did not, as a matter of law, defeat the homestead exemption as to that house. An owner is entitled to a reasonable time after purchase to occupy the whole of a homestead lot, and temporary renting of part of it pending consolidation of the buildings does not conclusively show abandonment. Whether the renting was temporary (and thus consistent with continued homestead use) or evidenced a permanent commercial diversion was a fact question for the jury.

quotes.text: the smaller house, being at the time of the purchase rented, continued to be occupied by the tenant until the levy of attachment on March 14, 1927, some three months after the date of the purchase
Any temporary renting would not defeat the homestead right.
Any temporary renting would not defeat the homestead right.

new.notes: Concerns a full separate house rented to a tenant on part of a homestead lot, not room-letting to lodgers/boarders in an owner-occupied dwelling; included because the court treats temporary letting of part of one's property as an ordinary, non-disqualifying incident of ownership rather than abandonment or commercial diversion. Duration is approximate (at least ~3 months at time of levy; tenant's occupancy predated the purchase).

Tort case on scope-of-employment liability for an employee's assault; 'rooming house' appears only once, identifying where the injured brakeman intended to go after work, with no bearing on lodging law.
Zoning nonconforming-use case concerning automobile wrecking/salvage yards; no lodging, boarding, or dwelling-letting issue present.
Mineral deed construction dispute over royalty/bonus/rental fractions from an oil and gas lease; 'lease' here refers exclusively to a mineral lease, unrelated to dwelling occupancy.

Validity-of-spot-zoning case concerning rezoning a small tract to local retail; a 'tourist court' is mentioned only in passing as one existing use on nearby already-rezoned lots, with no adjudication of any lodging-related right or regulation.
Master-servant premises-liability case (employee slip-and-fall on spilled oil in a warehouse); the citation to Houston National Bank v. Adair concerns a stairway, not lodging.

Contempt proceeding over an alleged sham lease/sale between brothers used to evade a non-compete covenant in the wholesale gasoline business; the string citation to Owen v. Willis regarding restrictive covenants is incidental and unrelated to dwelling letting.
Contract dispute over a cigarette-supply agreement tied to the sale of corporate stock; 'incident to the ownership thereof' refers to stock ownership, not any dwelling or room-letting arrangement.
Mandamus action over the State's mineral royalty reservation and oil/gas leasing rights under public land sales acts; entirely a mineral-lease/royalty dispute, unrelated to dwelling occupancy.

Fraud/limitations dispute arising from the sale of a tourist court whose highway frontage title was misrepresented; the tourist court is only an incidental identifier of the property sold, and the holding concerns discovery of fraud and limitations, not any lodging-related right or regulation.
Mineral-deed/pooling case concerning whether production elsewhere in a unit extends a term mineral interest; no lodging or dwelling-letting issue.
Mineral deed construction dispute over the royalty fraction conveyed under future oil and gas leases; 'lease interest' refers to a mineral lease, not dwelling occupancy.
Mineral-deed construction dispute between two conflicting deeds over the fraction of minerals conveyed; unrelated to dwelling letting.

Suit to enforce a 'residence purposes only' restrictive covenant against a tract where churches had been built nearby; concerns waiver/changed-conditions doctrine as to church use, with no boarding-house or paying-lodger issue present.
Challenge to a zoning ordinance banning front-yard fences on police-power grounds (traffic safety, firefighting access, crime prevention); no lodging or boarding-house regulation involved.

The underlying dispute concerns a city's attempt to enjoin use of land as a 'trailer coach park' / 'mobile home residence area' under a zoning ordinance, but the only issue actually decided here is res judicata (whether a prior judgment bars the new suit); the case is reversed and remanded for trial on the merits without any holding on the legality or characterization of the trailer-park use. Also, a trailer/mobile-home park (renting parking spaces) is a distinct use-type from letting rooms or dwellings to lodgers/boarders, so even a merits holding here would only be loosely analogous.

Suit for damages from diversion of dedicated parkland to highway construction; 'tourist court units' are mentioned only as improvements the plaintiff purchased on the abutting property, with no adjudication of any lodging-related right or regulation.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fourth Circuit
new.holding_summary: The court affirmed denial of a preliminary injunction sought by neighborhood groups to stop a French Quarter property from continuing to operate as a transient-rental guest house/hotel, finding no manifest error in crediting affidavits that the hotel was never vacant for six continuous months and that no completed structural changes disqualified its nonconforming-use status. The court preserved the operator's ability to continue short-term transient rental use while reaffirming that nonconforming uses are construed narrowly against continuation.

quotes.text: Appellees and their predecessors in right have operated 517 Dumaine as a hotel since before the enactment of the Comprehensive Zoning Act in 1982.

it should, consistently with the property rights of the individuals affected and substantial justice, be viewed narrowly and have all doubts resolved against continuation or expansion of the nonconformity
Based on the foregoing reasons, the denial of Appellants’ motion for preliminary injunction is affirmed.

new.holding_summary: Dispute over whether a building-restriction violation (operating a trucking/vehicle-repair business from a residential lot) had prescribed; no lodging or dwelling-rental issue.
new.notes: Building-restriction/commercial-vehicle-use case; no compensated occupancy of a dwelling or lodging arrangement at issue.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Second Circuit
new.holding_summary: Dispute over a hunting-privileges lease, a right of first refusal, and co-ownership partition of rural land; no dwelling or lodging occupancy at issue.
new.notes: Hunting lease and land-partition dispute; unrelated to letting rooms/dwellings for compensated occupancy.

new.holding_summary: Wrongful-death case addressing employer vicarious liability and Recreational Use Immunity Statutes for a duck-hunting lease accident; no lodging or dwelling occupancy issue.
new.notes: Duck-hunting-lease tort case; addresses a lease of hunting rights (an incorporeal), not compensated dwelling/room occupancy.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, First Circuit
new.holding_summary: The court held that a homeowner's rental of the family residence to successive tenants at $200/month, occurring in eleven of fifteen months (including periods of "holding for rental" between tenants), was continuous rather than "occasional" rental for dwelling purposes, and thus fell within the homeowners policy's "business pursuits" exclusion. Coverage for tort liability arising from the property during that period was therefore denied.

quotes.text: The evidence of record shows that the Newmans either rented or held for rental the residence premises continuously, and not occasionally, from October of 1979 to December of 1980.

The trial judge determined that following the departure of the elder Newman from the property, it “was rented almost exclusively until the time of the loss ...” and found that the “business pursuits” exclusion was applicable.
Por the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the trial court is correct and is affirmed at the appellants’ costs.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fourth Circuit
new.holding_summary: Equitable reversal of denial of an alcoholic-beverage permit for a bar where a sublessee had falsely reported the business closed; concerns bar licensing continuity, not dwelling lodging.
new.notes: Alcoholic-beverage permit/nonconforming-use case for a bar; no dwelling or lodging occupancy issue.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fifth Circuit
new.holding_summary: Commercial office-space lease dispute over roof repairs and disturbance from an adjacent adult bookstore tenant; the lessee was found to have breached the lease by vacating without cause.
new.notes: Commercial office lease dispute; not residential lodging or dwelling occupancy.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Second Circuit
new.holding_summary: Eviction of the widow of a longtime employee who had occupied a residence by permission of the employer-landowner as an incident of employment; occupant status under eviction statute upheld.
new.notes: Occupancy was gratuitous employer-provided housing tied to employment, not compensated lodging for pay.

new.holding_summary: Answering certified questions, the court held that Civil Code article 2971's $100 cap on innkeeper liability limits only the innkeeper's contractual liability as depositary of a paying guest's effects, not the innkeeper's or its employees' delictual (tort) liability for negligence. A paying hotel guest whose property is stolen due to employee negligence may recover beyond the statutory cap.

quotes.text: An innkeeper is responsible as depositary for the effects brought by travelers who lodge at his house; the deposit of such effects is considered as a necessary deposit.
On or about May 22, 1976, the Laubies were paying guests at the Royal Sonesta Hotel, which at all material times was under the management and control of Sonesta.

Article 2971 of the Civil Code, as amended and reenacted by Act 231 of 1912, provides for a limitation of only the contractual liability of an innkeeper as depositary. It does not diminish the delictual responsibility of the innkeeper, his officers of his employees.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Third Circuit
new.holding_summary: Mandamus ordering issuance of a beer and liquor permit for a bar/lounge as a preexisting nonconforming use after rezoning; no dwelling/lodging occupancy issue.
new.notes: Bar/liquor-permit zoning case; unrelated to lodging or dwelling letting.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, First Circuit
new.holding_summary: The court held that although numerous homeowners in a restricted subdivision had rented rooms or garage apartments to unrelated tenants in violation of covenants limiting lots to single-family use, these violations were not sufficiently frequent, substantial, or widely known to establish abandonment of the restrictions. Conversion of accessory living quarters to rental use was treated as a violation of the single-family restriction, which remained enforceable against a proposed apartment complex.

quotes.text: a restriction against the erection of a particular type of building is construed as prohibiting the conversion to that use
The owner of Lot 4 admitted to renting rooms but not apartments.

We have come to the conclusion that there has been insufficient violations of a substantial nature to evidence abandonment of the plan for the subdivision, a subversion of the original scheme of the sub-dividers.

new.notes: Duration of occupancy varies widely across the many lots surveyed (some multi-year, some single-season), so left unclear rather than forcing a single bucket.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fourth Circuit
new.holding_summary: Commercial restaurant sublease dispute over unpaid rent, indispensable parties, and repairs; possession alone found sufficient to let a thing.
new.notes: Commercial restaurant sublease case; not residential lodging.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, First Circuit
new.holding_summary: The court held that a motel had no duty to give a room key to the wife of its registered, month-to-month occupant where she was not herself registered and the husband had not authorized her admission, regardless of whether the occupant's relationship to the motel was lessor-lessee or motel-guest. The motel's affirmative duty to protect a paying occupant's privacy and peaceable possession from unauthorized third parties barred the claim, and summary judgment for the motel was affirmed.

quotes.text: In fact, the motel had an affirmative duty, stemming from a guest’s rights of privacy and peaceful possession, not to allow unregistered and unauthorized third parties to gain access to the rooms of its guest, (cf. LSA-C.C. art. 2965-67). This duty is the same regardless of whether we consider the contractual relationship one of lessor-lessee or motel-guest.
Mr. Campbell rented a double room on a month to month basis at the Rodeway Inn, in Morgan City, Louisiana.

Having found that Mrs. Campbell was not entitled to demand a key to the motel room, and further that no authorization to admit her was communicated to the motel by her husband, there was no breach of contract.

new.notes: Characterization left null: the court expressly declined to decide whether the paying occupant's relationship to the motel was lessor-lessee or motel-guest ('This duty is the same regardless...'), so no quote supports a definitive characterization.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, First Circuit
new.holding_summary: Zoning-ordinance dispute over placement of house trailers in a single-family residential district; a mobile home was found to violate the ordinance.
new.notes: The ordinance's definition of 'dwelling' excludes hotels/boardinghouses/lodginghouses, but this is incidental boilerplate in a mobile-home placement dispute, not an adjudicated lodging-house issue -- passing mention only.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, First Circuit
new.holding_summary: Nuisance suit under La. C.C. arts. 667-669 over polyvinyl chloride powder contaminating a neighboring residence from an industrial plant; injunction and damages affirmed.
new.notes: Industrial-nuisance case; no lodging or letting issue.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fourth Circuit
new.holding_summary: Post-foreclosure dispute over occupancy of and personal property in a commercial nursery-school building; found to be an 'occupant' relationship (not a lease), with recovery for conversion of school equipment and mental anguish.
new.notes: Concerns commercial school-building occupancy and conversion of school property, not residential lodging or dwelling letting, despite discussing 'occupant' doctrine similar to eviction-statute cases.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fourth Circuit
new.holding_summary: Zoning variance upheld allowing structural renovation of a nonconforming maternity residence housing unwed mothers, to relieve overcrowding; the Board's variance was found within its authority.
new.notes: Residents of the charitable maternity home are not paying lodgers/boarders; rooming-house zoning classification is mentioned only in passing regarding relocation feasibility, not adjudicated here.

new.court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Second Circuit
new.holding_summary: Zoning dispute over whether a mobile home placed on a residential lot qualifies as a permitted 'one-family dwelling'; court held it does.
new.notes: Mobile-home zoning classification case; not about lodging houses or compensated short-term occupancy of a dwelling.
Eviction proceeding against a deceased lessee's heirs occupying agricultural land by permission; concerns the C.C.P. eviction 'occupant' definition, not compensated short-term lodging or letting.
Family dispute over a usufructuary's sons occupying the family home by permission and jurisdiction to summarily evict co-owners; no compensated lodging or letting arrangement at issue.

Divorce case addressing whether a spouse occupying the family home pending property settlement retroactively owes rent to the other spouse; a co-ownership/community-property rent dispute, not short-term letting for pay.
Community-property partition case disallowing a rental-value offset between divorced co-owner spouses for occupancy of the marital home; not a short-term letting/lodging arrangement.
Zoning nonconforming-use case concerning loss of status for a seven-unit apartment building left vacant six months; involves ordinary long-term apartment leasing, not short-term letting or boarding.

new.holding_summary: The court affirmed denial of nonconforming-use status for a Garden District residence used intermittently over years to host paid tours and parties for tourists, holding that occasional commercial use of a private home, no matter how longstanding, is not sufficiently continuous to qualify as a legal nonconforming use under the city's zoning ordinance.

quotes.text: The Weislers’ sought review of a decision of the Board denying them nonconforming use status for the commercial purpose of conducting tours and parties for out-of-town tourists in a residentially zoned neighborhood.
The Board classified the commercial use of the property as intermittent and as such it did not qualify for nonconforming status.

As a matter of law we find that such usage is not sufficiently continuous or consistent to qualify for legally nonconforming status, i.e., we agree with the Board that and the trial court that the use was intermittent.
It is uncontested that the property in question, 2915 Chestnut St., is the Weislers’ residence in the middle of the Garden District.
in 1968 and 1969 he “worked at least a dozen paid details for the Weislers” at commercial “pay-parties.”

new.notes: Householder's own residence was periodically rented out for paid parties/receptions for tourists; zoning board and courts treated this compensated short-term use as insufficiently continuous commercial use, denying it protection — adverse to a householder's claimed right to let for pay.
Divorce case denying a spouse's second rule for use/occupancy or rent for the family home under La.R.S. 9:374; a co-ownership rent dispute, not short-term letting for pay.
Recreational Use Statute case defining 'occupant' of leased hunting-club land for immunity purposes; no lodging, boarding, or letting of a dwelling is at issue.
Restrictive-covenant dispute over operation of a used-car lot on subdivision lots; the 'commercial purposes' restriction concerns retail vehicle sales, not lodging or letting of dwellings/rooms.

new.holding_summary: The court affirmed the denial of a permit to operate a bed and breakfast at the owner's own Garden District residence, holding the Board of Zoning Adjustments reasonably found the owner had not established a legal nonconforming use of the property as a lodging business.

quotes.text: On May 1, 1997, Plaintiff filed an application with the Department of Safety and Permits for a permit to operate a bed and breakfast at his residence.
The Department of Safety and Permits denied the Plaintiff’s request for the bed and breakfast permit on the grounds that the Plaintiff had not attained a nonconforming use of his residence.
Plaintiff-Appellant Louis R. Koerner, Jr. (“Plaintiff”) is an attorney who purchased a residence located at 1204 Jackson Avenue in the city of New Orleans on October 26, 1979.

Plaintiff alleges that he inherited the nonconforming use of a “ten occupancy temporary lodgings” from the previous owner which he expanded into the additional commercial use of the premises through the years as an office for attorneys and for charitable and civic groups.

Plaintiff alleges that he inherited the nonconforming use of a “ten occupancy temporary lodgings” from the previous owner which he expanded into the additional commercial use of the premises through the years as an office for attorneys and for charitable and civic groups.

For the foregoing reasons, we affirm the judgment of the trial court and find that there was a reasonable basis for the Board of Zoning Adjustments to conclude kthat n0 nonconfirming commercial use of 1204 Jackson Avenue was acquired by the Plaintiff.

new.notes: Squarely on point: a householder sought to operate short-term paid lodging (a bed and breakfast) out of his own residence and was denied on zoning nonconforming-use grounds — an adverse precedent restricting a householder's ability to let short-term.
Commercial ground-lease and mortgage-foreclosure dispute over a restaurant leasehold and whether the foreclosing bank owed rent; no residential letting, lodging, or boarding is involved.

Community-property lesion case addressing whether the rental value of a family home occupied by an ex-spouse should count as consideration in a partition; a co-ownership rent dispute, not short-term letting for pay.

new.holding_summary: The court upheld a permanent injunction requiring a group-home operator to obtain parish planning-board and council approval under the state community-home statute before housing developmentally disabled residents in a residentially zoned area, rejecting an equal-protection challenge and analogizing the required local approval to the zoning variance a boarding-house operator would need in the same district.

quotes.text: We agree with the defendant that the closest definition applicable to the home is that of a boarding house, “a building other than a hotel where, for compensation and by prearrangement for a definite period, meals or lodging and meals are provided for three (3) or more persons, but not exceeding twenty (20) persons.”

The statute places essentially the same burden on a sponsor seeking to open a community home as the parish zoning ordinance places on anyone seeking a variance or exception. Since the community home is not a permitted use under the ordinance in an R-2 area, Normal Life would be obliged to request an exception or variance, as would any party seeking to operate a boarding house in an R-2 district.
For the foregoing reasons, the judgment appealed from is affirmed. Costs are taxed to appellant.

new.notes: Marginal/tangential: the facility is a state-licensed community home for disabled residents, not ordinary compensated lodging, but the court substantively invokes the zoning ordinance's 'boarding house' definition (compensation, prearrangement, meals/lodging) as the closest analogous use category, which bears on how such regulation classifies and burdens compensated multi-occupant residential use.

new.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Third Circuit
new.holding_summary: In a summary tax-collection proceeding against a hostel/bed-and-breakfast business that furnished sleeping rooms to transient guests for a fee, the appellate court found the trial court never actually ruled on the merits of the parish's sales and occupancy tax assessment and remanded for a decision on the merits.

quotes.text: On or about March 4, 2016, IMAGINE MANAGEMENT, LLC, through its owner, TOBY DORE, registered with Petitioner as a dealer for sales, use and occupancy tax purposes, for its operation of a hostel/ guesthouse/ bed and breakfast business in Lafayette Parish, Louisiana, under the trade name "CAJUN HOSTEL."

Upon information and belief, at all times pertinent hereto, Taxpayer was engaged in business as a "dealer" as defined in La. R.S. 47:301(4)(f)(ii) by furnishing sleeping rooms, cottages, or cabins at residential locations (as defined in La. R.S. 47:301(6)(a)(ii) ) in Lafayette Parish to transient guests for a fee, as well as by offering sales at retail of other taxable items.

Upon information and belief, at all times pertinent hereto, Taxpayer was engaged in business as a "dealer" as defined in La. R.S. 47:301(4)(f)(ii) by furnishing sleeping rooms, cottages, or cabins at residential locations (as defined in La. R.S. 47:301(6)(a)(ii) ) in Lafayette Parish to transient guests for a fee, as well as by offering sales at retail of other taxable items.

Because the trial court herein failed to issue a ruling on the merits of the Summary Sales Tax Proceeding brought by the Collector, this court has no jurisdiction to decide this appeal. Accordingly, we must reverse the appealed judgment and remand this matter to the trial court for further proceedings.

new.notes: A commercial hostel/B&B business furnishing sleeping rooms to transient guests for a fee is the subject of an occupancy-tax enforcement action; the merits of the tax liability were never actually decided (remanded), but the case documents modern regulatory treatment of short-term paid lodging.

new.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Fourth Circuit
new.notes: Premises-liability slip-and-fall case involving a roof-repair worker who fell off a rental property's roof; concerns invitee/trespasser duty analysis, not the letting or lodging arrangement itself.
Constitutional challenge to a parish local-option alcohol-prohibition ordinance under the police power; no lodging, boarding, or letting of dwellings is involved.

Police-negligence case about a fire in a locked patrol car while an intoxicated arrestee was left unattended; a hearsay fire-department report contains a passing, discredited reference to a 'rooming house,' unrelated to the holding on negligence and contributory negligence.

new.court: Civil Court of the City of New York
new.notes: Rent-control succession/family-member dispute (daughter passing on apartment); no compensated lodging or boarding-house issue.
Tenant-in-common vs. cotenant's commercial lessee dispute over business premises; no lodging/boarding issue.

new.court: Civil Court of the City of New York
new.notes: Loft Law 'residential occupant' priority dispute between prime tenant and one-year subtenant of loft space; not about lodging/boarding characterization.
Criminal larceny/extortion prosecution of landlords for forcibly evicting tenants; discusses license-vs-lease property theory only as analogy, not an actual lodging arrangement.
Overcrowding-statute/primary-residence dispute over tenant's daughter as additional occupant; not compensated lodging or boarding regulation.
Zoning challenge to floating-home (houseboat) district ordinance; concerns mobile-home/vessel zoning, not lodging or boarding.
Commercial holdover; dispute over use-and-occupancy liability after lease expiration and tender of keys. No lodging issue.

new.court: Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
new.notes: Roommate-law (RPL 235-f) applicability to an incarcerated tenant's absent-roommate arrangement; no compensated short-term lodging at issue.

new.court: Justice Court of the Village of Port Chester
new.notes: Criminal trespass prosecution over nursing-home visitation restriction; unrelated to lodging or boarding.
Zoning variance dispute over a group home's second kitchenette ('housekeeping unit' definition); no compensated lodging or letting issue.
Installment land-sale contract labeled 'landlord-tenant' by its terms; court holds it is a contract-vendee relationship, not a summary-proceeding-eligible tenancy. No lodging issue.

Case adjudicates whether a funeral home qualifies as a customary 'home occupation'; the ordinance's definitional list separately names 'Bed and Breakfast Home' as a permitted home occupation, but that category is not litigated or discussed by the court -- a passing background reference only.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
new.notes: Former building owners who sold to plaintiff and stayed on rent-free as owner-occupants sought Loft Law 'residential occupant' protection; court finds they are not tenants/lodgers at all. No compensated letting.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
new.notes: Loft Law window-period residential-occupancy proof dispute for former commercial building; no compensated lodging/boarding characterization issue.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
new.notes: Concerns whether the statutory warranty of habitability (RPL 235-b) applies to condominium unit owners vis-a-vis the board of managers; no compensated occupancy of another's dwelling/rooms by lodgers or boarders is at issue.

new.holding_summary: A rent-controlled tenant may not be evicted or ejected merely for charging a roommate a disproportionate share of the rent, since no rent control regulation forbids this, but where the tenant allegedly charged a roommate (and reportedly ran the apartment as an informal bed-and-breakfast for short-term foreign visitors) more than the entire legal rent, the landlord may still pursue injunctive relief and damages for profiteering. The court dismissed the declaratory-judgment and ejectment claims while allowing the profiteering-based injunction and disgorgement claims to proceed.

quotes.text: while defendant may not be evicted or ejected under the circumstances alleged herein, plaintiff may still seek injunctive relief enjoining defendant from profiteering and damages resulting from that purported conduct.

Plaintiff alleges in its papers that the building staff noticed that there were many individuals who appeared to be traveling from foreign countries who, on a continual basis, would stay for a few days or weeks in the apartment.

new.notes: Characterization left null: the court resolved rent-profiteering and roommate-law questions, not the lease/license/lodging character of the short-term arrangement. who_was_letting left unclear because the letter was a rent-controlled tenant, not an owner/householder, and it is unclear whether she resided alongside the transient occupants.

Dispute over whether a tenant who later performed janitorial services in exchange for free rent remained a tenant or became a mere licensee/employee; no letting of rooms to lodgers or boarders for pay.
