new.holding_summary: Upholds a municipal wharfage ordinance charging vessels for mooring as a lawful compensation for port facilities, not an unconstitutional tax, duty, or tonnage charge under the U.S. Constitution.
new.notes: Municipal wharfage/constitutional-commerce-clause case; wholly unrelated to lodging or boarding houses.

new.holding_summary: Holds that a police jury's location of a public road across a planter's land is subject to judicial review, and must be laid out with as little injury to the landowner as is compatible with the public interest.
new.notes: Road-location/police-jury power case, unrelated to lodging or boarding-house regulation.

new.holding_summary: Holds that a slave-yard keeper's expenses for boarding, clothing, and medical attendance furnished to attached slaves constitute a privilege on the slaves themselves as movable property.
new.notes: "Boarding" here refers to custodial care/maintenance of attached slaves as chattel property at a slave-yard, not to compensated human lodging or letting of a dwelling; outside project scope.

new.holding_summary: Holds that attaching creditors must be satisfied in the order their attachments were levied, and that the landlord's privilege for rent due takes preference over an attaching creditor's claim to the proceeds of a store's stock of goods.
new.notes: Commercial store rent/attachment-priority dispute; no dwelling, lodging, or boarding arrangement involved.

new.holding_summary: Holds that a tenant whose leased house is temporarily inconvenienced by an adjoining owner's lawful demolition and rebuilding of a party wall cannot dissolve the lease or abandon the premises, but is entitled only to a proportional reduction in rent for the period of inconvenience.
new.notes: Ordinary year-long house lease dispute about a landlord's structural/party-wall obligations; not about short-term letting, lodging, or boarding-house practice.

new.holding_summary: Trover action concerning a mortgagee's removal of distillery fixtures (copper stills, kettles) and their subsequent distress for rent by the landlord's bailiff; the court held the removed articles were personal property once severed and were properly distrained within the statutory period.
new.notes: Distress/fixtures case involving a distillery; no bearing on lodging, boarding, or short-term letting of dwellings.

new.holding_summary: Ejectment case addressing whether a vendee in possession under a parol purchase contract is entitled to notice to quit; the court surveys notice-to-quit doctrine and holds vendor-vendee relationships are an exception to the general notice requirement.
new.notes: Notice-to-quit/vendor-vendee ejectment doctrine regarding farmland; unrelated to lodging or boarding practice.

new.holding_summary: Forcible entry and detainer prosecution over a parol farm lease (six acres let for fencing as rent); the court held a void parol term still creates a tenancy for years within the meaning of the forcible-entry statute, and threats of bodily harm can constitute forcible detainer.
new.notes: Farm tenancy/forcible detainer case; no lodging, boarding, or dwelling-letting issue.

new.holding_summary: Dispute among tenants in common over whether one co-tenant's proportion of rents, collected by an agent purportedly acting under void letters of guardianship, could be set off against a separate debt; the court held the remedy lay in an action of account or bill in equity, not set-off.
new.notes: Guardianship/tenants-in-common accounting dispute. Mentions in passing that the agent was authorized to lease the premises 'to fit... for a tavern,' but the holding concerns set-off and account remedies, not the legal character or regulation of lodging/boarding letting.

new.court: New York Court for the Correction of Errors
new.holding_summary: Where the lessor was guilty of habitually bringing lewd women into other apartments under the same roof as the demised premises, causing nocturnal noise and disturbance, the court held this was evidence of a constructive eviction sufficient to go to the jury under a plea of eviction, barring the landlord's recovery of rent even absent a physical entry and expulsion.

quotes.text: two rooms upon the second floor and two rooms upon the third floor whereof had- been leased to the' defendant

Where the lessor was guilty of habitually bringing lewd women under the same roof with the demised premises, though in an apartment not demised, by which nocturnal noise and disturbance were made; and, in consequence, the lessee quitted the premises and remained away with his family; held, that this was evidence to go to the jury under a plea of eviction by the landlord, in answer to a declaration for the rent; and that the jury mighty upon such evidence, find the plea true; and the lessor would thereby be barred of his rent, the same as on an actual or physical entry and expulsion of the tenant.
This is, in its nature, a condition precedent to the payment of rent; and whether the possession was peaceable and quiet, was clearly a question of fact for the jury.

new.notes: The house was physically divided between rooms occupied by the landlord (first floor) and rooms leased to the tenant (second and third floors) -- a householder letting portions of his own dwelling, treated throughout the opinions as an ordinary lease governed by standard covenants (rent, quiet enjoyment). Central holding is constructive-eviction doctrine, not the legality of the letting itself; polarity is inferred from the court's unquestioning ordinary-lease framing of the arrangement rather than an explicit ruling on legitimacy.

new.holding_summary: The court held that property belonging to boarders at taverns or boarding houses is not liable to distress for rent owed by the tavern or boarding-house keeper, even though the property is in the keeper's possession and actual use by the boarders' permission and without the landlord's consent.

quotes.text: The property of boarders at taverns or boarding houses is not liable to distress for rent, although such property is not in their possession, but in the possession and actual use of the tenant, by their permission, and without the consent of the landlord.

The property of boarders at taverns or boarding houses is not liable to distress for rent, although such property is not in their possession, but in the possession and actual use of the tenant, by their permission, and without the consent of the landlord.

The property of boarders at taverns or boarding houses is not liable to distress for rent, although such property is not in their possession, but in the possession and actual use of the tenant, by their permission, and without the consent of the landlord.

new.notes: Court for the Correction of Errors reversed on a procedural ground (verdict already found for plaintiff below) but a majority of members separately adopted a resolution protecting boarders' property from distress for the innkeeper/boarding-house keeper's rent -- directly favorable to boarder status. Duration of the boarders' occupancy is not specified in the excerpt.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Ejectment for breach of a lease covenant limiting the lessee to one tenant or family per 100 acres; the court held that persons occupying parcels for a year on crop shares were 'tenants' within the covenant, and more than the permitted number rendered the lease void.
new.notes: Agricultural share-cropping tenancy and lease-forfeiture case; concerns farm tenants, not lodging or boarding of dwellings.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Trespass action by a lessor against a sub-tenant at will who removed a house he had built on the demised premises; the court held the lessor could not maintain trespass quare clausum fregit absent actual possession at the time of the alleged injury.
new.notes: Trespass/fixtures dispute over a sub-tenant's removal of a building he erected; no bearing on lodging or boarding regulation.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Replevin/avowry dispute between two claimants over the right to rent for a house let to the plaintiff for a year, submitted to arbitration in the tenant's presence; the court held the tenant was bound by the arbitrators' award without separate notice since he was privy to the submission.
new.notes: The underlying transaction is an ordinary year-long house letting, but the case turns entirely on arbitration and notice between two competing claimants to the rent, not on the character or regulation of lodging/boarding occupancy.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Trespass for unlawful entry into a dwelling house; the court held that while keeping an inn gives a general implied license to enter, the plaintiff's house was not shown to be an inn, so the defendant's uninvited entry and refusal to leave was a trespass.
new.notes: States the innkeeper implied-license-to-enter doctrine, but the house at issue was expressly found not to be an inn and no letting or boarding transaction is at issue; case is about trespass, not compensated occupancy or its regulation.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Action for use and occupation of a lot and dwelling house after the original lease term expired; the court held that because the original rent was reserved on the bare lot only, a tenant holding over after the landlord acquired title to buildings erected during the term must pay the higher value of land and buildings, not the old ground rent.
new.notes: Use-and-occupation rent valuation dispute after lease expiration; ordinary landlord-tenant law, not lodging or boarding.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Assumpsit for rent of a house and lot where the tenant, after his lease expired, attorned to a mortgagee whose mortgage had been forfeited; the court held a tenant of a mortgagor may lawfully attorn to the mortgagee after forfeiture and set this up as a defense against the mortgagor's rent claim.
new.notes: Mortgagor/mortgagee attornment and rent-privity dispute over a leased house; no lodging or boarding issue.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Replevin over a cider mill and press built by a tenant from year to year on a farm; the court held such machinery remained the tenant's personal property, removable at the end of the tenancy.
new.notes: Fixtures dispute between farm landlord and tenant; unrelated to lodging or boarding.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Motion to set aside a partition report between tenants in common of a woollen factory; the court confirmed the commissioners' treatment of loose, unattached machinery as personal property rather than realty.
new.notes: Fixtures/partition dispute over factory machinery; unrelated to lodging or boarding.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.holding_summary: Procedural ruling holding that a landlord seeking ejectment for non-payment of rent on unoccupied demised premises, where the tenant cannot be served personally, must proceed under the statutory summary proceedings rather than by affixing a declaration on the premises.
new.notes: Purely procedural ejectment-service ruling; no lodging or boarding issue.

new.holding_summary: Replevin/avowry dispute over a landlord's right to distrain under a parol lease for years; the court held a void parol demise for a term of years enures as a tenancy from year to year, sufficient to support distress for rent.
new.notes: General landlord-tenant distress/parol-lease doctrine (facts not specified beyond a house and lot rented at $140/year); not specific to lodging or boarding.

new.holding_summary: Trover action addressing whether a landlord could distrain for rent absent an express clause of distress; the court held a landlord with a reversionary interest may distrain at common law under the tenure of free and common socage, without needing statutory authority.
new.notes: General property-law doctrine on rent service/charge/seek and fealty; not specific to lodging or boarding.

new.holding_summary: Action against a deputy sheriff for seizing horses that a neighbor had left with an innkeeper for feeding and keeping; the court held the innkeeper had no lien because the horse owner was never a 'guest,' and the innkeeper's extraordinary liability and lien attach only where the goods' owner is actually or constructively a guest.
new.notes: Extensively discusses innkeeper liability and 'guest' status doctrine, but the property at issue is horses boarded at a stable/inn (agistment), not human lodgers or the letting of rooms/dwellings for pay; not on-topic for the corpus's human-occupancy focus.
Dispute is master-servant vs. landlord-tenant classification for farm labor housing incident to an employment contract, not compensated short-term lodging/boarding.

new.holding_summary: The court held that keeping an inn or tavern in the common-law sense is a lawful trade open to any citizen without a license; only the added privilege of selling spirituous liquors on the premises requires an excise license. Because the defendant's sign reading 'Entertainment' (paired with a 'Temperance' placard) did not indicate that he sold liquor, it did not amount to the statutory offense of displaying an unlicensed tavern sign.

quotes.text: But, at common law, any person may erect an inn for the public accommodation, without a license; as the keeping of it is not a franchise, but a lawful trade open to every citizen.
But, at common law, any person may erect an inn for the public accommodation, without a license; as the keeping of it is not a franchise, but a lawful trade open to every citizen.
As the sign in this case held out no such indication, the court below were right in deciding that it did not fall within the prohibition of the statute.

new.notes: Concerns a landlord's right to distrain for rent across successive annual farm leases; no lodging/boarding-house facts.

new.court: County Court of New York, Ontario County
new.notes: Procedural landlord-tenant summary-removal/notice-to-quit dispute over a yearly tenancy; not about lodging or boarding for pay.

new.holding_summary: Mrs. Switzer, a married woman, hired houses in her own name and ran a boarding-house business, contracting with boarders and receiving their payments; she gave defendant a note and chattel mortgage on the boarding-house furniture. The court held that because the mortgaged furniture went into the joint possession of husband and wife and was used for the family's support, it was not the wife's separate property under the Acts of 1848-49, so the husband alone was liable for its price and the wife's note and mortgage could not be enforced.

quotes.text: there was no separate property of the wife, the husband was liable for the debts contracted by the wife for its payment; consequently the note and mortgage given by the wife for its payment could not be enforced.

new.notes: Court's holding turns on married women's property/coverture law, not on the legal character (lease/license/lodging) of the boarding arrangement itself, so characterization and polarity are left null.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Addresses constructive-eviction/rent-suspension doctrine for an ordinary tenancy; no lodging or boarding-house facts.
Landlord's criminal liability for knowingly permitting tenants to run a house of prostitution; concerns a disorderly house, not licensing/regulation of an ordinary lodging or boarding trade.
Determines the defendant's legal domicile/residence for attachment jurisdiction; his hotel boarding is evidence of sojourning only, not a ruling on the legal character or regulation of letting.
Procedural dispute over injunctions against summary dispossession for nonpayment of rent on leased dwelling-houses; no lodging/boarding facts.
Concerns feudal tenures and restraints on alienation in fee-farm leases; not about short-term letting of rooms or dwellings for lodging.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.notes: Trespass/waste dispute between a reversioner and a life tenant's licensee over timber cutting; no lodging/boarding facts.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Pleading dispute over counterclaims in a landlord's rent action; no lodging/boarding-house facts.

Fuller appellate report of the same domicile/residence attachment dispute as Chaine v. Wilson, 16 How. Pr. 552; hotel boarding is evidence of sojourning for jurisdictional purposes, not a ruling on the character or regulation of letting.

new.holding_summary: An indictment will lie against excise commissioners who wilfully and corruptly grant a tavern license to an applicant they know is not of good moral character, lacks sufficient ability to keep a tavern, lacks the necessary accommodations for travellers, or where a tavern is not actually necessary at that place, notwithstanding the commissioners' ordinary discretion in licensing decisions.

quotes.text: that he is of sufficient ability to keep a tavern ; and has the necessary accommodations to entertain travellers; and that a tavern is absolutely necessary for the actual accommodation of travellers at the place where such applicant resides or proposes to keep the same

that he is of sufficient ability to keep a tavern ; and has the necessary accommodations to entertain travellers; and that a tavern is absolutely necessary for the actual accommodation of travellers at the place where such applicant resides or proposes to keep the same

By demurring, the defendants concede that they granted the license in question to a person whom they knew was not a mail of good moral character, nor a man of sufficient ability to keep a tavern; that he had not the necessary accommodations, and that a tavern was not necessary at the place where he proposed to keep it. This was a clear violation of duty, for which they were liable to be indicted.

new.notes: Dispute over the validity of a parol lease to commence in futuro and a use-and-occupation claim for commercial building space; no lodging/boarding facts.
Concerns an innkeeper's/livery-stable keeper's lien on a guest's horse; involves animal stabling, not compensated occupancy of a dwelling or rooms by a person.

new.holding_summary: The court enjoined the city of Brooklyn from enforcing, against a licensed innkeeper, a municipal ordinance that banned all liquor sales on Sunday, because state excise law expressly permitted licensed innkeepers to sell to their lodgers and lawful travelers on Sunday; the ordinance was therefore void as applied to the plaintiff's licensed privilege of serving his lodgers.

quotes.text: An ordinance, passed by a municipal corporation prohibiting the sale of spiritous liquors on Sunday, is void so far as relates to sales by innkeepers, to . their lodgers and to lawful travelers, pursuant to their licenses, and an injunction will be granted, to prevent its enforcement against them.

An ordinance, passed by a municipal corporation prohibiting the sale of spiritous liquors on Sunday, is void so far as relates to sales by innkeepers, to . their lodgers and to lawful travelers, pursuant to their licenses, and an injunction will be granted, to prevent its enforcement against them.

The defendants must be enjoined from enforcing so much of their ordinance as in effect prohibits the sale of spirituous liquors, by innkeepers, to their lodgers and to lawful travelers, on Sunday, pursuant to their license, so far as relates to the plaintiff, and others, in whose behalf he prosecutes this suit, until the further order of this court.

new.notes: Turns on whether an innkeeper's stabling of a traveling stud horse in a stall was a lease or an incident of the innkeeper-guest relationship; concerns animal stabling, not human lodging of a dwelling or rooms.
Ejectment dispute over a railroad's occupation of a public street; no bearing on compensated occupancy of dwellings/rooms or its regulation.
Manor leases in fee reserving perpetual rents and whether covenants to pay rent run with land to assignees; agricultural fee-farm tenure, not lodging/boarding of dwellings or rooms.
Dispute over use-and-occupation liability for a farm sold under a failed vendor contract, and guardian-in-socage rights; no lodging/boarding-house facts.
Farm purchase-vs-lease contract dispute and validity of a distress warrant/sheriff liability; no room/dwelling lodging facts.
Parol license to a railroad to build track across a farm; revocability of licenses to enter land, unrelated to lodging/boarding of dwellings.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.notes: Procedural ruling that a landlord in possession cannot bring ejectment against his own absconding tenant; no facts about lodging/boarding.

new.holding_summary: A married woman with no separate estate cannot bind property by her own contract; where she keeps a boarding-house in the family home as a means of supporting the family, with her husband's knowledge, the furniture and business are deemed his property. The husband is therefore liable to the vendor for goods purchased for the boarding-house, and a mortgage the wife gave over that property (to secure a note for rent, furniture, and provisions) is void absent his authorization.

quotes.text: When personal property is purchased by a married woman, with the knowledge of her husband, and is used by the wife in keeping a boarding-house, which is kept as a mode of supporting the family, the property is the husband’s, and he is liable for its price to the vendor, although it was bought in the name of the wife, and the boarding-house was conducted by her.

It went to the plaintiff’s house and possession, it was appropriated to his use, by being employed in a business prosecuted as a means of supporting his family. He is liable in law for its price, and it could be taken on execution to satisfy his debts.

new.notes: Boarding-house keeping is treated by the court as an ordinary, legitimate household enterprise for supporting a family (not restricted or penalized); the dispute concerns spousal property/agency law, not the legality of the letting itself.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
new.notes: Summary proceeding over a farm life-tenancy and the reversioner's rights against a sharecropping occupant; no lodging/boarding facts.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Use-and-occupation suit over renting of an entire house (via agent), turning on delivery of keys and proof of occupation; not a lodging/room-letting or boarding-house case.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Eviction/rent dispute over a landlord's use of a shared privy adjoining leased commercial space; no lodging/boarding facts.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Eviction dispute between co-occupying landlord and tenant of a store (paint shops) and exclusion of tenant's sub-lessee; commercial shop space, not dwelling lodging.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas
new.notes: Eviction/quiet-enjoyment dispute over a leased storefront and a landlord's waste-water interference; no lodging/boarding facts.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.notes: Dower ejectment turning on whether a farm laborer was a servant or the actual occupant, and whether ejectment lies against a remainder-man; agricultural land, no lodging facts.
Habeas corpus proceeding over a fugitive slave and the constitutionality of a State reclamation statute; wholly unrelated to lodging/boarding of dwellings.

new.holding_summary: The court held that an action for use and occupation may rest on an implied, not merely express, landlord-tenant agreement. Because summary proceedings to recover possession run against whoever is in actual possession, a landlord who unsuccessfully pursued summary proceedings against the boarding-house keeper in possession was not thereby precluded from later proving, in an ordinary suit, that a different person (who had sublet the premises to her, taking his own board as rent) was in fact his tenant.

quotes.text: The plaintiff purchased of one Voorhis'the premises Ho. 50 Maiden Lane, then in the occupation of Mrs. Leman as a boarding-house.

he had hired the premises of Voorhis and underlet them to Mrs. L., who was to board him and his apprentices for the rent, and that she had thus paid him all the rent except a balance of five or six dollars
The action for use and occupation is founded, it is true, on the conventional relation of landlord and tenant. But it is not necessary 1 hat the agreement should be express. It may be implied.

new.notes: A boarding-house sublease (rent paid in board) is treated as an ordinary, enforceable landlord-tenant arrangement; the legal dispute is about which party is liable as tenant, not about the legality of the boarding-house practice.
Inn-keeper's liability in trover for a non-guest's bag left at a hotel; concerns innkeeper bailment/custody of goods, not the letting of rooms or dwellings for pay.
Brief chancery note on a landlord's distress rights against a tenant's goods held by a receiver; no lodging/boarding facts.

new.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
new.notes: Double-rent statute case for a tenant wilfully holding over on a leased store/tenement after notice to quit; ordinary commercial tenancy, not lodging/boarding.
Dower action turning on who is 'tenant of the freehold' as between a vendor and vendee under articles of sale; no lodging/boarding issue. Retrieval matched on generic 'tenant of the freehold' phrase.
Debt action for rent on a family farm let by a now-deceased father to support the household; not a lodging or boarding-house case.
Covenant action for rent between co-tenants of a farm held under sealed articles resembling a partnership; no lodging issue.

new.holding_summary: A mail contractor's sub-agent boarded himself and stabled two teams of horses with Kimball at a stipulated weekly rate. The court held Kimball's claim arose as a livery-stable keeper rather than an innkeeper, since the arrangement differed from the entertainment of transient strangers and travellers, and upheld his joint and several lien on the horses for the keeping (including board).

quotes.text: The right of lien for the keeping of several horses of the same person at the same time is a charge; not against the horses, and therefore several and divided; but against the owner, secured by a lien upon all the horses, and therefore joint and several, and one horse may be detained for the keeping of all.

But it was not at all as innkeeper that the plaintiff became entitled to assert this claim against the defendant, but as livery-stable keeper; for it was under an arrangement totally different from that which tabes place in the entertainment of strangers and travellers.

It was a necessary part of that arrangement that the horses should be delivered to the defendant as they were needed, and this is part of the ordinary course of business of livery-stable keepers, and therefore must be consistent with the right of lien that belongs to the occupation.

new.notes: Core holding is about innkeeper/livery-stable lien law, but the court expressly distinguishes ordinary weekly-rate boarding-for-pay from the transient-guest innkeeper relation, bearing on characterization of compensated boarding arrangements. Marked mixed: enforces the boarding arrangement as ordinary business, but the case is not centrally about a householder letting a dwelling.

Partition action concerning a vendee's equitable estate and adverse possession; a lease of an absent heir's land share is mentioned only to show the defendant's possession was not adverse. No lodging issue.
Rent-apportionment dispute after a ferry-property landlord sold part of the reversion to a railroad; no lodging issue.

Trespass quare clausum fregit turning on whether a landlord of agricultural land had sufficient constructive possession to sue before entry, given a tenant-at-will occupant (son-in-law). Tenancy-at-will doctrine, not lodging.
Assumpsit for use and occupation against a tenant who paid rent to a decedent's administrator rather than the true heirs; estate-administration/landlord-tenant dispute, not lodging.
Distress-for-rent case on a leased, stocked dairy farm; addresses whether 'rent' can issue from land plus furniture/chattels. No lodging issue.
Trover action over ownership of steam saw-mill machinery/fixtures after a milling agreement expired; fixtures law, no lodging issue.
Landlord-tenant summary proceeding over an agricultural 'improving lease' (clear/fence land, pay taxes in lieu of rent); addresses timing of notice to quit, not lodging.

Dispute over an alien's right to vote in a Pittsburgh borough election as a 'freeholder, housekeeper, or inhabitant.' 'Housekeeper' functions as a voter-qualification term here, unconnected to letting rooms or dwellings.

Landlord-tenant-act jurisdiction case holding a roughly seven-month lease of a house (rent = taxes plus repairs) qualifies as a 'term of one or more years' for summary-possession purposes. Confirms short leases of a dwelling are treated as ordinary tenancies for years, but the case is purely procedural statutory construction, not about lodging/boarding characterization, and no household-letting facts are at issue; kept irrelevant per the no-quote/passing-mention standard.
Landlord-tenant summary proceeding quashed for defects in the inquisition record concerning a rent-free tenancy at will; no lodging issue.
Landlord-tenant summary proceeding quashed for defective inquisition findings on a one-year farm lease; no lodging issue.

Slave-freedom (homine replegiando) case turning on whether an enslaved person's 'sojourning' in Pennsylvania with a farm-lessee's family, without the master's consent, triggered the abolition statute. 'Sojourning' here concerns residency of an enslaved person, unrelated to lodger/boarder letting of dwellings.
Landlord-tenant summary proceeding on a one-year farm lease, addressing whether notice to quit must precede expiration of the term. No lodging issue.

Replevin over a distress for rent on a one-year lease of a tavern property; the tenant's covenant to 'keep a public house' and obtain the license is recited only as a lease term and is never adjudicated. The actual holding concerns whether rent payable in advance was a properly reserved, distrainable rent, not innkeeping/lodging characterization.
Concerns inheritance rights of foreign/domiciled heirs under Spanish and Mexican law and forfeiture of land grants by absentee colonists; no letting, lodging, or boarding-house issue present.
Concerns homestead exemption from forced sale and whether mortgaging a homestead is an 'alienation' requiring the wife's statutory consent; no room-letting or lodging issue.

Concerns validity of a Mexican-era colonization concession and title, including satisfaction of settlement/cultivation conditions (the land was cultivated 'by means of tenants' in an agricultural sense); not about letting rooms or dwellings for lodging.
Concerns proof of a lost ancient Spanish grant of town exidos (commons) to the city of San Antonio and the presumption of a grant from long, notorious possession; no lodging or boarding-house issue.

Purely procedural holding on pleading requirements under the 1840 summary forcible-detainer statute for landlords against a holdover tenant of unspecified 'lands'; no facts about a dwelling, rooms, or lodging arrangement are alleged or discussed.

Concerns the Catholic church's usufructuary tenure in a dedicated church-square lot in Victoria and the effect of the change of sovereignty from Mexico to Texas on that tenure; no letting or lodging issue.
Concerns the statutory right of a good-faith possessor of land to be reimbursed for permanent improvements against the owner's claim for rents; no lodging/room-letting issue.
Concerns whether a widow's headright certificate was granted in her personal right as head of family or as representative of her deceased husband's estate; no lodging issue.
Concerns adverse possession between co-heirs to slaves left with the parents after the co-tenant's death, and the statute of limitations; no letting or lodging issue.
Concerns whether a repealed licensing statute could support an indictment for retailing spirituous liquors without a license; a liquor-license regulation case, not lodging/boarding-house regulation.
Concerns a first-class settler's six-month statutory preference to locate a land certificate over his improvement before the land became open to other claimants; no lodging issue.

Concerns whether an allegation of 'residence' (as opposed to a 'fixed domicil or residence,' distinguished from a mere 'sojourner') sufficed to establish probate jurisdiction to appoint an administrator, and validity of the administrator's land sale; the sojourner/fixed-residence distinction is about domicile for probate venue, not compensated occupancy of a dwelling.
Concerns the validity of a decree for specific performance and land partition rendered against an absentee defendant, and alleged fraud in obtaining it; no lodging issue.
Concerns apportionment of a hire price when a hired slave dies during the hiring term without the hirer's fault; involves hiring of personal property (a slave), not letting of a dwelling or rooms.
Concerns usury, priority among successive mortgages/deeds of trust on real property, and competency of an agent-witness; no lodging or room-letting issue.
Concerns which body, the county court or an incorporated town council, has jurisdiction to require repair of a street/road; no lodging issue.

Concerns the constitutionality of statutory conditions limiting a landowner's recovery of rents/use-and-occupation value from a good-faith settler, and probate-court jurisdiction over an estate; not about letting rooms or dwellings.
Concerns sufficiency of pleading a claim for loss of a public ferry and its franchise privileges attached to riverfront land; no lodging or boarding-house issue.
Marital domicile/abandonment dispute over separation and divorce jurisdiction; no letting, lodging, or boarding arrangement at issue.

Tutorship accounting dispute over plantation rental value and a tutor charging his minor wards for their own board and lodging in his household; an intra-family maintenance/accounting matter, not a compensated letting to lodgers or a boarding-house arrangement.
Prosecution under a municipal ordinance against adulterated milk sales; no lodging or boarding house issue.
Companion case to Callac on the same milk-adulteration ordinance, addressing double jeopardy and delegated police power; unrelated to lodging or boarding regulation.
Nullity action attacking a divorce decree for defective substituted service on an absentee spouse; no lodging or letting issue.
Possessory action over farmland boundary lines following a land sale; no lodging or dwelling-letting arrangement.
License-tax dispute over whether travelling salesmen qualify as exempt 'clerks'; unrelated to lodging or boarding.

new.holding_summary: In a wife's suit against her husband and his concubine over community property, the court found the concubine's property was largely acquired through her own capital and industry, principally her occupation of keeping a boarding house. The court held she was entitled to her share of the jointly built-up estate as against the husband's community, splitting the property between her separate share and the marital community.

quotes.text: Prom the time she went to live with Malady she had no industry except that of keeping a boarding house.

She should be allowed to place her capital and industry against the capital and industry of William Malady, her paramour and copartner, and the property purchased during the time they have been living and working together, should be declared property in which they have a joint interest; one half of it should be decreed to be the property of William Malady, and said half to belong to the community which existed between himself and his lawful wife, Mary Malady.
That Mary Caldwell should be entitled to keep the proceeds arising from the employment of her patrimony and resulting from her industry, we think is unquestionable. She has a right to it all.

new.notes: Case centers on community-property/concubinage law, not on the legal character of the letting itself; boarding-house keeping (including nephews who 'always slept in the house' and draymen boarders at $100/month) is treated in passing as an ordinary lawful income-producing occupation of a householder, which is why it is coded favorable rather than adjudicated on licensing/nuisance grounds.

new.holding_summary: A city ordinance authorizing the Mayor to order occupants of a house of prostitution or assignation to remove, with fine or imprisonment for refusal, is a valid exercise of delegated police power and does not deprive the owner-keeper of due process, even though she owns the premises.

quotes.text: The charter of the city expressly delegates the power to “ regulate houses of prostitution and assignation ” and “exclude such houses from certain limits” and “to close the same,” and “to authorize the Mayor to close such places.”

It is the clearest possibleuexample of a police regulation, the exercise of the police power of the State — that power reserved to every State, as essential to social order and comfort, which subjects the most absolute rights of properly to the condition that they shall be so used as not to infringe the rights of others.

new.notes: Borderline relevant: deals with municipal police-power closure of a house of assignation (owner-occupied, used for short-stay occupancy) rather than an ordinary boarding/lodging house; court does not characterize the arrangement under lease/license/lodging/innkeeping terms, so characterization left null; duration of individual occupancies not stated.
Police jury lacked power to regulate railroad train speed; no lodging or boarding content.
Commercial store lease/eviction dispute between an express company and its lessor; not a dwelling/lodging occupancy.

new.holding_summary: A lodging housekeeper who retains a room in her house to be occasionally visited and occupied by her concubine, without any contract for payment of rent, cannot recover room rent or nursing fees, because the arrangement was merely incidental to the pre-existing concubinage rather than a genuine letting for pay.

quotes.text: 1. A woman who keeps a room in he? house to bo visited and occasionally occupied by lior concubine, without any contract for the payment of rent by the latter, cannot enforce such payment.
the plaintiff, a lodging housekeeper in this city, claims $1644 90 for room rent due by Joseph Mathis

But are we to hold that that woman or man who keeps a room in his or her house to be visited occasionally and occupied by a concubine, without any contract to pay rent, can claim or enforce such payment?

Nevertheless he continued to make regular weekly visits to the house of plaintiff, spending there Saturday night, Sunday and Sunday night. It was on these occasions that he occupied the room for which rent is claimed, and which was undoubtedly, retained for his occupancy and not rented to others.

new.notes: Court's reasoning implies an ordinary lodging-rent contract would have been enforceable (favorable-leaning dicta), but denies recovery on these facts because the occupancy was incidental to concubinage rather than a bona fide letting for pay; marked mixed.
Concerns whether a city-built market house is a 'public market' for purposes of private-market distance restrictions; no lodging or boarding content.

When O'Hern nonetheless pursued the writ of ejectment despite Deslonde's payment and tender of all rent, the court found the eviction malicious and increased the tenant's damages, including for mental suffering and humiliation.

quotes.text: On the 1st of October, 1884, the defendant leased to the plaintiff a dwelling-house situated in this city, for twelve months, at a rental of forty dollars per month, aggregating for the entire year $480.

When a lessor, in illegally issuing a writ of ejectment was actuated by malice, he is liable to a lessee for damages, as a recompense for an oufet age upon his rights and feelings as a citizen and a man.

When a lessor, after b© has obtained a judgment cancelling tbe lease, voluntarily receives from tbe tenant all tbe rent due according to tbe terms of tbe leas© and waives bis right to issue a writ of ejectment, bis act in receiving tbe rent recognizes tlie lease as still in force, and in lieu of possession accepts a specific performance of the contract of lease.

new.holding_summary: The city of Baton Rouge prosecuted Crémonini for renting his house to women of 'lewd and abandoned conduct' in violation of a council resolution, but the governing ordinance actually required that the tenants first be convicted as keepers of a disorderly house and the owner then notified before the owner could himself be prosecuted. Because the tenants had never been convicted or the owner properly notified, the court held Crémonini's conviction unauthorized and reversed it, while affirming that a municipality may, through a general ordinance applicable to all alike, regulate and punish owners who let houses to keepers of disorderly houses once due process is followed.

quotes.text: setting at defiance and refusing to comply with a resolution of the city council prohibiting him from renting a certain house to women of lewd and abandoned conduct.
The city ordinance, on the subject of disorderly houses, authorizes the prosecution and punishment of offenders, by fine or imprisonment, and by closing their establishments.

The ordinance further authorizes the prosecution and punishment, by fine or imprisonment, of the owners of such houses, after the conviction of the inmates thereof, as keepers of disorderly houses, and after notification of such conviction to said owners or their agents.
We, therefore, hold that the penalty imposed against him was absolutely unauthorized and is glaringly illegal.

new.notes: characterization left null: the court addresses municipal regulatory power and due-process procedure over an owner who let his house to disorderly tenants, but never classifies the letting arrangement itself as lease/license/lodging/innkeeping. who_was_letting and duration_of_occupancy left unclear: record does not state whether Cremonini resided in or near the house or the length of the tenancy.

Dispute over priority of vendor's privilege versus wife's legal mortgage on a plantation; purely a registry/priority-of-liens question, no bearing on lodging or letting of dwellings.
Dispute over an occupant's obligation to pay sums 'in lieu of rent' under a vente a remere/mortgage instrument for a plantation; agricultural land finance case, not about dwelling/room lodging.

Parish police jury license-tax dispute over a barroom/grocery business and municipal-annexation boundary jurisdiction; regulation of liquor and grocery licensing, not lodging houses.
Local-option election dispute over a city's authority to continue issuing liquor retail licenses versus a parish prohibition vote; liquor-license regulation, unrelated to lodging/boarding.
Damages suit for wrongful eviction of a commercial tenant under a reversed judgment; general landlord-tenant liability case, no facts about lodging/boarding of a dwelling or rooms.
Damages claim over provisional seizure and landlord's re-entry after lease expiration; ordinary commercial landlord-tenant ejectment dispute, not lodging/boarding related.
Workman's privilege dispute over a raft of timber; concerns privileges on movables under C.C. art. 3184, entirely unrelated to dwellings or lodging.

Upholds a New Orleans ordinance requiring a permit to open a drinking house/barroom under the police power; regulates liquor retail, not lodging or boarding houses despite the regulation-selector match.
Co-heirs' partition dispute over land possession, prescription, and reimbursement for taxes/improvements; no facts touching compensated occupancy or lodging.

quotes.text: It is of no consequence that she leased her houses by the month or year, or that she sometimes leased rooms, as she owned both the houses and the furniture.

Duration marked unclear because the court's phrase mixes house-lets 'by the month or year' with unspecified room-lets.
Challenges a market 'gardeners' tax' on produce carts as an unconstitutional revenue exaction disguised as a police regulation; concerns market-vendor taxation, not lodging/boarding regulation.

Suit on a family guaranty/donation contract concerning a paraphernal fund and conflict-of-laws issues; a witness's passing remark that the husband 'lives in furnished lodgings, and takes his meals at a restaurant' is offered only as evidence of his financial ruin, not a ruling on the legal character of lodging.
A 20-year 'lease' of community land (an orange grove) is recharacterized as an impermissible gratuitous donation by the husband; agricultural-land community-property dispute, not dwelling lodging.

new.holding_summary: The plaintiff-lessee's hotel business -- keeping boarders and lodgers, a bar room, and billiard tables -- was recognized as a legitimate enterprise protected by a lease covenant barring the lessor from renting the adjoining building for a competing hotel or similar business; the court found the covenant breached but denied damages for want of certain proof, remanding as a nonsuit rather than a final judgment for defendant.

quotes.text: carried on in the leased premises, the business of keeping boarders and lodgers, a bar room and billiard tables
carried on in the leased premises, the business of keeping boarders and lodgers, a bar room and billiard tables
there was evidently a breach of this covenant by the deceased.
We agree, however, with the judge a quo, that the evidence does not enable the court to fix accurately the damages resulting from this violation of the contract.

new.notes: Ordinary lessor/lessee rent-and-lis-pendens dispute; no facts about dwelling rooms, lodgers, or short-term letting.

new.notes: Dispute over lessor's privilege on furniture in a leased house; no discussion of lodging/boarding practice, duration, or characterization of the occupancy.

new.holding_summary: A police regulation authorizing the mayor to order removal of an occupant from a house of prostitution or assignation had not been triggered because the mayor had never issued such an order, so the occupant had not violated it and the recorder lacked jurisdiction.
new.notes: Regulation targets houses of prostitution/assignation under vice-suppression police power, not ordinary lodging or boarding houses letting rooms for pay; outside corpus scope despite selector match.

new.holding_summary: Municipal ordinance prohibiting Sunday liquor sales was a valid police-power regulation, not an establishment of religion; conviction reversed on the facts because an unauthorized porter, not the saloon keepers, made the sale.
new.notes: Concerns Sunday liquor-sale regulation; no connection to lodging, boarding, or room-letting.

new.notes: Ordinary residential house lease (whole house, disputed monthly vs. yearly term) and wrongful-eviction damages; no room-letting, lodging, or boarding-house doctrine.

new.holding_summary: A tenant leased a suite of rooms in the plaintiff's apartment house, the 'Four Seasons,' for one year, then abandoned the premises after about six months, claiming the rooms were rendered untenantable by vermin (bedbugs, cockroaches, water bugs, ants). The court held the landlord owed no implied warranty of habitability absent fraud or an express condition, applying caveat emptor to the leasing of the rooms just as to a sale, and affirmed judgment for the landlord for the unpaid rent.

quotes.text: The action is on a written lease of a suit of rooms in the apartment house of the plaintiff, known as the “Four Seasons.” The hiring was for one year from November 1, 1882

The maxim caveat emptor applies to the leasing as well as to the transfer of real or personal property, and the lessee or purchaser takes the risk of its quality and condition, unless he protects himself on the subject by express agreement.
The landlord, in the absence of fraud or express condition, is not responsible for the presence of rats, mice, bugs or roaches about his premises.

new.notes: Treats the letting of rooms/suites in an apartment house as an ordinary lease governed by caveat emptor, with no special duties or restrictions imposed because the subject is furnished living quarters — favorable to letting as an ordinary incident of ownership. who_was_letting is coded commercial_operator because the plaintiff owned and operated the multi-unit 'Four Seasons' apartment house as a rental business, not a single householder letting part of his own home.

The chattel mortgage given the plaintiff by the defendant, Green, not having been recorded until after all the indebtedness claimed by the defendant, Cushing, in this action accrued, was not a valid lien upon the furniture as against the defendant Cushing’s claim under the boarding house keeper’s act.

new.holding_summary: A husband and wife who agreed to jointly furnish a boarder with board, lodging, and use of a room -- the wife supplying the house and the husband the provisions, sharing proceeds equally -- validly created a joint debt owed to them both, since a husband may lawfully agree that his wife receive compensation for her own services and property.

quotes.text: The defendants set up as a counterclaim in this action a demand against the plaintiff for board, lodging and use of room, which were supplied and furnished to the plaintiff by the defendants jointly.

We think under the circumstances disclosed the defendants had a right and could legally make a contract by which the wife should receive a share of the proceeds of such board and use of room, for the use of her house and for her services, and that such contract having been made, and the plaintiff having promised to pay the defendants jointly for such board and use of room, with full knowledge of the agreement between the defendants, she cannot now insist that her debt was to the husband alone, and thus defeat the defendants’ counterclaim.
But even under such circumstances the husband might covenant and agree that his wife should receive pay for her services on her own account.

new.holding_summary: A boarding-house keeper is not an insurer of a boarder's goods as an innkeeper would be; rather, as bailee for mutual benefit she is liable for a patron's stolen property only upon proof she failed to exercise ordinary care, a burden plaintiff did not carry.

quotes.text: A boarder is not a guest in the sense in which it is applied with reference to an innkeeper’s liability (Hancock v. Rand, 94 N. Y. 1; 46 Am. Rep. 112); and unlike the latter, who is liable as an insurer of his patron’s goods (Hulett v. Swift, 33 N. Y. 571), a boarding-house keeper is answerable for a loss of the goods only if he has omitted to exercise ordinary care to prevent it.
A boarding-house keeper, furthermore, is in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, in contemplation of law a custodian of his patron’s goods.
The judgment should be reversed and a new trial granted, With costs to appellant to abide the event.

new.notes: Ordinary tenant-holding-over/landlord's-election dispute over a commercial tenancy; not about lodging or boarding.

Dispute over whether a hired farmhand's occupancy of employer-provided housing was a tenancy or mere service occupancy (with rent deducted from wages); this is tied/service housing between employer and employee, not compensated lodging/boarding let to a stranger.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
new.notes: Excise commissioners' discretion to refuse a hotel liquor license based on the applicant's moral character and the house being used as a resort for illicit purposes; concerns liquor licensing and disorderly-house conduct, not boarding/lodging-house regulation as such.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
new.notes: Extensive corporate-law dispute among family shareholders over promoters' agreements, by-laws, and corporate assets (including family mansion houses held by the corporation); no lodging, boarding, or short-term letting facts.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Trial Term, Sullivan County
new.holding_summary: Court held that a grantor's release of 'all claims, easements, privileges, and rights' under an agreement creating a mill pond released her right to fish and boat there, since those rights arose from the pond-creation agreement rather than as an incident of her ownership of the underlying soil. Plaintiff was therefore entitled to exclusive control of the pond, and defendants' fishing and removal of no-trespassing signs were unlawful.
new.notes: Water/easement dispute over a fishing pond; 'incident of ownership' language concerns riparian/fishing rights, not compensated occupancy of a dwelling.

new.court: County Court of New York, Oneida County
new.holding_summary: Court upheld revocation of a hotel keeper's liquor license after the licensee pled guilty to keeping a disorderly house, holding the excise board's summons was properly signed and that the board could take judicial notice that the disorderly conduct occurred on premises it had licensed. The decision turns on excise procedure and evidentiary sufficiency.
new.notes: Liquor-license revocation for keeping a disorderly (bawdy) house at a hotel; concerns excise procedure and vice regulation, not compensated short-term lodging as such.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
new.holding_summary: Where a flat was hired 'at the rate of' $35 a month with no term specified, the court held the hiring defaulted to a yearly tenancy under the applicable statute absent proof of a definite term, and that the tenant's advance payment of a year's and later six months' rent negated any inference of a month-to-month tenancy. The court also addressed a district court's power to direct and set aside a verdict.
new.notes: Ordinary landlord-tenant dispute over the term of a full-flat residential lease between landlord and tenant; not a lodger/boarder arrangement or its regulation.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Fourth Department
new.holding_summary: Court held a town's 20-year-old suit to recover railroad stock it had transferred was barred by laches and was not a proper action to remove a cloud on title, and that the governing statute did not require the sale of the stock be made for cash. The 'incident of ownership' language concerned the power to dispose of personal property (stock).
new.notes: Municipal railroad-stock dispute; no relation to dwelling occupancy or lodging.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term, First Department
new.holding_summary: Court held that a person who lives in New Jersey but conducts business in New York City 'sojourns' in New York for purposes of a statute governing where a witness may be subpoenaed under a deposition commission. The ruling construes 'sojourn' in a procedural/venue sense.
new.notes: Procedural deposition-venue case construing 'sojourner'; unrelated to compensated occupancy of a dwelling.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
new.holding_summary: Court held that a tenant's holding over after expiration of a one-year dwelling-house lease creates, at the landlord's election, a new lease for another year regardless of prior notice of intent to vacate, and that this rule is not relaxed even where the holdover resulted from a family member's illness rather than the tenant's own convenience.
new.notes: Ordinary full-dwelling-house lease/holdover-tenancy dispute between landlord and tenant; not about short-term room letting or lodging-house regulation.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term, Second Department
new.holding_summary: Court affirmed the validity of preferences in an assignment for the benefit of creditors, finding the debts owed to the assignor's wife and sister-in-law were bona fide loans and not fictitious. The trial finding recited, as background, that the wife had kept boarders under an arrangement with her husband whereby she retained the profits and he paid for his board.
new.notes: Passing factual reference to a wife 'keeping boarders' as background for a creditor-preference/assignment dispute; the court never adjudicates the legal character of the boarding arrangement itself, so treated as a passing mention under the coverage rule.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
new.holding_summary: Majority held the city of New York holds absolute fee title to the tideway under its colonial charters, so an upland owner whose title derived from a post-charter grant had no compensable riparian rights when the city filled in the tideway to build a street; the dissent argued a pre-charter Harlem-patent grantee retained riparian rights requiring compensation.
new.notes: Waterfront/riparian-rights and land-reclamation dispute; 'incidents of ownership' language concerns tideway title, unrelated to dwelling occupancy.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas
new.holding_summary: Court held a landlord holding a chattel mortgage on a tenant's furniture did not satisfy the mortgage debt merely by taking possession of furniture the tenant had abandoned, and that excluding the landlord's testimony that he never used or profited from the property, and excluding evidence of its value, was reversible error. The dispute arose after the landlord let the flat to a new occupant for the remainder of the original tenant's term.
new.notes: Chattel-mortgage/conversion dispute; the subletting of the flat is incidental to the mortgage issue, not an adjudication of lodging or short-term letting law.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas, General Term
new.holding_summary: Court held a steamboat company liable, without proof of negligence, for money taken from a passenger's locked stateroom at night, applying to water carriers a liability analogous to an innkeeper's. The court declined to extend to steamboat companies the contrary rule for sleeping-car companies, which furnish lodging alone (not victuals and lodging) to a limited class of ticketed passengers and so are not treated as innkeepers.
new.notes: Carrier-liability case analogizing steamboats/sleeping-cars to innkeepers for lost-property purposes; discusses 'lodging' only as a doctrinal analogy for baggage liability, not compensated occupancy of a household dwelling or lodging-house regulation.

new.court: New York Superior Court, Equity Term
new.holding_summary: In a divorce action, the court found circumstantial evidence of adultery sufficient, including that the defendant and the co-respondent (who kept the flat where he boarded) were seen undressed and kissing, and had misrepresented their relationship as in-laws. The court remarked that their conduct exceeded ordinary relations between a 'boarding-house keeper and boarder.'
new.notes: Divorce/adultery case; the 'boarding-house keeper and boarder' reference is a passing rhetorical comparison, not a ruling on lodging law or its regulation.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term, Fourth Department
new.holding_summary: Court reversed a defense verdict in a wrongful-death boat-collision case, holding it was error to admit testimony about a nonparty boat operator's general drinking habits, elicited in part through mention that he 'kept a boarding house' with a bar, where there was no evidence he was intoxicated on the night of the accident.
new.notes: Negligence/evidentiary case; boarding-house reference is incidental background used to introduce impeachment testimony about drinking habits, not adjudicated lodging-house law.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, Special Term, Ulster County
new.holding_summary: Court held a newly enacted certiorari-review statute for excise-license denials applied to a license refusal predating the statute's passage, and that an excise board could not refuse to consider an application on its merits merely because a majority of the board had campaigned on refusing licenses, absent an actual local-option vote prohibiting licensing.
new.notes: Liquor-license (hotel/innkeeper's license) refusal and excise-board procedure case; concerns liquor licensing, not lodging-house regulation or compensated dwelling occupancy.

new.holding_summary: Court held that money found on a customer-use desk inside a bank was not 'lost property' recoverable by the finder, because its location indicated it had been voluntarily placed there and merely forgotten by its owner, distinguishing cases (cited in passing, including one involving a hotel servant finding money left by a 'transient guest') where property found on a floor was genuinely lost.
new.notes: Lost-property/finders-law case; the hotel-transient-guest reference is a passing citation to another jurisdiction's case, not an adjudication involving lodging here.

new.court: County Court of New York, Rockland County
new.holding_summary: Court held that an agreement letting the defendant quarry stone on the plaintiff's land in exchange for one-fifth of sale proceeds, with no fixed term, created a tenancy at will removable by summary proceedings, since the arrangement was a landlord-tenant relationship (rent) rather than a joint-ownership share arrangement.
new.notes: Landlord-tenant dispute over commercial quarrying rights on land, not a dwelling or lodging arrangement.

new.court: New York Court of Common Pleas, General Term
new.holding_summary: Court held an oral assignment of rents to become due was void under the statute of frauds because rent is an incident of real-property ownership requiring a writing to assign, and that the defendant had constructive notice of a recorded deed transferring ownership and was estopped from claiming the disputed rents after accepting an agency from the new owner.
new.notes: Rent-assignment/statute-of-frauds dispute concerning ownership of rental income; unrelated to the character or regulation of lodging or short-term letting.

new.holding_summary: Court held that a tenant of commercial store premises could raise, as a defense to a rent claim, damages caused by the landlord's permitted interference with the tenant's beneficial use of the premises (removing a partition that forced patrons through a disreputable bar-room below), even absent a technical eviction, entitling the tenant to abandon the premises and defeat the rent claim.
new.notes: Commercial lease/constructive-eviction dispute over a store and offices; not a dwelling or lodging-house case.

new.holding_summary: Court upheld a gift mortis causa where the decedent, on the day of her death, delivered to her sister a receipt evidencing money held on deposit and declared she was giving her that money; delivery of the receipt sufficed since the sister already possessed the funds. The court also held a general objection to deposition testimony on 'mental capacity' too unspecific to preserve error.
new.notes: Gift mortis causa and testamentary-capacity case; the decedent's prior boarding-house keeping is background biography establishing the source of the money, not adjudicated lodging law.

new.court: Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Second Department
new.notes: Municipal police-power case about banning soft-coal burning in factories; no connection to lodging, boarding, or letting of dwellings.

new.court: Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Fourth Department
new.notes: Fraudulent-conveyance action against a wife who used boarding-house income to buy a home to shield it from her husband's creditors; boarding is background fact only, court never addresses the legal character or regulation of the boarding arrangement itself.

Use-and-occupation claim for a store, apartments, and a shed under an oral commercial lease; ordinary landlord-tenant law, not lodging/boarding regulation.

new.notes: Railroad fare-transfer penalty statute construed against a lessee operating a leased rail line; no connection to dwelling letting.

new.court: Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Fourth Department
new.notes: False-imprisonment action arising from arrest for unlicensed hawking/peddling at a resort village; no connection to lodging or dwelling letting.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
new.holding_summary: Where a householder contracted to board and lodge a family for a year and the boarder abandoned the arrangement without cause, the boarding-keeper could sue immediately for breach rather than waiting out the term, recovering damages only to the date she gave up the house, measured as the profit she would have made had defendant performed, less profits earned by reletting the vacated rooms to other lodgers.

new.notes: Dispute over a railroad's exclusive coach/hackman concession at its depot under common-carrier statutes; unrelated to lodging or letting of dwellings.

new.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
new.holding_summary: The court held that statutory summary proceedings for non-payment of rent apply to a lessee of a fully furnished house let at a gross rent, because the furniture is a mere incident to the letting and the rent, in law, issues out of the land only; the injunction restraining the landlord's summary proceedings was therefore reversed.

quotes.text: The provisions of the Revised Statutes authorizing the dispossession of a tenant by summary proceedings, for non-payment of rent, are applicable to a lessee of a furnished house at a gross rent; the furniture in such a case is but an incident, and the rent issues out of the land only.

Ejectment/tenant-estoppel case arising from a sheriff's-sale purchaser's proceedings against a farm tenant; no letting of rooms or a dwelling for pay, and no regulation issue.

new.notes: Guardian's coal-mine lease accounting dispute; mentions miners' company dwelling-houses only as a trade custom for allocating rent within coal leases, not the legal character or regulation of letting dwellings for pay.

new.holding_summary: The court held that a parol agreement by which Shamburg would occupy several rooms in the leased farmhouse and be boarded there by the lessee's wife was a valid collateral contract, not barred as evidence varying the written farm lease. quotes.text: Notice to a boarder and occupant of a room to quit, followed by no other action than a continuance of boarding and occupancy as before the notice, makes no change in the contract as regards compensation.
Had Beaver ceased to board Shamburg and his family, the case would be different. Telling him to go, and afterwards inducing him to stay, leaves the case as if Beaver had said nothing.

Child-adoption jurisdiction case turning on meaning of 'resident'/'temporary resident' in the adoption statute; no connection to letting rooms or lodging.

Fire-insurance vacancy-clause dispute over occupancy between successive dwelling-house tenants; concerns insurance-law 'occupancy,' not lodging/boarding letting or its regulation.

The court applied the same reasoning to the products of the farm she operated. The Supreme Court affirmed judgment for the wife on the sheriff's interpleader.

new.cite: Crosland v. Mutual Saving Fund, 121 Pa. 65
new.holding_summary: In a mortgage-priority dispute, the court held that a jury instruction was misleading where it treated facts common to any jointly-built double house (shared roof, tenant occupancy of one part, absence of front porches, occasional payment of rent to the co-owner) as sufficient by themselves to relieve a mortgagee of the duty to inquire into the separate owner's title. The proper test was whether the building was suitable for and fairly capable of separate occupancy, and whether that was apparent to an observer from its access and appearance.

quotes.text: The possession of the tenant is the possession of his landlord.
The fact that both parts of a double house are built together affords no presumption against the occupant of either part. They could not be conveniently or economically built in any other manner.

The question for the jury, so far as this subject was concerned, was whether the building was suitable for or fairly capable of separate occupancy, and whether the modes of access to its parts and its external appearance were such, as to make this apparent to an observer. If so, inquiry was a duty.

new.notes: Mrs. Crosland, owner, let one unit of a jointly-built double house to tenants for rent; court treats subdivision and letting of part of a dwelling as an unremarkable, economical incident of ownership, though the litigated holding concerns mortgage notice doctrine rather than the letting practice itself; duration of tenancy not stated in the facts.

Sunday-closing-law injunction against a passenger railway running cars on the Sabbath; the retrieved 'lodging-houses' passage is a verbatim quote of the 1786 Act's proviso exempting lodging-houses from Sunday-labor prohibition, cited only in passing and not adjudicated.
Procedural sufficiency of notice-to-quit and service of summons under the 1863 Landlord and Tenant Act; no facts on nature or duration of the letting.
Testamentary trust construction (dry trust, incidents of fee ownership including alienability); unrelated to letting or lodging of dwellings.
Church corporation's power to sell/alienate its real estate under an 1853 statute; not a case about letting rooms/dwellings for occupancy.

Fire-insurance dispute over a vacant 'watering-place' resort building; that a Mrs. Cooper had 'kept a few boarders' in prior summers is recited only as background on occupancy/vacancy for insurance purposes -- the court never rules on the legal character of the boarding arrangement itself, holding instead on occupancy warranties and negligence defenses in fire policies.
Jurisdictional dispute under the 1863 Landlord and Tenant Act over a tenant's attornment to a sheriff's-sale purchaser; procedural, property type and occupancy facts not given.
Municipal police-power license fee on passenger-railway cars; regulates common carriers, not lodging or boarding houses.
Follow-on decision affirming the same passenger-railway license-fee police-power regulation as Frankford & Philadelphia Passenger Railway; unrelated to lodging/boarding.

Constitutional challenge to Philadelphia's election Registry Act; the statute's classification of voters by 'hotels, taverns and restaurants ... sailors' boarding-houses or restaurants' is a voter-residency assessment mechanism, not adjudication of a letting/lodging arrangement's legal character.

Common-law innkeeper liability for a guest's money embezzled by the barkeeper; concerns an innkeeper's duty of care and bailment, not the legal character of letting rooms/dwellings for pay or regulation of lodging/boarding houses under the police power.

Upholds a borough's police-power license tax on bars, saloons, oyster saloons, restaurants, billiard/bowling establishments -- doctrinally adjacent (police-power licensing of a class of businesses) but the taxed class does not include lodging or boarding houses, so it does not bear on the corpus's letting/boarding question.
Farm tenancy dispute over a justice's jurisdiction, tenant's ability to dispute landlord's title, and jury discharge procedure; no lodging/boarding facts.

Divorce/desertion case; husband's scheme to move himself and wife into Mrs. Neilson's boarding house is factual backdrop to a fraud/desertion analysis, not an adjudication of the legal character or regulation of boarding/lodging.
Sheriff's interpleader over ownership of rafted lumber and admissibility of a grantor's declarations; passing mention that a witness boarded near the rafts is immaterial to the holding.
Ordinary landlord-tenant case on the doctrine of attornment following sale of the reversion; no lodging/boarding facts or regulatory issue.
Testamentary trust case on whether an active trust executed on the beneficiary's discoverture; trustees' authority to let vacant lots on ground-rent is incidental and unrelated to short-term lodging.
Limited-partnership/sheriff's-interpleader dispute over ownership of liquor-store stock; no occupancy or lodging issue.
Constitutional-law case invalidating a statute compelling extinguishment of irredeemable ground-rents; unrelated to lodging or boarding.

Assumpsit action between tenants in common over rent for farm use and occupation; no lodging/boarding facts.
Fiduciary-accounting dispute over an assignee's responsibility for funds lost in a bank failure; unrelated to lodging.

Fraudulent-conveyance case on whether a sale of hotel furniture/stock had the actual, continued change of possession required against creditors; hotel boarders/transient guests appear only as facts bearing on possession, not on the legal character of guest occupancy.

Municipal-taxation case construing a Wilkesbarre licensing ordinance; holds the enabling act's police-power license tax on 'bowling-alleys and billiard-tables... and other places of business or amusement' does NOT extend to hotel-keepers, merchants, or bankers. Hotel-keepers appear only in the ordinance's (invalidated) list, not in an adjudicated holding about lodging/boarding regulation.
Contract-for-sale dispute over a malt-house and the leasehold ground beneath it; commercial/industrial lease, no lodging or boarding facts.
Procedural landlord-tenant case on justice's jurisdiction under the 1830 Act; record fails to show the demised term. No lodging/boarding facts.

Family conveyance/inheritance covenant dispute; the underlying agreement lets the father retain 'the privilege to rent away the house, garden and stable' on the conveyed farm, but this letting term is never litigated or characterized by the court -- the holding concerns advancement/distribution doctrine in the Orphans' Court.

Landlord-tenant procedural case (Act of 1772) concerning a commercial office building and whether an assignee of part of the reversion may proceed against the whole tenant; no residential lodging facts.
Municipal police-power/eminent-domain case on liability for repairing Delaware River meadow banks; unrelated to lodging or boarding.

Landlord-tenant forfeiture/jurisdiction dispute over a farm lease under which the tenant built up a hotel business; the hotel operation is background to damages/jurisdiction questions, not an adjudication of lodging's legal character or regulation.
Dispute over agency in a lease of a house used as a young ladies' boarding school, wrongful eviction and distress for rent; concerns agency and eviction procedure, not lodging/boarding arrangements.
Construes an innkeeper's statutory bond as security for dram-shop/liquor-liability damages, not licensing of lodging or boarding houses; no bearing on the character of letting rooms.
